6.3 Subchronic studies
Reyes et al. (2023) conducted a 90-day dietary study in CRL Sprague-Dawley CD® IGS
rats (80 rats; four groups; 20/group; ten/sex) to evaluate the safety of LegH Prep. The groups were
assigned as basal diet control (Group 1), low dose (Group 2), intermediate dose (Group 3), and
high dose (Group 4) (Table 9). An additional ten male and ten female test animals were randomly
assigned to each of Group 1 and Group 4 (five/sex) as recovery animals for a 28-day recovery
period. Animals were selected for the study based on adequate body weight gain, lack of injury or
clinical signs of disease, and a body weight that was within ± 20% of the mean within a sex.
Animals that were selected for the study were randomly distributed according to stratification by
body weight so that there was no statistically significant difference among group body weight
means within a sex. The study was conducted under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP): 21 CFR §
5818 and in accordance with OECD 40819 guidelines. Body weights, food consumption, clinical
observations, estrus determination, ophthalmological observations, hematological and clinical
chemistry parameters, coagulation, thyroid hormones, urinalysis, histopathology, organ weights,
and individual necropsy records were recorded. Individual body weights were measured weekly
and body weight gain was calculated for selected intervals and the overall study. Individual food
consumption was measured at the same time as body weight measurements as well as food
efficiency and dietary intake of LegH Prep. At terminal sacrifice, vaginal smears were collected
from all female rats on the day of terminal sacrifice to determine the stage of estrus.
Ophthalmological examinations included focal illumination, slit lamp biomicroscopy, and indirect
ophthalmoscopy prior to study initiation and on Day 87 of the study (for all surviving animals).

All animals within the study (including decedents) were subjected to a gross necropsy,
which includes examination of the external surface of the body, all orifices, musculoskeletal
system, and the cranial, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic cavities, with their associated organs and
tissues and all gross lesions were recorded. The following organs were evaluated by histological
examination in all animals of all groups: accessory genital organs (prostate and seminal vesicles),
ileum with Peyer's patches, rectum, jejunum, salivary glands (sublingual, adrenals, kidneys,
submandibular, and parotid), larynx, skeletal muscle, aorta, liver, skin, bone (femur), lungs, spinal
cord (three levels: cervical, mid-thoracic, and lumbar), bone marrow (from femur and sternum),
lymph node mandibular, lymph node mesenteric, spleen, brain (sections including medulla/pons,
cerebellar, and cerebral cortex), mammary gland, sternum, nasal turbinates, stomach, nose,
thymus, cecum, ovaries, thyroid, cervix, oviducts, trachea, colon, pancreas (with islets), urinary
bladder, duodenum, parathyroid, uterus, esophagus, peripheral nerve (sciatic), vagina, Harderian
gland, pharynx, heart, pituitary gland, eyes, optic nerve, testes, and epididymides. The following
organs were weighed after dissection: adrenals (combined), kidneys, testes (combined), brain,
liver, thymus, epididymis (combined), ovaries with oviducts (combined), uterus, heart, spleen,
prostate, and seminal vesicles with coagulating gland (combined), thyroid, parathyroid, and
pituitary gland (Reyes et al., 2023).
There were no mortalities nor clinical observations attributable to LegH Prep
administration observed in this study. All observations noted were considered incidental and of no
toxicological significance, as there were no trends in observations that increased with dietary level.
There were no changes in body weight, body weight gain, or food consumption in male and female
rats attributed to the dietary administration of LegH Prep. Mean weekly body weights and mean
daily body weight gains for male and female rats in Groups 2 - 4 were comparable to control Group
1 throughout the main test and the recovery period. Dietary administration of LegH Prep, for a

period of at least 90 days in male and female rats, at target dietary levels of 30,000, 60,000, and
90,000 ppm, did not induce any changes in hematology coagulation, clinical chemistry, thyroid
hormones, and urinalysis parameters. At the end of the study there were significant increases (p <
0.01) in MCV and MCH in the male Group 4 as compared to Group 1 (Table 10).
There were no statistically significant changes in any of the clinical chemistry parameters
for any of the groups receiving LegH Prep as compared to the control (Table 11). Analysis of the

changes were not attributable to LegH Prep administration and deemed clinically insignificant. In
the recovery phase, there was a significant (p < 0.05) increase in the epididymis-to-body weight
and decrease in the pituitary-to-bodyweight as compared to the control in males (Table 17). In

as compared to the control (Table 17); however, these changes were deemed incidental and not
toxicologically significant. Under the conditions of the study and based on the observation of the
clinical endpoint evaluated, the authors concluded, “the no-observed-adverse-effect level

90,000 ppm for male and female Sprague-Dawley rats, a level calculated to provide dose levels of
4798.3 and 5761.5 mg/kg/day, the highest level tested in male and female rats, respectively, in this

6.4 Other studies
6.4.1 Potential toxigenicity/pathogenicity
Banerjee and Verma (2000) evaluated the ability of P. pastoris to produce secreted toxins
and inhibit the growth of different yeast cells. The P. pastoris strain was obtained from the
Research Culture Collection of Northern Research Laboratory (NRRL, Peoria, IL; strain NRRL
No. Y 4290). Two cultures of P. pastoris strain (NRRL No. Y 4290) were grown (1 × 106 cell/ml)
and cultured for 2, 3 and 14 days, after which the cell suspensions were centrifuged, and the
supernatant filtered and concentrated (50X). The concentrated supernatant was then spotted on the
surface of dextrose agar in a 24-well microliter dish and then overlaid with top agar containing
viable indicator strains of pathogens and yeasts. As controls, toxins from Kluveromyces lactis and
Pichia acacia were plated with the indicator strain Dabaryomyces tamarii. The authors reported
that the K. lactis toxin produced a clear zone of growth inhibition, confirming the ability to show
toxin effectiveness in this study. The P. pastoris concentrated supernatant did not show any
toxigenic activity against any of the indicator strains, showing that the (NRRL No. Y 4290) strain
of P. pastoris did not produce toxins against sensitive indicator strains (Banerjee and Verma,
2000).
França et al. (2015) evaluated the pathogenicity/toxigenicity of P. pastoris X-3320, by the

administration of viable P. pastoris to male BALB/c mice. To this end, two separate experiments
were conducted: in the first study, mice (15/group) were administered a single dose of either P.
pastoris X-33 [7 log CFU (1 × 107 CFU/day) in 1 ml 0.9% saline] or 1 mL 0.9% saline suspension
(served as a control) daily by oral gavage for 20 days. Whereas, in the second experiment, male
BALB/c mice (10/group) were either fed an antibiotic-free diet ad libitum containing P. pastoris
X-33 (1 × 107 CFU/g), the antibiotic-free diet alone, or the diet containing Saccharomyces
boulardii (1 × 107 CFU/g) for 20 days. In both experiments, animals were monitored for behavioral
effects daily, and subsequently on the 20th day after the start of gavage administration; feces were
collected 24, 48, and 72 hours post yeast administration. Mice from both experiments (5/group)
were euthanized, tissues and organs were collected (specific tissues/organs not stated) and
histopathological analysis was conducted; whereas the remaining ten mice, from both experiments,
were challenged by oral gavage with one dose of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (strain
29630) at 5 log CFU/mouse, which is the LD dose. The survival rates were then calculated ten
50
days later. Fresh feces from the surviving animals were collected on the 13th day after challenge
and mice were subsequently euthanized. For histopathological analysis, the intestine, liver, and
spleen were removed, specifically to evaluate intestinal colonization of S. enterica Typhimurium
and possible translocation to the liver and spleen.
The authors reported that mice administered exclusively P. pastoris X-33 did not exhibit
any reported behavioral changes nor signs of injury as evidenced by histopathological analysis.
Moreover, there were no changes in the intestinal microvilli and lamina propria reported as
compared to the saline control group. The group of mice that received P. pastoris X-33 in the diet
and were subsequently challenged with an LD dose of S. typhimurium had a significantly

Becerril-García et al. (2022) evaluated the potential pathogenicity of P. pastoris in BALB/c
mice by intravenous administration of live cells. P. pastoris GS115 and Candida albicans (ATCC

66027) yeast cultures were maintained in Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30 and 37°C, respectively.
C. albicans is a well-defined pathogen and was used as a positive control for pathogenicity in this
study. Female BALB/c mice (5 - 7 weeks old; four groups; 20/group) were anesthetized with
ketamine and xylazine (80 and 120 mg/g bw, respectively) inoculated intravenously (IV) with
either P. pastoris or C. albicans, or PSS solution (200 µl) via the lateral tail vein. The fourth group
was maintained as a housing control and did not receive any injection. Yeast cells were washed
with physiological saline solution (PSS) (0.89%) and counted with a hemacytometer to be adjusted
at 5.0 × 106 viable yeast cells/ml in the PSS injection. Animals were then monitored daily for
adverse effects, behavior, and bodyweight changes. Subsequently, five mice of each group were
euthanized at 4, 24, and 48 hours post injection (hpi) and six days post infection (dpi). The sera
and tissue of the kidney, liver, brain, spleen, heart, and lung were collected. Only one mouse was
euthanized at six dpi due to illness, according to humane end points stated by the local Institutional
Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), whereas all the other survived until study termination.
Fungal burden was measured in homogenized organs (log CFU/g tissue) after 48 hours of
10
incubation at 30°C for P. pastoris and 37°C for C. albicans. Histological analysis included the
identification of polymorphonuclear (PMN) and mononuclear (MN) inflammatory infiltrate
sections stained with H-E according to their staining characteristics, cell size, and cell nucleus
morphology (PMN cells: the nucleus contains multiple lobes, MN cells: a round nuclei). Periodic
acid-Schiff base (PAS)-stained sections were used to visualize the presence of fungi in tissues.
The pathogenicity of P. pastoris was also evaluated utilizing an in vivo delayed-type
hypersensitivity test (DTH), with C. albicans being utilized as a positive control. This involved a
sensitization phase, which was done by the epicutaneous administration of P. pastoris or C.
albicans (2 × 108 CFU) in 50 µl of PSS on exfoliated stratum corneum. The PSS control mice
underwent the same procedure, except with just PSS alone, whereas the other control did not
undergo exfoliation of the stratum corneum, which were used to assess the baseline status. Animals
were monitored for seven days for adverse effects and behavioral changes. The efferent phase was
then conducted by the inoculation of 10 µl with either heat-killed yeast species (1 × 107 CFU) and
the subsequent swelling that was induced after 24 hours was calculated based off the baseline

6.5 Genotoxicity
For the LegH Prep that is the subject of this GRAS notification, a bacterial reverse mutation
assay was conducted (Reyes et al., 2023) to evaluate the potential for genotoxicity of LegH Prep.
The assay was conducted under GLP, and the protocol was based on OECD Guideline 47122 and
ICH Guidelines S2A23 (ICH, 1996) and S2B24 (ICH, 1997). The LegH Prep was evaluated for
mutagenicity in five bacterial strains using Salmonella typhimurium (TA98, TA100, TA1535, and
TA1537) and Escherichia coli (WP2 uvrA) according to the plate incorporation (Experiment I)
and preincubation (Experiment II) methods, in the presence and absence of a metabolic activation
system (S9). The concentrations of LegH Prep with and without S9 activation were 0, 31.6, 100,
316, 1000, 2500 and 5000 µg/plate. Cell toxicity was ascertained by a clearing or a depletion of
the background lawn or a reduction in the number of revertants down to a mutation factor of
approximately ≤ 0.5 as compared to the negative (solvent) control. The mutation factor was
calculated for each experiment by dividing the mean value of the revertant counts by the mean
values of the negative control. LegH Prep would be considered mutagenic if a biologically
significant positive response for at least one of the dose groups was observed in at least one tester
strain with or without metabolic activation or if there is a clear and dose-related increase in the
number of revertants. The authors reported no biologically relevant increases in revertant colony
formation in any of the tester strains, neither in the absence or presence of metabolic activation,
utilizing any concentration of LegH Prep. In experiment I (Table 18), LegH Prep treated plates
exhibited toxic effects in tester strain TA1535 at a concentration of 5000 µg/plate (without
metabolic activation). The positive controls for this experiment were 4-nitro-o-phenylenediamine
(4-NOPD), 2-aminoanthracene (2-AA), sodium azide (NaN ), and methyl methanesulfonate
3
(MMS). In experiment II (Table 19), toxic effects of LegH Prep were noted in tester strain TA1537
at concentrations of ≥2500 µg/plate in the absence of metabolic activation. The mutation factors
for experiment I (Table 20) and experiment II (Table 21) did not indicate signs of toxicity and
were within historical ranges. The authors reported that no other toxic effects of LegH Prep were

observed in experiment I or II. Therefore, the authors concluded, “LegH Prep is non-mutagenic in
this bacterial reverse mutation assay” (Reyes et al., 2023). Therefore, under the conditions of the
study, LegH Prep was non-mutagenic in this bacterial reverse mutation assay.

carbohydrate, ash, and moisture content to the original LegH prep in GRN No. 737 (see Table 3).

To ascertain whether any of the proteins within LegH Prep contained digestion-resistant
polypeptides, an in vitro digestion assay was conducted using simulated gastric fluid (SGF). The
in vitro pepsin digestion protocol used is comparable in procedure as to the one used in a multi-
laboratory study demonstrating the power, versatility, and reproducibility of this procedure in a
total of nine laboratories (Thomas et al., 2004). This assay is utilized as there is a strong predictive
value of the digestibility of a protein when comparing the stability of allergenic and non-allergenic
dietary proteins (Bannon et al., 2003). To simulate gastric fluid, assays were conducted at pH 2.0
with pepsin-protein ratios of 10:1 (U/µg) or 1:1 (U/µg), and the proteins in LegH Prep were
compared to three control proteins [hemoglobin (Hb), bovine serum albumin (BSA), and
ovalbumin (OVA)]. Hb and BSA were digested within 30 seconds, whereas OVA possessed more
stability, with 10% visually stainable full-length protein band remaining after 30 minutes of
digestion using 10 U of pepsin. The original LegH protein was rapidly digested by pepsin, to below
10% of the band intensity detected in a control digestion, in two minutes. In addition, the 17 P.
pastoris proteins found in the original LegH Prep product were digested and no longer visible at
0.5 minutes under the conditions of the in vitro digestion assay. The authors concluded that:
[T]he results demonstrated that the LegHb [LegH] protein and the associated Pichia
pastoris proteins were more than 90% digested within 2 min in SGF plus pepsin at 37oC,
at ratios of either 10 units or 1 unit of pepsin activity per 1 µg of total protein, based on
Coomassie Blue staining detection (Jin et al., 2018).
In summary, based on the work to assess the potential allergenicity of the original LegH
Prep product, the authors concluded “…our analysis found no evidence to suggest that food
products containing the LegH protein and associated minor components from Pichia pastoris pose
any significant risk of allergy or toxicity to consumers” (Jin et al., 2018).
In addition, Reyes et al. (2021) conducted an in vitro digestion assay to determine if any of the
protein of interest might include digestion-resistant polypeptides (Thomas et al., 2004). The acidic
(pH = 2) gastric fluid environment was simulated using pepsin-protein ratios of 10:1 (U/µg) or 1:1

(U/µg), and compared the proteins found in the LegH Prep to pepsin only or LegH Prep alone. The
results show the protein was digested to non-detectable levels within two minutes (Figure 2). The

6.7 Summary and conclusions
Based on the literature and database evaluations, bioinformatics and comparisons to known
allergens and toxins, and the in vitro digestibility assays, there is minimal likelihood of allergic
reactions when consuming LegH Prep in the intended food categories of use.

The GRAS notices for LegH Prep and the production organism, Pichia pastoris, are listed
in Table 30. LegH Prep has been the subject of two GRAS conclusions, one for LegH derived from

6.9 Safety evaluation summary
LegH Prep is an ingredient derived from the methanotrophic yeast, Pichia pastoris
(Komagataella pastoris), which is to be used as a flavor and nutrient component (providing iron)
in plant-derived meat analogue products up to 2.0%. The LegH protein contained within LegH
Prep exhibits at least 65% purity and comprises up to 15% of the LegH Prep. The LegH Prep
described in this GRAS notification has not changed in terms of how it is manufactured and has
comparable composition, specifications, and stability as the LegH Prep described in GRN No. 737.
The only thing that has changed with this LegH Prep, with respect to LegH Prep described in GRN
No. 737, is the number and types of meat analogue products into which LegH Prep is to be added
and the maximum amount that is to be added to these products (≤2.0% as opposed to ≤0.8% in
GRN No. 737). LegH Prep passed all microbial and heavy metal specifications, and all of the
compositional specifications set by IFI, which are the same as those provided for LegH Prep in
GRN No. 737. LegH Prep exhibited an average LegH protein content of 11.68%, a LegH protein
purity of 85.2%, a salt concentration of 75 mM, a total protein content of 12.96%, a fat content of
0.10%, a carbohydrates content of 2.41%, an ash content of 1.25%, consisting of 16.92% solids,
and a moisture content of 83.10%. These compositional parameters were comparable to those in
the LegH Prep that was the subject of GRN No. 737. Stability studies also indicated the neat
substance is stable for up to 91 days at -20°C, and comparable to the LegH Prep in GRN No. 737.
The potential allergenicity and toxicity of Pichia pastoris proteins in IFI’s LegH Prep 2.0 was also
included in this dossier to support the lack of toxicity and allergenicity of LegH Prep. Although
LegH Prep 2.0 is a less purified version of the original LegH Prep and therefore contains more P.
pastoris components, it is comparable in composition, macronutrient LegH protein (≥ 65%) and
overall protein content and utilizes the same production organism as described in GRN No. 737
(and as described for the LegH Prep that is the subject of this GRAS notification). Therefore,
studies for LegH Prep 2.0 were also utilized to establish the lack of allergenicity and toxigenicity
of this LegH Prep.
The calculated EDI for LegH Prep at the 90th percentile of consumption is 40.43 mg/kg
bw/day, which is based on the amount of dried LegH Prep (from dried solids) that would be
required to be added to the selected food categories, described in Table 5, to get the desired LegH
protein concentration in the meat analogues present in these foods. The LegH protein represents
approximately 11.7% of the total hydrated version of LegH Prep; however, the NOAEL derived
from the 90-day study utilized the dried LegH Prep (see Section 5.2), with dried solids representing

approximately 17% of the LegH Prep. Therefore, to achieve the desired amounts of LegH protein
within the selected foods provided in Table 5, and to calculate an accurate estimation of the EDI
for the LegH Prep, the percentage of LegH protein within the dried solids (which is approximately
17% of the LegH Prep) was utilized, which provided the 90th percentile EDI of 40.43 mg/kg
bw/day (Table 7).
The NOAEL for LegH Prep in rats is 4798.3 mg/kg bw/day in male rats and 5761.5 mg/kg
bw/day in female rats (equivalent to 287,892 and 357,213 mg/day, respectively, in a 60 kg human).
Normally, it is desirable to have a 100-fold safety factor between the Acceptable Daily Intake
(ADI) of the substance and the experimentally achieved NOAEL from a 90-day safety study.
However, LegH Prep and LegH protein have a documented history of use, and LegH Prep has

P. pastoris is a non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic organism used as a protein expression system
for use in human food), potable water treatment, animal feed, and FDA approved therapeutics.

LegH Prep, like the original LegH Prep (GRN No. 737), did not exhibit any adverse effects,
clinical signs of toxicity, or palatability issues. When IFI conducted a 14-day palatability study,
LegH Prep was palatable, well tolerated, and did not induce any clinically significant effects up to
12,500 mg/kg day. The 90-day toxicity study also corroborated the lack of toxicity for the LegH
Prep. All observations noted were considered incidental and of no toxicological significance, as

there were no trends in observations that increased with dietary level. There were no changes in
body weight or body weight gain or food consumption in male and female rats attributed to the
dietary administration of LegH Prep. There were significant increases noted in some
hematological, urinary, and thyroid hormone parameters; however, all statistically significant
changes were within historical control ranges, and without histopathological correlate, were not
considered adverse. Histopathological analysis revealed that there were no LegH Prep attributable
macroscopic observations, organ weight changes, or microscopic findings. There were significant
changes in the absolute and relative thymus weight, epididymides-to-body weight, and significant
increases in kidney-to-brain weights; however, these changes did not exhibit a dose-dependent
relationship and were not associated with any clinically adverse effects, and therefore deemed
incidental.
Utilizing studies not conducted by IFI and provided by publicly available literature, the
pathogenicity of P. pastoris was assessed in mice by oral gavage and IV administration, which
resulted in no adverse effects, behavioral changes, or indications of deleterious effects as
evidenced by histopathological analysis. Studies also indicated that P. pastoris does not induce
any adverse effects in the GI tract or other organs, when consumed as viable, probiotic cultures.
P. pastoris was also well tolerated and did not induce any adverse effects in broiler chicken chicks
up to 49 days. Genotoxicity of LegH Prep was assessed using the bacterial reverse mutation assay

Good afternoon, Ellen.
Please find below our responses to FDA’s additional follow-up questions for GRN 001202:
1. The batch analyses data provided was on the hydrated LegH preparation. The dried
preparation was used in the EDI calculations in the GRAS notice to determine how much
LegH Prep would need to be added to achieve the desired concentrations of LegH
Protein in the selected food categories at the selected amounts in each food category
(please refer to pgs. 20-22 of GRN 001202 “Part 3: Dietary Exposure 3.1 Estimated Daily
Intake). The NOAEL derived from the 90-day study utilized the dried LegH Prep.
Therefore, to achieve the desired amounts of LegH protein within the selected foods
provided in Table 5 of GRN 001202, and to get an accurate estimation of the EDI for the
LegH Prep, the percentage of LegH protein within the dried solids (which is
approximately 17% of the LegH Prep) was used and considered.
Regarding the discrepancy with the dietary exposure of iron from the 90th percentile
level of consumption of LegH protein, this was discussed internally, and we utilized the
calculations provided to FDA from the notifier’s CAP submission for determining the
amount of iron derived from LegH protein. LegH protein has a MW of about 16kD, with
each LegH molecule containing one heme molecule, which contains one iron
molecule.
Therefore, the amount of iron in LegH is calculated as:
Fe/LegH = 55.845g/mol/16,000 g/mol = 0.349% = 0.349 g/100g =0.00349g/g = 3.49
mg/g. This corresponds to 1 g of LegH protein containing approximately 3.5 mg iron.
Therefore, based on 1.788 g of LegH protein/day at the 90th percentile level of
consumption (as stated in GRN 001202), the 90th percentile level of iron consumption
from LegH protein contained within LegH Prep would be 6.258 mg/person/day.

2 IDENTITY, METHOD OF MANUFACTURE, SPECIFICATIONS, AND PHYSICAL OR

This section reviews and cites publicly available information, as well as data provided by ACC and
Changing Bio, pertaining to the composition, manufacturing process, and specifications of Kluvy®
Protein that is the subject of this GRAS determination. This information characterizes the notified
substance intended for use as an ingredient in food products.

2.1 Identity
The subject of this GRAS determination is Kluvy® Protein, a yeast protein derived from the CJ3113
strain of Kluyveromyces marxianus (referred to as “K. marxianus”). The strain was isolated from a
special type of Mongolian cheese, locally called “milk tofu” and is used to produce yeast protein via
aerobic fermentation in a defined medium. Following fermentation, the entire biomass of the CJ3113
strain is collected, autoclaved, and dried into powder, which results in a product containing ≥55% w/w
yeast protein, as well as natural fermentative by-products and yeast cell debris. Such a product is named
Kluvy® Protein and it is intended for use as a substitute for animal-source protein in conventional
foods. Kluvy® Protein is predominantly composed of protein (>55%), along with dietary fiber (~30%),
moisture (<7%), and fat (~5%).
2.2 Manufacturing Process
2.2.1 Strain Used as Production Strain
K. marxianus, a nonpathogenic and nontoxigenic yeast, is well known due to its frequent connection
with traditional dairy products like fermented milk, kefir, yogurt, cheese, and so on (Coloretti et al.,
2017). It is a dairy yeast that has also been previously described by synonyms in scientific literature,
notably Kluyveromyces fragilis and Saccharomyces keyfr (Karim et al., 2020, Morrissey et al., 2014).
In general, K. marxianus is considered a safe yeast used in the food and biotechnology sectors (Varela
et al., 2017, Wu et al., 2024). Because of its history of association with food, K. marxianus, like
Kluyveromuces lactis (referred to as “K. lactis”), has been designated European Food Safety Authority
(EFSA) Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) status (EFSA BIOHAZ, 2024, Varela et al., 2017, Wu
et al., 2024). In general, yeast, including K. marxianus, are not known to produce toxic metabolites
(Alasmar et al., 2020).
The subject of this GRAS Determination is manufactured from a non-genetically modified K.
marxianus CJ3113 strain. This strain was isolated from self-made edible “milk tofu” collected from
herdsmen in Mongolia, China, by culturing it in Kluyveromyces Differential Medium (KDM),
containing yeast extract, peptone, malt extract, dextrose, agar, 5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-b-D-
galactopyranoside, isopropyl-beta-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG), and chloramphenicol. This medium is a
screening and identification medium that can be used to selectively screen wild-type yeast (K.
marxianus and K. lactis) with β-galactosidase activity. Single, blue-colored colonies growing on the
medium are selected as candidate strains. The ideal strain was selected based on rapid growth rate,

6.1 History of Use of K. marxianus
K. marxianus was first isolated from grapes (Barone et al., 2021). K. marxianus is closely related to

the better-known K. lactis (Lachance, 1998; Llorente et al., 2000). They are morphologically identical
with the exception of their spore shape and other characteristics, most notably the ability to ferment
lactose. Their DNA homology, however, is only 15–20%, and as a consequence, they are distinct
species (Batt, 2014). Both strains belong to the family Saccharomycetaceae and can assimilate lactose,
a trait absent in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, making these non-conventional yeasts valuable in the food
industry. Additionally, due to its ability to assimilate lactose as a carbon source, K. marxianus is
commonly found in lactose-rich edible dairy products such as fermented milk, yogurt, and cheeses,
and is often referred to as dairy yeast. Recent attempts to characterize the microbial content of
fermented milk, that is kefir, find that the major yeast species present in the product is K. marxianus,
accounting for up to 90% of the yeast population (Kim et al., 2019, Youn et al., 2022). According to
the Codex Alimentarius (Codex Stan 243-2003), a typical kefir (fermented milk obtained from kefir
grains) should contain not less than 104 CFU/mL of the total amount of yeast (including K. marxianus).
Another study has reported that the population of yeast (including K. marxianus) and acetic acid
bacteria in kefir are around 105 to 106 CFU/g (Cho et al., 2018).
Moreover, K. marxianus is considered an emerging non-conventional food-grade yeast, possessing a
unique set of beneficial traits, such as rapid growth, thermotolerance, and a broad substrate spectrum
which makes this yeast a particularly attractive host for applications in a variety of food and
biotechnology industries (Bilal et al., 2022). The long history of safe association with food products
helped this yeast achieve regulatory acceptance for food ingredient production in the US and European
Union (EU), respectively (Fonseca et al., 2008, Lane & Morrissey, 2010).
In 1995, Caballero et al. (1995) assessed two strains of K. marxianus (NRRL-Y-2415 and NRRL-Y-
1109) as baker's yeasts, finding them to have superior proofing activity compared to commercial strains,
which led to their successful use in bread making. Subsequently, K. marxianus was integrated into the
baker's yeast industry, and various studies explored its applications in food baking. In another study,
mixed starter cultures of K. marxianus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus or Lactobacillus helveticus were
found to improve the quality, shelf life, and consumer preference of sourdough bread (Plessas et al.,
2008). Struyf et al. (2017) found fermentation of dough with an inulinase-secreting K. marxianus strain
allowed the reduction of fructan levels in the final product by more than 90%, while only 56%
reduction was achieved when a control Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain was used. The use of K.

6.2 Regulatory History of K. marxianus
As mentioned, the use of K. marxianus to produce food ingredients has been reviewed by the regulatory
bodies in the US and EU (Fonseca et al., 2008, Lane & Morrissey, 2010). K. marxianus was used to
produce a lactase enzyme preparation as described in GRN 000088. The use of this species as the
production organism was reviewed by the FDA and GRN 000088 had received “no questions” letter
from the FDA on April 3, 2002. Other than in the US, the safety of K. marxianus has also been reviewed
by EFSA, an EU regulatory body. K. marxianus is included in the current QPS list, version v20 (EFSA
BIOHAZ, 2024). The QPS assessment process was first outlined by the Scientific Committee in 2007,
establishing the initial list of biological agents. This list is reviewed and updated annually by EFSA's
Panel on Biological Hazards (BIOHAZ). This assessment covers K. marxianus’s use in enzyme
production and novel foods, indicating that the organism’s safety has already been pre-assessed.
Consequently, no additional toxicological data are required to establish its safety in the European
Union.
6.3 Safety of Using K. marxianus
Kluvy® Protein is produced from a non-genetically modified, food-derived strain of K. marxianus
CJ3113. This strain is fermented and inactivated, and the resulting biomass is collected. The final
product (i.e., yeast protein) is designed to serve as a protein substitute for both animal and plant
proteins. As mentioned in Part 6.2, the use of this species to produce food ingredients has already been
reviewed by the US FDA and EFSA and has no concerns on its safe use. Other supporting evidence of
safety is also included in the following section to further demonstrate the safe use of K. marxianus and
in turn, justify the safety of yeast protein derived from it, i.e., Kluvy® Protein.
A literature search was conducted on September 1, 2024, using PubMed and Google Scholar to identify
relevant safety studies. The search terms “Kluyveromyces marxianus” or “K. marxianus” were used to

organisms or those reporting safety parameters such as anthropometric measures, clinical chemistry,
hematology, and adverse events in the abstract were considered relevant and were subsequently
summarized.

6.4.4 Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Elimination Profile
No information on the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME) of Kluvy®
Protein (K. marxianus protein) was identified in the literature search. However, Kluvy® Protein is
majorly composed of >55% protein and approximately 30% dietary fiber. The ADME profile of
Kluvy® Protein could be extrapolated by analyzing the ADME of these two major portions.
The majority of dietary proteins are fully degraded and absorbed in the small intestine: after a meal,
proteins are denatured by acid and hydrolyzed by gastric pepsin in the stomach, further hydrolyzed by
pancreatic proteases, subsequently degraded by small intestinal enterocyte membrane exopeptidases
and absorbed across the small intestinal enterocytes into the bloodstream as individual amino acids for
use in the body (Dallas et al., 2017). It is expected that Kluvy® Protein would undergo similar ADME
pathways as other protein products, providing all sources of amino acids to the body.

On the other hand, fermentation using K. marxianus has been reported to generate angiotensin-
converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitory peptides and antioxidant peptides in certain fermentation
conditions (García-Tejedor et al., 2014, Mirzaei et al., 2018). These peptides are reported to improve
the quality of the end products by enriching the nutritive value and enhancing the flavor characteristics.
Current studies on bioactive peptides in fermented foods primarily focus on general screening and
identification. After this, the identified peptides are synthetically produced for further characterization
of their biological activity. Quantification of bioactive peptides from food sources has not been studied
extensively. Since these bioactive peptides naturally occur in foods, people have already been exposed
to them, and to date, no adverse effects have been reported from their consumption. In the case of
Kluvy® Protein, it is a yeast protein derived from the fermentation of K. marxianus. During the
manufacturing process, K. marxianus is heat inactivated via an autoclaving step (105 – 125°C, 0.1 –
0.15 MPa, for 15 – 30 mins). As a result, the yeast loses all metabolic activity and is unable to produce
any proteins or peptides. Although bioactive peptides may be produced during fermentation, heat
treatment can cause protein denaturation, leading to a loss of their biological activity. Therefore, the
likelihood of bioactive peptides being present in Kluvy® Protein is low.
Most fiber-containing foods include approximately one-third soluble and two-thirds insoluble fiber
(Wong & Jenkins, 2007), including Kluvy® Protein. Therefore, it is expected that Kluvy® Protein
would undergo a similar ADME pathway as most fiber-containing foods. Dietary fiber can be broadly
categorized according to its solubility into two major types of fiber: water-insoluble/less fermented
fibers – cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin; and water-soluble/well-fermented fibers – pectin, gums, and
mucilages. Both soluble and insoluble fibers are not digested in the human gastrointestinal tract.

Soluble fiber absorbs water to become a gelatinous, viscous substance and is fermented by bacteria in
the digestive tract. Insoluble fiber has bulking action, is not fermented, and is excreted in feces without
any absorption. Given the lack of metabolism and absorption, insoluble fiber is unlikely to cause any
adverse effects. On the contrary, soluble fiber can be readily and quickly metabolized by gut bacteria,
which could significantly influence the abundance and diversity of the human gut microbiota (McRorie
& McKeown, 2016).

EXPERT PANEL STATEMENT
An independent panel of experts (GRAS Panel), qualified by scientific training and experience to
assess the safety of food and food ingredients, was convened by the Anchor Center for Certification
(ACC) on behalf of Shanghai Changing Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Changing Bio).The panel conducted
a critical and comprehensive evaluation of the available data and relevant information to determine
whether Kluvy® Protein, when used in selected conventional human foods, is safe and Generally
Recognized As Safe (GRAS) under the conditions of its intended use. This determination was made in

accordance with scientific procedures outlined in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C
Act), as specified in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (21 CFR) §170.30(b).
The GRAS Expert Panel convened by teleconference on October 17, 2024 and unanimously concluded
that Kluvy® Protein, meeting the specifications detailed in “GRAS Determination for the Use of
Kluvy® Protein in Selected Conventional Foods,” when used as an ingredient in conventional foods
as a source of protein, and when manufactured under current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP),
is GRAS based on scientific procedures. A summary of the basis for the GRAS Expert Panel’s
conclusion is provided herein.
Summary and Basis for a GRAS Conclusion
Changing Bio’s Kluvy® Protein is produced by fermentation of non-genetically modified
Kluyveromyces marxianus (K. marxianus). The finished product is composed of protein (>55%), along
with dietary fiber (~30%), moisture (<7%), and fat (~5%). Kluvy® Protein is intended for use as an
ingredient in select conventional foods (i.e., baked goods and baking mixes, beverages, breakfast
cereals, condiments and relishes, dairy product analogs, frozen dairy desserts and mixes, grain products
and pastas, gravies and sauces, milk products, plant protein products, processed fruit and vegetable
juices, snack foods, soft candies, and soups and soup mixes) at use levels ranging from 1% to 20% by
weight.
The GRAS Panel independently, collectively, and critically examined Changing Bio’s GRAS dossier
for Kluvy® Protein as well as publicly available scientific information and data compiled from the
literature and other published sources through October 17, 2024. The data evaluated by the GRAS
Panel included information pertaining to the methods of manufacture and product specifications,
analytical data, intended use levels in conventional foods, consumption estimates, and comprehensive

literature related to the safety of Kluvy® Protein.
Composition
Kluvy® Protein consists primarily of protein (over 55%), along with dietary fiber (around 30%),
moisture (less than 7%), and fat (approximately 5%). Kluvy® Protein is a complete protein, consisting
of all twenty naturally occurring amino acids. This includes nine essential amino acids that the human
body cannot produce and must be supplemented by food. The amino acid composition of Kluvy®
Protein was presented in the dossier and the GRAS Panel concurs that it compares favorably to other
protein replacement products used as meat and dairy analogs.
The GRAS Panel has reviewed the analytical data provided in Changing Bio’s GRAS dossier for
Kluvy® Protein and confirms that it demonstrates the absence of the K. marxianus production
organism.
Production Strain
Kluvy® Protein is manufactured from the fermentation of non-genetically modified K. marxianus
CJ3113. K. marxianus has a long history of safe use in food production (e.g., cheese and kefir) and is
used to produce GRAS food ingredients including the lactase enzyme (per GRN 000088). It is also
recognized by European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) to be safe for human food use and has been
included in the latest Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) list, version v20 (EFSA BIOHAZ, 2024).
K. marxianus is nonpathogenic and nontoxigenic and is not known to produce any toxic secondary

metabolites (Alasmar et al., 2020).
Manufacturing Process
Kluvy® Protein is manufactured by Changing Bio under cGMP with food-grade raw materials and
processing aids. The GRAS Panel notes Changing Bio’s statement that none of the raw materials used
in the production process are derived from major allergens. As detailed in the GRAS dossier, the
production process consistently yields a reproducible product. In addition, Kluvy® Protein is
extensively analyzed to ensure the product meets the established specifications, including protein,
moisture, ash, heavy metals, and microbial limits.
Microbiological analyses include total plate count, yeast, mold, Escherichia coli, Enterobacteriaceae,
Salmonella, and Staphylococcus aureus. The GRAS Panel notes the absence of production organism
in the finished product was demonstrated by testing three non-consecutive batches using an
appropriately verified method.
The GRAS Panel reviewed the manufacturing process and does not have any concerns with the
information provided in the GRAS dossier.
Product Specifications
The GRAS Panel notes that the product specifications established by Changing Bio for Kluvy® Protein
are sufficient to characterize the ingredient. The GRAS Panel reviewed batch analysis results for five
non-consecutive lots of Kluvy® Protein as presented in the GRAS dossier, and notes that the ingredient

is well-characterized and that the analytical data obtained using internationally standardized methods
includes protein, moisture, microbiological, and heavy metal content. Stability data indicate that
Kluvy® Protein is shelf-stable for up to one year when stored at ambient conditions.
Proposed Uses and Estimated Intake
Estimated intakes of Kluvy® Protein were based on its proposed use in selected conventional foods
and the maximum usage levels outlined in the GRAS dossier. The estimated conservative mean daily
intake for consumers only and the 90th percentile intake for consumers only are 25 g/day and 53 g/day,
respectively, for the total population aged 2 years and older.
To compare with dietary reference intakes for protein, the estimated total protein intake from the
proposed uses of Kluvy® Protein was calculated by assuming a maximum protein content of
approximately 63%, based on representative batch results provided in the GRAS dossier. The
conservative mean and 90th percentile estimate of daily protein consumption from Kluvy® Protein are
approximately 16 g/day and 33 g/day, respectively, for the total population aged 2 years and older. The
GRAS Panel notes that this intake falls within or below the recommended and typical dietary protein
intake levels. Additionally, Kluvy® Protein is intended to substitute other protein sources in the diet,
rather than increase overall protein consumption. Therefore, the GRAS Panel concurs with Changing
Bio that the risk of adverse effects from excessing protein intake due to Kluvy® Protein consumption
is unlikely. The GRAS Panel also concurs that the dietary intake of fiber and sodium from consuming
Kluvy® Protein falls within the recommended daily levels and is therefore not a safety concern.
Pivotal Safety Data
The safety of Kluvy® Protein is supported by several factors:
1) The production organism, K. marxianus, has a long history of safe use in food manufacturing, with
no evidence of pathogenicity or toxigenicity. The production organism has been confirmed to
belong to the K. marxianus species, is derived from a food source, and has not undergone genetic
modification; therefore, the GRAS Panel agrees that the safety information associated with K.
marxianus is relevant and supports the safe use of this organism.

2) Kluvy® Protein is produced in accordance with cGMP standards, using food-grade raw materials
and processing aids.
3) The absence of live production organisms in all batches is ensured through analytical testing and
monitoring of yeast counts according to established specifications, which have been confirmed to
be appropriate for the intended use.
4) Kluvy® Protein has an amino acid profile similar to other dietary protein sources, making it a
suitable dietary protein substitute.
5) The protein intake from consuming Kluvy® Protein is within or below recommended dietary
protein levels and background dietary protein intakes, ensuring no overall increase in protein
consumption.
6) The GRAS Panel concurs that there is no evidence to suggest that Kluvy® Protein derived from
the fermentation of K. marxianus poses an increased allergenic risk.

1.0 Introduction.
The Shanghai Changing Biotechnology Company, Ltd has developed a non~transgenic, or native
yeast organism culture as a protein-rich food protein source for foods. The company and the
Anchor Center for Certification have considered food characteristics including nutritional
properties, potential toxicity and potential food .allergy for the product. Based on the literature
search for risks for possible toxicity and allergenicity, they have concluded that the food
products should be generally recognized as safe. l have reviewed the pr,oduct description and
their evaluation focusing on food allergy risks based on my knowledge of food allr:rgy from
GMO evaluations with CODEX guidelines, and based on aJlergen identification in managing the
www.AllergenOnlin .org database and have concluded the products should be considered
Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS}.
A report from Changing Biotechnology or ACC describes the species compositional analysis,
protein identification based on liquid cbr-omatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MSMS)
and comparison of protein sequences to the major allergenic proteins in the eight-priority
allergenic sources listed by the US FDA I have reviewed their report and performed
independent investigation of public data to consider possible risks of food allergy from the
material that would be used as a human food protein source. My analysis is reported here.
Comparisons in www.AllergenOnline.org used a sliding 80 amino acid window looking for
minimum Identity matches of 35% or more. Additional searches were made with the NCBJ
Protein database using BLASTP and looking for long alignments of> 35% identity.
2. Purpose. The purpose of this study is to perform an evaluation of potential food allergy risks
that might arise for consumers with existing allergies. The risks are best judged by whether the
source organism is a oommon food allergy source, or if the protein amino acid sequence
matches the identity of known allergens.
3. Method·.

3.1 cientific literature search strategies. The PubMed database
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nib.gov/pubmed) maintained by the U.S. National Library of
Medicine was used as th.e primary data source for scientific literature on allergy. Allergy to
the yeast species, .Kluyve1·omyces marxlan11s was performed by a general search oftbe
species name AND "allergen" AND "allergy". In addition, Wikipedia was also searched
with the species name. Information from those two searches were evaluated for evidence of
allergy. The CBI Taxonomy database was searched with the species name to investigate
the apparent re!ationshlps with other fungi.

Biotechnology Company/ ACC lists he top 100 proteins identified by LC-MSMS based on
proportion relative to the total protein mass of the product. They compared the detected

4. Results.
4.1 Literature searches. No evidence of any allergy was found for this species. ot in
PubMed, nor in Wikipedia. There were no publications identified in PubMed with keywords
"Kluyveromyces marxianus" AND "allergen". Two papers were identified with
"Kluyveromyces marxianus" AND "allergy" but they showed a lack of allergy with
exposure. One was by Amelia and Ciprandi jn 2019, suggesting recurrent respiratory
infections could be avoided by supplementary feeding with fuis species plus bovine
colostrum. The other by Tullio in 2024 described probiotic use •of this species or a fev
other yeasts that might reduce allergy.
Other publications were reviewed to describe the AUergenOnline database (Goodman et al.,
2016), and to oonsider possible allergy and cross-reactivity for those who are already
allergic (Aalberse, 2000). Proteins predicted from genomes are sometimes used to compare
to allergen databases (Machida et al, 2005 and Abdebnoteleb et al., 2020). Most allergy
protocols were to consider possible risks from transgenic or genetically modified organisms
(Goodman, 2006), but are often over-predictive if based on the CODEX guidelin.es (2003
(Goodman et a. 2008), aod would lead to unnecessary human serum IgE studies and
possibly to basophil histamine release assays (Knol, 2006),
4.2 Bioinformatics 1111ing proteins identified by LC-MS/MS ,detected peptid.es. The
report by Shanghai Changing Biotechnology Company describes and shows the results of
LC-MSMS identification of proteins. The more abundant ones are of the same overall
protein types that have sometimes been called allergen for instance in WHO/lUJS Allergen
Nomenclature database but the proof of reactivity for those proleins are not listed in peer
reviewed publications. Furthermore, there are no publications demonstrating allergy to
proteins from this species, KJuyveromyces marxianus. The report from the company did not

find any significant sequence match to clear allergens from the eight major allergenic foods.
There are many proteins listed in both the AllergenOnline.org database and the WHO/IlilS
allergen nomenclature database that do not have clear IgE binding or clinical allergy
associated with them. It is therefore reasonable to assume based on scientific evid~ce, that
proteins from this species are unlikely to cause allergy.
5. CONCLUSIONS
My overall conclusion from reviewing the data and information provided by the developer
and based on literature searches is that the protein material generated from thls product
should be assUIJled to be Generally Recogniz.ed as Safe (GRAS).

RE: GRAS Determination for Onego Bio, Inc., for the use of ovalbumin from fermentation by
Trichoderma reesei in baked goods and baking mixes, beverages and beverage bases (alcoholic
and non-alcoholic), breakfast cereals, cheeses, confections and frostings, dairy product
analogs, egg products, fats and oils, frozen dairy desserts and mixes, fruit and water ices,
gelatins, puddings, and fillings, grain products and pastas, gravies and sauces, milk products,
plant protein products, snack foods (protein and snack bars), and soft candy.
Dear GRAS filing team,
Please find enclosed the Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) determination for the use of ovalbumin
from fermentation by Trichoderma reesei. The substance is intended to be used as a general-purpose
protein ingredient in a wide range of FDA-regulated food categories which include baked goods and
baking mixes, beverages and beverage bases (alcoholic and non-alcoholic), breakfast cereals,
cheeses, confections and frostings, dairy product analogs, egg products, fats and oils, frozen dairy
desserts and mixes, fruit and water ices, gelatins, puddings, and fillings, grain products and pastas,
gravies and sauces, milk products, plant protein products, snack foods (protein and snack bars), and
soft candy.
The protein ingredient is intended to replace fresh or powdered whole eggs and egg white protein
powder in FDA-regulated food products, providing dietary protein along with functional properties such
as foaming, gelling, and binding. These uses are not expected to increase the overall protein
consumption of the general population. Information regarding the product identification, intended uses,
the manufacturing process and safety is presented in the attached GRAS notice.

2.1. Identity of the notified substance
2.1.1. Introduction
Onego Bio produces a highly purified ovalbumin by precision fermentation using a genetically modified
strain of T. reesei expressing the ovalbumin gene from Gallus gallus. T. reesei is a filamentous fungus
with a long history of safe use in the production of food enzymes by precision fermentation. The notified

substance is referred to as ovalbumin from fermentation by T. reesei or NON-ANIMAL OVA (NOVA)
throughout this GRAS determination, although other common names may be used as detailed in
Section 1.3.
NOVA is a water-soluble, white to off-white powder with a moisture content of maximum 10% and
protein content of minimum 75%, out of which at least 80% is ovalbumin. Onego’s NOVA is substantially
equivalent to its native counterpart and can be used as an ingredient in a range of food products as a
replacement for fresh or powdered eggs and egg white protein powder.
The levels of impurities, namely heavy metals and microbial contaminants are all below limits of safety
concern. NOVA contains no residual recombinant DNA or viable cells from the production organism.
No mycotoxins of food safety concern were detected.
2.1.2. Chemical name and physicochemical properties
Egg albumin, or ovalbumin (OVA), is the predominant protein in the egg white of Gallus gallus (chicken),
accounting for about 54% of the total albumen by weight. It is also known as “Gal d 2”, which
corresponds to its allergen designation (Mathew & Pfleghaar, 2023).
Native OVA is a water-soluble globulin. It is a monomeric, phosphorylated glycoprotein with a
polypeptide chain consisting of 385 amino acids, including six cysteines with a disulfide bond. N-
terminal and C-terminal of the protein are acetylated glycine and proline, respectively, with a
carbohydrate group attached to the N-terminal. The ovalbumin's crystal structure consists of a three-
turn α-helix loop, a reactive center, and six strands of β-sheet A (Aro, 2023; Razi, 2023; Guha, 2019).
Hen egg ovalbumin is a mixture of three kinds of proteins, A1, A2, and A3 with two, one, and no
phosphoryl residues, respectively, with isoelectric points (pI) ranging from 4.75 to 4.94 (Kitabatake,
1988).
2.1.3. Substantial equivalence to native protein
Onego Bio has conducted a comprehensive characterization of ovalbumin from fermentation by T.
reesei to conclusively determine substantial equivalence to its native counterpart. The amino acid
sequence, glycosylation pattern, molecular weight, isoelectric point, secondary structure,
thermostability, and in vitro digestibility were evaluated and compared to native OVA, as detailed below.
The results from all the analyses confirmed that ovalbumin from fermentation by T. reesei is
substantially equivalent to ovalbumin from chicken egg white.
For the analyses described below, two commercial reference OVA samples were used: 1) Worthington
OVA (Worthington Biochemical Corporation, LS003059) and 2) Sigma OVA (Sigma Aldrich, A5503).
Both Worthington and Sigma OVA samples were purchased as lyophilized powders with a purity higher
than 95% and 98%, respectively. Both originate from chicken egg white.

2.1.3.1. Amino acid sequence: LC-MS/MS peptide mapping
A high-resolution peptide mapping (PepMap) analysis using liquid chromatography coupled with
tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) was performed on samples of NOVA and native OVA from

chicken egg white to compare their protein sequences. LC-MS/MS is a widely used method in
proteomics, favored for its high sensitivity, precision, and ability to provide detailed protein
characterization (Neagu, 2022).
For this analysis, Worthington OVA and NOVA samples from three non-consecutive production lots (ID-
7695, ID-6309, and ID-8711) were denatured and reduced using a urea-DTT solution, alkylated with
iodoacetamide, and digested with trypsin into peptides. LC-MS/MS analysis was carried out using an
ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) system coupled with a quadrupole time-of-flight
(QTOF) mass spectrometer, employing positive electrospray ionization (ESI). The mass range for data
acquisition was m/z 67–2490, and results were filtered to retain only high-confidence peptide
identifications.
As recorded in the UniProt database (accession number P01012), native ovalbumin consists of 386
amino acid residues, representing the full-length precursor that includes an N-terminal methionine. In
Gallus gallus, this methionine is removed post-translationally in the mature protein, resulting in a
sequence of 385 amino acids, as detailed in Table 1. The PepMap results for the commercial OVA
sample were consistent with the reported sequence, with a sequence coverage of 100%.
For Onego's NOVA, PepMap analysis confirmed an amino acid sequence of 385 residues, identical to
the native protein (UniProt accession number P01012), with 100% sequence coverage (Figure 1).
Notably, the expression cassette designed by Onego Bio omits the N-terminal methionine residue, as
T. reesei does not remove it as efficiently as Gallus gallus. This modification ensures that ovalbumin
produced by T. reesei corresponds exactly to the mature native OVA commonly consumed from chicken
eggs and egg-containing products. While the sequence of Onego’s ovalbumin expressed in T. reesei
has not been submitted to the NCBI or UniProt, it is fully detailed in Table 2 as determined
experimentally via LC-MS/MS in at least three non-consecutive production batches. To further support
the sequence equivalence of NOVA to its native counterpart, a comparison of the percentages of each
amino acid in OVA and NOVA is presented in Section 2.5 - Batch analysis, Table 8, where the mean
levels of each amino acid in NOVA are compared to theoretical values for native ovalbumin,
demonstrating a similar amino acid composition.

2.1.3.3. Molecular weight: SDS-PAGE
The molecular weight of NOVA was compared to that of its natural counterpart by means of Sodium
Dodecyl Sulfate–Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). Results are displayed in Figure 2.
For this analysis, NOVA samples from three non-consecutive production batches and Worthington
OVA, all in powder form, were dissolved in ultrapure water to a concentration of 1 mg/mL. The protein
samples were then denatured by boiling in denaturing buffer for 5-10 minutes.
Both OVA and NOVA were analyzed with and without PTMs. PTM removal was essential for this
comparison, as differing PTM patterns would otherwise result in distinct electrophoretic profiles.
To this end, CIAP (calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase, Invitrogen) was used to remove OVA's
phosphate groups, while PNGase F (Peptide-N-Glycosidase F, New England Biolabs) was used to
remove the N-glycans in both NOVA and OVA. Given that NOVA lacks the phosphate groups present
in OVA, CIAP treatment was not required for its analysis. Denatured samples designated for PTM
removal were treated with PNGase F and CIAP according to manufacturer's protocols. NOVA and OVA
samples from which PTMs have been removed are referred to as "treated".
All samples - treated and untreated NOVA and OVA - were loaded onto a Criterion TGX Precast Gel
(BioRad) which was run at constant 250 V for 30 minutes. The gel was stained with PageBlueTM staining
solution. In all cases, the sample amounts loaded on each gel corresponded to 600 ng of ovalbumin (8
to 9 µL).

2.1.3.4. Secondary structure: circular dichroism
The secondary structural motifs of NOVA and its native counterpart were analyzed by circular dichroism
(CD) spectroscopy. Far-UV (190 to 260 nm) CD measurements were performed at 20°C, using a 0.1
mg/mL protein concentration in 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.2). For each sample, CD spectra
were recorded in duplicate and averaged using a bandwidth of 1 nm, a wavelength step of 0.5 nm, and
a time-per-point setting of 0.5 s. The CD spectra are presented in measured ellipticities (mdeg) without
smoothing and with baseline correction for buffer contribution. Three non-consecutive production
batches of NOVA (ID-7695, ID-6309, and ID-8711) were analyzed against a control OVA sample
(Sigma).
As shown in Figure 3, both NOVA and native OVA displayed typical features of an alpha-helical protein,
including negative bands at 208 and 222 nm and a positive band at 193 nm. The CD spectra of both
proteins exhibited similar conformational motifs, confirming their equivalence in secondary structure.

The melting temperatures (Tm) of NOVA from three non-consecutive production batches (ID-7695, ID-

Ovalbumin from precision fermentation with T. reesei is produced by submerged fermentation of a T.

reesei strain that has been constructed as described in Section 2.2.2. The fermentation process takes
place in a liquid culture medium composed of standard ingredients used in the food/enzyme industry in
facilities that adhere to current cGMPs and have a Food Safety Plan, in accordance with 21 CFR Part
117. All raw materials, including processing aids, are obtained from qualified suppliers and are safe and

Fermentation
The production of each batch of ovalbumin via precision fermentation with T. reesei begins with the

to off-white powder with a protein content of minimum 75%, out of which at least 80% is ovalbumin.

6.1. Introduction
The subject of this GRAS determination is recombinant ovalbumin produced by Onego Bio via precision
fermentation using a genetically modified strain of filamentous fungus T. reesei. Onego Bio has
determined the product to be GRAS based on scientific procedures, in accordance with 21 CFR §
170.30(a) and § 170.30(b). The GRAS status is supported by publicly available safety data on
ovalbumin from fermentation and the production organism, T. reesei.
NOVA is a water-soluble powder with a protein content of minimum 75%, out of which at least 80% is
ovalbumin. NOVA is substantially equivalent to its native counterpart and can be used as a general-
purpose ingredient to replace eggs and white protein powder in a range of food products, as a source
of dietary protein providing nutritional value and functionality due to its foaming, gelling, and binding
properties. These uses are not expected to increase the overall protein consumption of the general
population.
The production platform for NOVA, T. reesei, is widely recognized as a safe production host for
enzymes, with a long history of use in the food industry. It has been used to produce numerous GRAS
proteins and enzymes, many of which have received “no questions” letters from the FDA.
The fermentation process takes place in a liquid culture medium composed of standard ingredients
used in the food/enzyme industry in facilities that adhere to current cGMPs with the implementation of
a Food Safety Plan in compliance with 21 CFR Part117. All raw materials are of high purity and quality,
regulated and suitable for their intended use and are food-grade, in accordance with 21 CFR §
170.230(c).
The food safety aspects of Onego’s ovalbumin from fermentation by T. reesei, the production process,
and the production platform are discussed in the following sections.
6.2. Safety of ovalbumin
6.2.1. History of consumption of ovalbumin
Egg albumin, or ovalbumin (OVA), is the predominant protein in the egg white of Gallus gallus (chicken),
accounting for about 54% of the total albumen by weight (Guha, 2019).

As a major component of egg white, OVA has an extensive history of safe consumption worldwide.
Eggs have long been a fundamental part of the human diet due to their rich nutrient content and culinary
versatility, with ovalbumin significantly contributing to their nutritional value and functional properties.
Ovalbumin is an excellent source of high-quality dietary protein, as it contains all essential amino acids
and is highly digestible. Additionally, its intrinsic functional properties – gelling, foaming, binding,
emulsifying – make it very valuable for the food industry (Razi, 2023)
OVA was one of the first proteins to be purified from egg whites and it has also been expressed in
several microbial platforms, including E. coli, P. pastoris, and T. reesei, as reported in peer-reviewed
scientific journals. The final product of recombinant production by precision fermentation is a protein
powder that typically shows comparable functional properties to chicken ovalbumin and can be used as
a replacement in food formulations (Järviö, 2021; Pereira, 2016; Ito & Matsudomi, 2005), offering a
sustainable alternative to the conventional food industry to reduce its reliance on animal farming.
Recombinant ovalbumin produced by fermentation using Komagataella phafii (P. pastoris) has also
been determined GRAS in GRN 1104 (2022), which has received a “no questions” letter from the FDA.
Other egg white proteins have also been determined GRAS (Table 13), such as ovomucoid from
fermentation with Komagataella phafii as described in GRN 967 (2020) and egg-white lysozyme isolated
from hen eggs as described in GRN 64 (2000), both of which have also received “no questions” letters
from the FDA. In a proposed rule from 1998 to include egg-white lysozyme in 21 CFR § 184, Direct
Food Substances Affirmed as GRAS, the FDA states that that proteins derived from egg whites do not

Notably, native egg white proteins are less digestible compared to those subjected to moderate heat
treatments (60–90 °C). Such treatments alter the secondary and tertiary structures, exposing previously
buried hydrophobic and sulfhydryl groups, thereby enhancing the accessibility of enzymatic cleavage
sites and improving overall digestibility (Farjami, 2021; Evenepoel, 1998). Heat treatment can also
modulate the allergenicity of egg white proteins, especially ovalbumin by destroying IgE and IgG-
reactive epitopes, which reduces allergenic potential as will be detailed in section 6.2.3.
Given the demonstrated substantial equivalence to native ovalbumin in terms of thermostability and
digestibility (section 2.1.3), the ADME profile of ovalbumin from fermentation by T. reesei is expected
to resemble that of dietary proteins, and comparable to OVA derived from chicken eggs.
6.2.3. Allergenicity of ovalbumin
Eggs are one of the nine major food allergens identified by the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer
Protection Act of 2004 (FALCPA) and the FASTER Act of 2021, along with milk, fish, crustacean
shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybean, and sesame. Together, these food groups account for
90% of food allergies in the US (FDA, 2024; USDA, 2024; FDA, 2022a). After milk, eggs are the second

most common allergen in childhood, typically appearing in the first two years of life. In 50 to 80% of
children, egg allergies resolve spontaneously by school age. Egg allergies rarely appear in adulthood
(ECARF, 2016; Jiaqi, 2023; Caubet, 2011).
The most common egg allergens are found in the egg white, where, despite OVA (Gal d 2) being the
most abundant protein, ovomucoid (Gal d 1) is the primary allergen. Other significant allergens in egg
white are ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), egg white lysozyme (Gal d 4), and ovomucin (ECARF, 2016; Mathew,
2023; Caubet, 2011). In contrast, egg yolk allergies are less common, with chicken serum albumin (Gal
d 5) being the main allergen in the yolk (Tomei, 2023; Quirce, 2001)
Egg allergy is mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE). While healthy individuals can produce antigen-
specific IgE without adverse effects, those with egg allergies experience an exaggerated immune
response, even to minimal egg protein exposure. This can lead to a range of symptoms from cutaneous
reactions (most common) to severe, potentially life-threatening anaphylaxis. A genetic predisposition
likely contributes to egg allergies, as children of atopic individuals are more prone to developing this
allergy. Asthmatic patients are particularly at high risk of severe reactions (Mathew, 2023; Caubet,
2011).
The allergenicity of Gal d 2 has been validated in various animal models mainly aimed at developing
valid sensitization models for the study of food protein allergenicity. For instance, Knippels et al. (1999)
explored oral sensitization with ovalbumin in different rat strains, administering 1 mg of OVA daily via
gavage for six weeks. While all strains developed OVA-specific IgG responses, only Brown Norway
(BN) rats also developed OVA-specific IgE responses, indicating that genetic background influences
the outcomes of oral sensitization. This pattern of IgG and IgE responses observed in orally sensitized
BN rats was later found to be comparable to that seen in food-allergic pediatric patients. Local and
systemic immune-mediated effects observed in rats were in accordance with observations from human
clinical practice (Knippels, 2000).
Similarly, a study by Batista et al. (2014) demonstrated that mice sensitized to ovalbumin through
subcutaneous injection (2 x 10 mg OVA) exhibited food allergy-like symptoms after consuming a 14%
OVA diet for seven days. These symptoms, including increased anti-OVA IgE, intestinal inflammation,
and significant metabolic alterations, notably improved after 7 additional days of OVA ingestion,
suggesting that prolonged OVA ingestion may mitigate the metabolic effects of experimental egg
allergy.
It is important to note that food protein allergenicity largely depends on their resistance to heat and
digestive enzymes, as food allergens must remain stable during cooking and digestion to reach the
intestinal mucosa, where absorption and sensitization can occur (Astwood, 1996). OVA (Gal d 2) is
known to be heat-labile, undergoing structural changes during cooking that reduce its immunogenic
potential. This likely explains why some individuals with egg allergies can tolerate cooked and baked
egg products (Caubet, 2011) a finding extensively documented in interventional studies involving
sensitized patients (Upton, 2023; Lemon-Mulé, 2008). In contrast, ovomucoid (Gal d 1) is resistant to

Given that the primary and secondary structures of NOVA, along with its thermostability, have been
shown to be equivalent to those of native OVA through experimental data (Section 2.1.3), it is expected

Furthermore, given that most products containing NOVA are intended to be cooked, the use of OVA as
an ingredient, rather than whole eggs or egg-white protein, could somewhat reduce allergenicity

and the FD&C Act section 403(w), all food products containing NOVA must still be labeled as containing
egg. Labels will clearly indicate the presence of egg allergen, specifying the source (FDA, 2022b), to
assist consumers in avoiding allergens.
6.2.4. Toxicity of ovalbumin
Given the long history of egg consumption worldwide, research has primarily focused on the
allergenicity of OVA, with fewer studies addressing its toxicity. Generally, OVA is considered non-toxic
and safe for consumption as part of a regular diet, with the primary concerns related to allergenicity
rather than inherent toxicity. Most of the studies conducted with OVA focus on the benefits of its
consumption instead.
In a study by Nicklin and Miller (1987), researchers explored the impact of early dietary exposure to
OVA on the development of OVA-specific antibody responses in Piebald Virol Glaxo (PVG) rats.
Pregnant and lactating rats were fed a diet containing 21% OVA, and their offspring were later
challenged with OVA either parenterally (10 µg OVA) or orally (200 mg OVA). The study found that
early exposure during gestation and the post-partum period led to increased biliary anti-OVA antibody
activity while maintaining systemic tolerance following parenteral OVA challenge. This suggests that
early dietary antigen exposure plays a crucial role in shaping immune responses later in life. Although
not designed as a toxicity study, the absence of reported deaths (both control and treatment groups)
and the seemingly well-tolerated prolonged OVA exposure in both adult and neonatal rats indirectly
indicates a lack of developmental toxicity.
In a human clinical context, other studies have explored the potential effects of OVA and its hydrolysates
on human health. Lucey et al. (2019) assessed the cardiovascular effects of OVA-derived protein
hydrolysates in a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial involving adults aged 50–70 with
elevated systolic blood pressure. Despite promising animal and in vitro data, the study found no
evidence that the hydrolysate reduced blood pressure or modified cardiovascular risk factors. However,
it is worth noting that the treatment did not lead to any adverse effects, reinforcing the general safety of
egg-derived proteins in human diets.
Further supporting the safety of egg-derived proteins, Nijssen et al. (2023) assessed the effects of egg-
derived protein hydrolysates on arterial stiffness and cardiometabolic markers in adults with metabolic
syndrome. While the preparation did not significantly impact arterial stiffness, it did modestly reduce
fasting pulse pressure and acutely lowered central augmentation index and diastolic blood pressure,
demonstrating some cardiovascular benefits. As in Lucey et al. (2029), no adverse effects were

observed, further reinforcing the safety of egg protein hydrolysates in adults with metabolic syndrome.
While these studies suggest positive health effects, egg white protein has been linked to a reduction in
biotin absorption, although this is not attributed to OVA itself. The interaction between avidin in raw egg
white and biotin, which renders the vitamin non-absorbable, is a well-known phenomenon, though biotin
deficiency from egg consumption remains rare (Saleem & Soos, 2023, Wallig & Keenan, 2013). These
concerns, however, are primarily relevant to the consumption of raw egg whites and do not extend to
the typical dietary intake of cooked egg proteins.
These studies collectively suggest that OVA and egg white protein are safe under normal dietary
conditions, with no significant toxicity reported outside of allergenic responses.

6.3.3. Safety of NOVA
6.3.3.1. Substantial equivalence to native ovalbumin
As outlined in Section 2.1.3, Onego Bio has conducted a comprehensive structural characterization of
ovalbumin derived from fermentation by T. reesei, demonstrating its substantial equivalence to the
native chicken ovalbumin, which has a well-established history of use in the human diet as the main
component of chicken egg white.
The amino acid sequence of NOVA has been confirmed to be 100% identical to that of native chicken
OVA (Section 2.1.3.1), with only minor differences in amino acid composition (Table 8, Section 2.5)
which were expected and can be attributed to the different production organisms. Notably, Onego Bio
has intentionally designed the expression cassette to match the amino acid sequence of mature chicken
OVA, ensuring that the ovalbumin produced by T. reesei corresponds exactly to the OVA molecule

commonly consumed as part of a regular diet from eggs and egg-containing products. Furthermore,
experimental analysis confirmed that the molecular weight and secondary structure of NOVA are
equivalent to native OVA, as demonstrated by SDS-PAGE and CD spectroscopy (Sections 2.1.3.3 and
2.1.3.4).
The main structural difference between NOVA and its native counterpart lies in the post-translational
modification (PTM) pattern, which was expected due to differences in the biosynthetic machinery of T.
reesei compared to that of chickens. Native ovalbumin is phosphorylated, with phosphate groups at
Ser-68 and Ser-344 (Harvey, 2000), whereas NOVA lacks phosphorylation. Although T. reesei has
been reported to perform this PTM (Ramos-Pedersoli, 2021; Rodriguez-Iglesias and Schmoll, 2019) its
phosphorylation capabilities are limited compared to those of higher organisms.
Additionally, NOVA’s glycosylation pattern was found to differ slightly from that of native OVA. LC-MS
glycan analysis revealed the presence of mannose-based N-glycans with chains ranging from 5 to 11
mannose units, linked to the polypeptide chain by GlcNAc residues (Section 2.1.3.2). This glycosylation
pattern is consistent with proteins produced in T. reesei (Kolaczkowski et al., 2020; Beckham et al.,
2012), and while it is not identical to that of native ovalbumin, it remains highly similar - both NOVA and
native OVA are primarily glycosylated with mannose-based structures and share one predominate
glycoform (Man) (GlcNAc) which is the main N-glycan on NOVA. The overall difference in
5 2,
glycosylation is consistent with what is expected from fungal expression systems, which typically
produce glycosylation patterns that are closer to those of higher eukaryotes than bacterial or yeast
systems (Garvey, 2022; Su, 2012). However, as these differences could introduce food safety concerns,
the stability of NOVA was further assessed.
Despite minor differences in PTMs, the stability, function, and safety of ovalbumin from fermentation by
T. reesei were shown to be unaffected, as demonstrated by thermal stability and digestibility
comparisons with its native counterpart (Section 2.1.3.5). The thermostability of NOVA was assessed
by measuring its melting temperature (Tm), which indicates the protein’s ability to maintain its three-
dimensional structure under heat stress. NOVA’s Tm was found to be equivalent to that of native OVA,
suggesting that NOVA will perform similarly under food processing conditions, such as cooking or other
thermal treatments, thereby ensuring its safety in food products.
In addition, protein digestibility data (PDCAAS) confirmed that NOVA is digested in a manner
comparable to native OVA, further supporting their substantial equivalence. The similarity in both
thermal stability and digestibility demonstrates that NOVA provides the same nutritional benefits,
particularly in terms of essential amino acids, without altering its safety or bioactivity.
Based on the comprehensive structural characterization, thermal stability, and digestibility data, it can
be concluded that NOVA produced by T. reesei is substantially equivalent to native chicken OVA. The

including heavy metals and mycotoxins. The product is also confirmed free of residual viable cells and
recombinant DNA from the production organism. NOVA contains a protein level of at least 75%, with a

originating from the host strain. The consistency of batch analysis results across all lots demonstrates
