6.3.3.3. Dietary exposure to protein and ovalbumin
As described in Section 3, the proposed uses of Onego's recombinant ovalbumin are substitutional for
existing uses of egg and egg white and are not expected to increase the overall dietary protein
consumption of the general population.
The EDI of NOVA for the general US population is 0.32 g/kg bw/day at the mean intake levels (0.74
g/kg bw/day at the 90th percentile). These values fall below the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution
Range (AMDR) for protein, which is 1.05 to 3.67 g/kg bw/day as recommended in the US by the Food
and Nutrition Board (FNB) of the Institute of Medicine (Wolfe, 2017). In terms of grams per day, the
intake NOVA at its intended conditions of use is also below the FDA’s Daily Reference Value (DRV) of
50 g of protein per day for a 2,000-calorie diet (21 CFR § 101.9(c)(9)), with an EDI of 18.89 g/day at
mean intake levels (39.17 g/day at the 90th percentile). Furthermore, exposure to protein from NOVA
will be even lower, as the product contains at least 75% protein, of which at least 80% is ovalbumin as
detailed in Section 2.5. It is also worth mentioning that these exposure values represent a worst-case
scenario, assuming maximum use levels across all proposed food categories, and are therefore an
overestimation.
NOVA is intended to replace fresh or powdered whole eggs and egg white protein powder in the
selected food categories and will be substitutional for animal-derived ovalbumin in the diet. Given the
proposed uses for ovalbumin from fermentation by T. reesei, the cumulative exposure to ovalbumin
(both from dietary exposure from eggs and egg-containing products and from the intended uses of
NOVA) is not expected to increase in the general population. Consumer exposure to dietary protein is
not expected to increase either, as the majority of the population’s protein intake comes from
unprocessed foods, including meat, poultry, fish, and legumes, and will likely continue to do so.
Ovalbumin has a long history of safe consumption as a dietary protein, as detailed in Section 6.2. Given
the substantial equivalence of NOVA to its native counterpart and consistent compliance to quality
specifications of the final product, we anticipate that this established safety profile extends to the
consumption of NOVA under its proposed conditions of use. The proposed uses and levels of use of
NOVA are not expected to increase exposure or pose unintended safety risks to consumers.

The production strain and manufacturing process for Onego’s NOVA from fermentation by T. reesei are

humans, as discussed in Section 6.3.1.
NOVA is manufactured in facilities that meet US regulations for food production by adhering to cGMPs
with the implementation of a Food Safety Plan in compliance with 21 CFR Part 117, and the product
meets predetermined batch-release specifications (see Section 2.4).

6.3.5. Allergenicity of NOVA
None of the raw materials or the production organism used to manufacture NOVA are (or are derived
from) major food allergens as defined by the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act
(FALCPA) of 2004 and the Food Allergy Safety, Treatment, Education and Research (FASTER) Act of
2021.
Besides ovalbumin, which is the main constituent of the protein fraction in NOVA (85.8% to 90.9%) and
whose allergenicity is discussed in Section 6.2.3, no significant allergens are expected in Onego's
finished NOVA preparation. To address allergenicity concerns, all food products containing NOVA will
be clearly labeled to indicate the presence of egg, in accordance with the requirements of the Food
Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act (FALCPA) (Public Law 108-282) and Section 403 (w)
of the FD&C Act.
Allergenicity concerns are not expected to arise from the production platform of NOVA. T. reesei has a
well-established history of safe use in food enzyme production and is not reported in the scientific
literature as a known producer of allergens. As detailed in Section 6.3.1, a review of the FDA GRAS
Notice Inventory identified 32 GRAS notices for proteins produced using T. reesei. None of the 29
publicly available notices, including those withdrawn by the applicant, report allergenicity concerns
related to the production organism. Furthermore, no scientific publications or reviews have documented
widespread allergenic reactions resulting from the ingestion of proteins derived from fermentation by T.
reesei.
As further discussed in Section 6.3.1, T. reesei is widely regarded as a safe organism for food enzyme
production. While repeated occupational exposure to commercial enzyme preparations (e.g.,
cellulases) derived from T. reesei or other Trichoderma species has occasionally been associated with

allergic responses such as dermatitis, rhinitis, and asthma due to handling or dust inhalation, such
cases are rare (Health Canada, 2018). Importantly, the likelihood of these occupational aeroallergen or
contact allergen sensitivities leading to food-related allergic reactions is considered extremely low.
Nonetheless, Onego Bio evaluated the allergenic potential of residual T. reesei proteins in the final
ovalbumin preparation by analyzing the peptides and proteins from the production organism present in
NOVA. To this end, the protein fraction in three non-consecutive production batches (ID-7695, ID-6309,
and ID-8711) was characterized through quantitative proteomic analysis (LC-MS/MS), as described in
Section 2.5.2. The analysis confirmed that ovalbumin was the predominant protein in all batches. In
addition to ovalbumin, 541 peptides derived from T. reesei were identified in NOVA.
All T. reesei amino acid sequences detected at levels exceeding 0.01% (290 sequences) were further
assessed for sequence homology using the AllergenOnline database (version 22;
http://www.allergenonline.org), maintained by the Food Allergy Research and Resource Program
(FARRP) at the University of Nebraska. This analysis aimed to identify potential homology between the
identified T. reesei peptides and known allergens, to assess the risk of allergenic cross-reactivity that
could potentially trigger reactions in sensitized individuals consuming NOVA.
Sequence homology testing took place in two steps. In the first step, we evaluated potential cross
reactivity with documented allergenic proteins using an 80-amino-acid sliding window search with a
35% homology threshold, as recommended by the Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO, 2001). It is
worth noting, however, that sequences with > 35% identity over an 80-amino-acid window are common
among highly conserved proteins and this threshold alone is not predictive of allergenicity, often
resulting in a high number of false positives (Abdelmoteleb, 2021; EFSA, 2022). The scientific literature
indicates that greater sequence or structural conservation (typically > 50% identity) is generally required
for allergenic cross-reactivity, while sequences with at least 25% identity over 200 or more amino acids

As detailed in Table 17, sequence matches included various protein groups such as transaldolases,
heat shock proteins, xylosidases, peptidyl-prolyl cis–trans isomerases (cyclophilins), superoxide
dismutases, enolases, elongation factors, aldehyde dehydrogenases, peroxisomal membrane proteins,
translationally-controlled tumor proteins, triosephosphate isomerases, and a disulfide-isomerase. Many
of these proteins are evolutionarily conserved across species and genera, and their biological
importance in a wide range of organisms results in significant sequence homology across diverse
species (Dogan, 2013; Sharan, 2005).
The majority of identified matches were aeroallergens and contact allergens derived from mites
(Dermatophagoides spp. and Tyrophagus putrescentiae), molds and yeasts (e.g., Aspergillus spp.,
Penicillium spp., Alternaria alternata, Cladosporium cladosporioides, Malassezia sympodialis, and
others), and insects (Periplaneta americana and Aedes aegypti). Matches were also found with pollen

allergens from edible and non-edible plants (e.g., Olea europaea, Salsola kali, Catharanthus roseus,
and others) as well as contact allergens from non-edible plants (e.g., Hevea brasiliensis). It is important
to note that the AllergenOnline database includes proteins from a variety of sources, not only food
allergens, but also airway, contact, venom, and salivary allergens with IgE binding data. In Onego’s
case, the identified matches to aeroallergens and contact allergens are primarily associated with
respiratory allergies and contact dermatitis, not food-related allergic reactions. A review of the scientific
literature found no evidence linking these allergens to allergic reactions upon ingestion, further
supporting the conclusion that they are unlikely to pose a food safety concern. Therefore, these
allergens are not considered relevant to the allergenicity assessment of T. reesei as the production
organism for NOVA.
Notably, a few matches with minor allergens from major allergenic food sources were identified for 5 of
the 23 potentially allergenic T. reesei proteins in NOVA (proteins 3, 12, 13, 15, and 17 as listed in Table
17). These included matches to cyclophilins, enolases, and triosephosphate isomerases from fish
(Salmo salar, Thunnus albacares, and Pangasianodon hypophthalmus), crustaceans (Procambarus
clarkii, Scylla paramamosain, Crangon crangon and Fenneropenaeus merguiensis), peanut (Arachis
hypogaea), and wheat (Triticum aestivum).
Three of these five proteins were identified to share significant sequence homology with a cyclophilin
from peanut, Arachis hypogaea (GenBank accession XP_025675300, WHO/IUIS allergen Ara h 18).
Ara h 18 is not part of the pool of major peanut allergens (Ara h 1, Ara h 2, Ara h 3, and Ara h 6) that
are associated with severe allergic symptoms and anaphylaxis. Instead, Ara h 18 is classified as a
minor allergen and is considered a cross-reactive determinant, with IgE-binding properties attributed to
sensitization to other allergen sources, such as pollen, rather than direct peanut exposure (Mattsson,
2021). Furthermore, Ara h 18 has not been associated with severe allergic symptoms upon exposure
and is unlikely to pose a food safety concern (Mattsson, 2021). Cyclophilins are essential enzymes for
most organisms, widely distributed in nature, and highly conserved across prokaryotes and eukaryotes;
they have been identified in plants, insects, fungi, bacteria, and mammals, including humans (Singh,
2023; Wang and Heitman, 2005). Due to their conservation, cyclophilins commonly appear in in silico
sequence homology tests for allergens. However, major allergens are generally not highly conserved
across species, which explains why individuals sensitized to a specific food allergen typically do not
exhibit allergic reactions to a wide range of unrelated food sources (Abdelmoteleb, 2021). Notable
exceptions include tropomyosins, which are conserved among shellfish and certain insects (Smeekens,
2024; Kamath, 2023). Importantly, no clinical evidence suggests widespread cross-reactivity involving
cyclophilins. Based on these considerations, the observed matches between T. reesei proteins and Ara
h 18 do not present a significant allergenic risk to NOVA consumers.

One more protein from T. reesei showed sequence homology greater than 50% with a set of
triosephosphate isomerases (TPI) from wheat (Triticum aestivum), crawfish (Procambarus clarkii), mud
crab (Scylla paramamosain), brown shrimp (Crangon crangon), iridescent shark catfish
(Pangasianodon hypophthalmus), and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The TPI from wheat (GenBank
accession CAC14917, WHO/IUIS allergen Tri a 31) has been reported only as an aeroallergen
associated with occupational baker's asthma or rhinitis due to inhalation exposure and is not a primary
wheat allergen (Sander, 2011). Therefore, Tri a 31 is not relevant to this allergenicity assessment.
Regarding the TPIs from crawfish, mud crab, shrimp, catfish, and salmon (WHO/IUIS allergens Pro c
8, Scy p 8, Cra c 8, Pan h 8, and Sal s 8, respectively), none correspond to the major allergens of these
food sources (Jasim, 2021; Ruethers, 2021; Yang, 2017; Bauermeister, 2011). TPI is a highly
conserved enzyme involved in glycolysis, found in a wide range of organisms, from bacteria to humans,

where it plays a critical role in energy production (Myers and Palladino, 2023). Given that TPI is highly
conserved across species and is essential for glycolysis in virtually all organisms, it is reasonable to
expect that humans would generally be tolerant to homologous TPI proteins. This is further supported
by the fact that there is no clinical evidence of widespread cross-reactivity associated with TPI. In
Onego’s case, none of the TPI matches identified for T. reesei proteins showed an identity greater than
70%, making clinically significant IgE cross-reactivity highly unlikely (Aalberse, 2000; Goodman et al.,
2008; Abdelmoteleb et al., 2021; Sharma and Vitte, 2024). Therefore, the allergenicity risk posed by
these TPI matches from food sources is not considered a significant concern for NOVA consumers.
The fifth T. reesei protein that matched minor allergens from major allergenic foods showed sequence
homology with a series of enolases derived from Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), iridescent shark catfish
(Pangasianodon hypophthalmus), yellowfin tuna (Thunnus albacares), and banana prawn
(Fenneropenaeus merguiensis). While enolases from fish, shrimp, and chicken have been identified as
IgE-binding proteins and, in some cases, linked to mediator release (Khanaruksombat, 2014; Kuehn,
2013; Andreassen, 2009), they do not correspond to the major allergens in fish or prawn (Kamath,
2023). Similarly, the enolases identified in this analysis—Sal s 2, Pan h 2, and Thu a 2—are not
classified as major allergens (Ruethers, 2021; Faisal, 2019; Kuehn, 2014). Enolases are ubiquitous and
among the most abundant cytosolic glycolytic enzymes, highly conserved across taxonomically diverse

organisms, including humans (Morales-Amparano, 2021). Despite their high sequence conservation
across taxonomical groups, widespread clinical cross-reactivity between enolases from all organisms
producing homologs has not been reported. Cross-reactivity has primarily been observed between
enolases acting as aeroallergens from fungi and yeasts, as well as enolases acting as food allergens
within specific fish species (Morales-Amparano, 2021). As such, the matches to enolases derived from
food sources are not considered to present a significant risk of allergenicity in the context of NOVA.
Moreover, none of the enolase matches identified for T. reesei proteins exceeded 70% sequence
identity, further reducing the likelihood of clinically relevant IgE cross-reactivity.
In conclusion, the sequence homology analysis of T. reesei proteins present in NOVA at levels
exceeding 0.01% predominantly identified matches with proteins classified as aeroallergens and
contact allergens, with no major food allergens detected. While some matches were observed with
allergenic proteins from major allergenic foods, these were limited to minor allergens not associated
with severe allergic reactions or anaphylaxis. These minor allergens are primarily conserved across
diverse taxa due to their essential biological functions, reflecting their evolutionary importance rather
than a heightened potential for cross-reactivity. Although IgE binding has been reported for some of
these proteins, there is no evidence of widespread clinical cross-reactivity. Furthermore, none of the
matched proteins demonstrated greater than 70% sequence identity across their full length with the T.
reesei proteins in NOVA, a threshold generally associated with significant IgE cross-reactivity. This
indicates a minimal likelihood of clinically relevant cross-reactivity.
It is also important to note that allergenicity risk is dose dependent. Minor allergens are unlikely to pose
significant food safety concerns unless present in high concentrations (Abdelmoteleb, 2021). In the
case of NOVA, the T. reesei proteins in final products are expected to be present at concentrations
unlikely to elicit significant allergenic responses. Moreover, T. reesei has a well-established history of
safe use in food enzyme production, with no documented reports of food allergies linked to T. reesei-
derived proteins. This history, combined with the outcomes of the sequence homology analysis, strongly
supports the conclusion that proteins from T. reesei in NOVA, other than ovalbumin, do not present a
significant allergenic risk. The allergenicity concern posed by ovalbumin, as detailed throughout this
document, will be addressed by clearly labeling all food products containing NOVA to indicate the
presence of egg, in accordance with the requirements of the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer
Protection Act (FALCPA) (Public Law 108-282) and Section 403 (w) of the FD&C Act.

2.1. Description and Characterization
The subject of this GRAS assessment is a standardized highly pure (≥96%) lycopene
preparation, manufactured by genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain JZL03. This
strain is derived from the S. cerevisiae HESHEHG001 strain and has been genetically modified to
produce lycopene (see section 2.4). The recombinant strain JZL03 is constructed from the parental
strain HESHEHG001. Lycopene is produced by fermentation of genetically engineered S.
cerevisiae JZL03, followed by extraction and recovery (downstream processing), and final product
treatment. It is a red to dark red powder that primarily consists of lycopene (≥96%) that is identical
to lycopene found in tomatoes. Lycopene is a type of organic pigment called carotenoid. It is
related to beta-carotene and gives some vegetables and fruits (e.g., tomatoes) a red color. General
descriptive characteristics of lycopene are summarized in Table 1. The sensory requirements shall
meet the specifications outlined in Table 1.

In order to ensure a consistent and safe product, Hesheng Technology has established food

Lycopene is an acyclic, nonpolar hydrocarbon chain, consisting of a C40 isoprenoid
skeleton and 2 open-end rings with relative molecular mass of 536.89 Dalton and CAS Registry
number 502-65-8. Similar to other carotenoids, each of the polyene chain double bonds of
lycopene could exist in cis or trans conformation, resulting in a large number of geometric isomers.
However, the vast majority of carotenoids exist in the all-trans configurations. Lycopene contains
thirteen double bonds. Naturally occurring carotenoids are in the all-trans-configuration. Storage,
cooking, food processing and exposure to light may result in some isomerization of the all trans
form to various cis forms including the 5-cis, 9-cis, 13-cis, and 15-cis forms. All-trans form of

lycopene predominates in foods, while the cis isomers, along with trans isomers, are common in
human blood and tissue. Specifically, in human plasma all-trans-lycopene and 5-cis-lycopene have
been identified as the most abundant lycopene isomers (Hadley et al., 2003). All-trans lycopene is
a red crystalline powder with a melting point of 172-175ºC that is soluble in fats and certain organic
solvents but insoluble in water ethanol and methanol. Lycopene is classified as a non-provitamin
A carotenoid, with other examples being lutein and zeaxanthin.

2.4.3 Biosynthetic Pathway of Lycopene
S. cerevisiae does not naturally produce lycopene, but it can synthesize farnesyl
pyrophosphate (FPP), a precursor for lycopene bio-synthesis. The production of lycopene from
FPP requires three enzymes, geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) synthase, phytoene synthase,
and phytoene desaturase.
The biosynthetic pathway of lycopene is described as follows:
Acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase, and then to
HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA) by HMG-CoA synthase. HMG-CoA reductase
then reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid (MVA). After multiple enzymatic steps, MVA is

converted to FPP.
FPP is then converted to GGPP under the catalysis of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate
synthase. Phytoene synthase catalyzes the synthesis of phytoene from GGPP. Finally, phytoene is
dehydrogenated to lycopene by phytoene desaturase.

(2) Stability of Target Gene Transcription Levels:

3.3. Natural Sources and Intake
The primary source of natural lycopene in the human diet is tomatoes and products derived
from it. Additionally, fruits like pink grapefruit, water melon, rosehip, papaya and guava are also
sources of lycopene (Nguyen and Schwartz, 1999). Lycopene from tomatoes, synthetic lycopene
and lycopene synthesized by the fungus B. trispora are permitted for uses in food. In the US, over
80% of dietary lycopene intake is derived from processed tomato products such as ketchup, tomato
juice, spaghetti sauce, and pizza sauce (Clinton, 1998). The amount of lycopene present in
processed foods is often much higher as compared to that found in fresh foods, as processing often
involves concentration via water loss. Tomatoes and tomato-based products are the major and the
best sources of lycopene in the human diet. A list of tomato products with lycopene is given n
Table 8, while main dietary sources of lycopene are given in Table 9.
As mentioned earlier, lycopene is present in human diet, primarily in dark red fruits and
vegetables, such as tomatoes, watermelons, and sweet red peppers. Thus it has been ingested for
hundreds of years from foods without any harmful health effects. The available information
suggest that a 130 g serving of fresh tomatoes contains 4-10 mg of lycopene, while ketchup
contains 3.3 mg per tablespoon. The mean level of lycopene consumed from food is estimated as
8 mg/day. Lycopene is available as dietary supplement (2,446 labels found) and it is most often
used by adults in doses of 15-45 mg by mouth daily for up to 6 months. As per 21 CFR 73.585,
tomato lycopene extract; tomato lycopene concentrate are approved as color additive. Tomato
lycopene is included in EAFUS list, it is also recognized by Flavor and Extract Manufacturers
Association as GRAS ingredient (FEMA No.: 4110).

6. PART VI- NARRATIVE
The safety determination of lycopene produced by genetically engineered S. cerevisiae
strain JZL03 is based on the totality of the available evidence, including animal experimental
studies, in vitro studies, human studies of naturally occurring and synthetic lycopene, as well uses
of lycopene as a food ingredient. As lycopene preparation (≥96% pure), the subject of this GRAS
determination, produced by S. cerevisiae, is substantially similar to lycopene naturally present in
food, derived from tomato and synthetic, the available safety database that exists for lycopene and
its preparation can be applied to establish the safety of lycopene preparation. The FDA raised no
questions in response to GRAS notices submitted for use of lycopene derived from Blakeslea
tripspora (GRN 173), tomato lycopene (GRN 185; GRN 156), and synthetic lycopene (GRN 119)
for use in numerous foods. Similarly, European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has extensively
evaluated the safety in use of lycopene as a food color, and the included sources of lycopene were
tomatoes, synthetic lycopene and lycopene synthesized by the fungus B. trispora. Studies of acute
oral toxicity, subchronic toxicity, chronic toxicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity,

genotoxicity and carcinogenicity were included in the EFSA evaluation. In an expanded abstract
on safety of lycopene, Trumbo (2005) from FDA concluded that dietary lycopene intake at levels
typically consumed in the US appears to be safe among the general healthy population.
For the present GRAS assessment, efforts have been made to present both the data
supporting safety of lycopene as well as any data on potential adverse effects. An attempt has been
made to interpret these findings from relevant studies as they relate to the present GRAS
assessment. The assessment of efficacy studies is limited to a review of the results related to safety
and tolerability. For this assessment, a comprehensive search of the scientific literature was
conducted through December 2024 to identify publications on the safety of lycopene. In the
following sections, relevant biological and toxicological studies on lycopene are described that
provide support for the conclusions reached in this determination.

6.2.1. Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion of Lycopene
The available information suggest that fat soluble carotenoids, such as lycopene, are
absorbed in the intestine and transported in chylomicrons to the blood stream via the lymphatics.
Several studies related to the absorption, distribution and excretion of lycopene from various
sources, including natural lycopene from tomato concentrate and synthetic lycopene, have been
performed. The findings from animal and human intervention studies with tomato extract as
lycopene source and with synthetic lycopene indicate that lycopene from these sources is
bioavailable. The bioavailability of synthetic, formulated lycopene is comparable to tomato-based
lycopene (Cohn et al., 2004; Hoppe, 2003). It is expected that lycopene from S. cerevisiae when
used in food products of comparable composition will be bioavailable to a similar extent as
lycopene from tomatoes.
Bioavailability of lycopene can be affected by several factors, including food processing
and dietary composition (Story et al., 2010). Lycopene occurs in several forms in fresh plant foods,
including carotenoid-protein complexes in chloroplasts or in crystalline form inside chromoplasts.
Thermal processing generally improves lycopene bioavailability by disrupting cellular membranes,
which allows lycopene to be released from the tissue matrix. The available evidence suggest that
lycopene from thermally processed tomato products is more bioavailable than lycopene from fresh
tomatoes. The absolute amount of lycopene absorbed does not appear to vary greatly with dose.
Inter-individual differences, not dose, has the greatest impact on the amount of lycopene absorbed.
Lycopene bioavailability is greatly affected by dietary composition. Given that lycopene is a lipid-
soluble compound, consuming it with fat increases its bioavailability. In vivo studies indicate that
the cis-isomers of lycopene appear to be more bioavailable than the all-trans isomer. Diwadkar-
Navsariwala et al. (2003) reported that the lack of toxicity of high doses of lycopene may be due
to the fact that lycopene absorption has an upper limit of saturated concentration and is not
absorbed when the dose exceeds 60 mg.
Lycopene GRAS Page 23 of 46 Hesheng Technology
Following ingestion, lycopene must first be released from the food matrix before it is
incorporated into mixed micelles (Story et al., 2010). The available information indicate that
lycopene was absorbed by the same route as dietary lipids, i.e., passive diffusion. Subsequent
studies reported that lycopene absorption can be facilitated by a cholesterol membrane transporter
known as scavenger receptor class B type I. Once inside the enterocyte, lycopene is packaged with
other dietary lipids into chylomicrons that are transported across the basolateral membrane and
make their way into the lymphatic system, which eventually releases chylomicrons into the blood.
Competition with other carotenoids or cholesterol may also influence lycopene absorption.
The available studies suggest that lycopene is stored in human organs at varying degrees
(Kun et al., 2006). Lycopene is found in the highest concentrations in the liver, testes, adrenal
glands, and adipose tissues, while it is found in lower concentrations in the kidney, ovary, lung,
and prostate. The available data indicate that in rats lycopene is absorbed in systemic circulation

and is distributed to the tissues in similar pattern as seen in humans. Tissue levels of lycopene in
rats are comparable with that in humans. This also suggest that rat can be considered as a useful
and appropriate animal model for lycopene studies.
In a recent review article on lycopene digestion, absorption, metabolism, and excretion,
Arballo et al. (2021) reported that majority of lycopene is cleaved eccentrically by the enzymes ß-
carotene oxygenase 2 (BCO2), yet further research is needed to probe the enzymatic cleavage
activity at the tissue level. Additionally, results indicate that single nucleotide polymorphisms and
dietary fat influence lycopene absorption and thus modify its health effects. These investigators
noted, high inter-individual variability in lycopene levels in humans, attributed in part to food
preparation procedures, differential bioavailability depending on the presence of co-consumed
dietary fat, and differences in genetic polymorphisms associated with lycopene absorption and
metabolism.
6.2.2. Specific Corroborative Studies
In a series of unpublished toxicity studies, potential adverse effects of lycopene preparation,
subject of present GRAS, containing >96% lycopene were investigated. These safety studies of
lycopene preparation included, acute toxicity, and mutagenicity and genotoxicity (Ames test, in
vitro mammalian chromosome aberration test and in vivo mammalian micronucleus test). All
studies were conducted according to the China National Food Safety Standards (known as Guo Jia
Biao Zhun, or GB Standards). Translated copy of the study report was provided by Hesheng
Technology.
6.2.2.1. Acute Toxicity of Lycopene Preparation
In an unpublished acute oral toxicity study, conducted as per National Standards of the
People’s Republic of China: GB 15193.3-2014 National Food Safety Standard - Acute Oral
Toxicity Test, oral toxicity of lycopene preparation was evaluated in SPF healthy adult SD rats.
For this study, lycopene preparation from Hesheng Technology was used. In this study, 20 (10/sex)
adult Specific Pathogen-Free (SPF) Sprague-Dawley rats were used. The test was carried out as a
limit test and only one dose group was included. Purified water was used as the solvent and the
test article was prepared immediately before use. Lycopene preparation was administered by a
single oral gavage at a dose of 10 g/kg bw. Onset time, extent and duration of changes in animals
were comprehensively observed and documented to evaluate possible target organs of toxicity.
Observations were made on the skin, hair coat, eyes, mucous membranes, and respiratory, urinary,
digestive, and nervous systems.
Lycopene GRAS Page 24 of 46 Hesheng Technology
Rats were observed for toxicity immediately after administration, and the onset time and
end time of toxic symptom as well as death were recorded. The observation period was 2 weeks.
Euthanasia was performed on animals that were moribund, suffering from severe pain, and still
alive at the end of test. Oral gavage administration of lycopene preparation did not result in
significant toxicity or death in the animals during the 14-day observation period. Weight
measurements on days 7 and 14 post-dose showed weight gain in surviving animals. The animals
were euthanized at the end of the test, and no abnormalities were found in gross necropsy. The
LD for the acute oral toxicity test of lycopene preparation is >10 g/kg bw. The findings from this
50
study suggest that lycopene preparation was actually non-toxic in the acute oral toxicity test in rats.

6.2.2.2. Mutagenicity and Genotoxicity Studies of Lycopene Preparation
6.2.2.2.1. Bacterial Reverse Mutation Test of Lycopene Preparation
This test was conducted as per National Standards of the People’s Republic of China:
Bacterial Reversion Mutation GB15193.4-2014. The bacterial reverse mutation was conducted
using five standard histidine-deficient Salmonella Typhimurium mutant strains (TA97a, TA98,
TA100, TA102, and TA1535). Rat liver microsomal enzymes (S9 mixture, 0.5 ml/dish) induced
by a combination of phenobarbital sodium and β-naphthoflavone were used as the in vitro
metabolic activation system. Five dose groups (5000, 2000, 1000, 500, and 200 µg/dish) were
tested in the pilot test. The results showed no significant difference in background bacterial lawn
between each dose group and the untreated control group, indicating that the test article did not
induce bacterial toxicity to the test strains at doses of 5000 µg/dish and below. Based on the pilot
test results, 5 dose groups (5000, 1582, 500, 158, and 50 μg/dish) were set up for the main test,
along with an untreated control group, a solvent control group (DMSO), and a positive mutagen
control group.
In the formal and validation tests, lycopene preparation precipitation was not observed after
the addition of test solutions in ≤ 5000 µg/dish groups with or without metabolic activation. There
was no significant difference in the background lawn of each test strain between each dose group
and control group, indicating that the test article had no bacterial toxicity at doses ≤ 5,000 µg/dish.
The number of revertants for each test strain in each dose group did not exceed 2 times as compared
with the untreated control group with or without metabolic activation. No dose-response
relationship and no test points with reproducible positive results were observed. The mean number
of revertants for each test strain in the positive control group was over 2 times that in the untreated
control group, showing a significant positive reaction. These findings indicate that the lycopene
preparation did not induce an increase in the number of reversion colonies for the five strains.
Lycopene preparation is negative for the bacterial reverse mutation test.
6.2.2.2.2. In Vitro Mammalian Chromosome Aberration Test of Lycopene Preparation
This assay was conducted in accordance with the People’s Republic of China: National
Food Safety Standard - In Vitro Mammalian Chromosome Aberration Test GB 15193.23-2014.
For this test, the Chinese hamster lung (CHL) cell line was selected. The rat liver microsomal
enzyme (10% S9 mixture) induced by phenobarbital sodium and β-naphthoflavone served as the
in vitro metabolic activation system. DMSO was used as the vehicle. The maximum available
solubility of the sample was approximately 160 mg/ml. Cells were treated with lycopene
preparation at concentrations (doses) of 100, 200, 400, and 800 µg/ml for 4 hours without
metabolic activation, with purified water as the vehicle. The results showed that the test article did
not affect cell count. Cell viability in the 100, 200, 400, and 800 μg/ml groups at the end of culture

were 96.12%, 103.88%, 75.19%, and 58.14%, respectively. Additionally, cells were also treated

with the same concentration of lycopene preparation and without metabolic activation, for 24 hours.
The results showed that the lycopene preparation did not affect cell count. Cell viability in the 100,
200, 400, and 800 μg/ml groups at the end of culture were 102.20%, 95.60%, 71.98%, and 56.59%,
respectively. Based on the results of the pilot experiment, three dose groups (200, 400, and 800
µg/ml) were set for the formal test along with a vehicle control group (DMSO) and two positive
control groups [without S9 mixture: methyl methanesulfonate (MMS, 20 µg) /ml), with S9
mixture: cyclophosphamide (CP, 10 µg/ml)].
The results of three test conditions (without or with S9 for 4 hours, and without S9 for 24
hours), lycopene preparation solution did not affect the cell observations and counts in the 200,
400, and 800 µg/ml groups. After 4 hours of treatment with and without S9, the chromosome
aberration rates of CHL cells were 2.0% and 2.0% in the vehicle control group, and 1%, 2%, 1%,
and 2%, 2%, 0% in the lycopene dose groups, respectively. There was no significant difference in
the chromosome aberration rate between the lycopene dose groups and vehicle control group. The
chromosome aberration rates of CHL cells in the positive control groups (MMS and CP) were 9%
and 9%, respectively, which was significantly higher than those in the vehicle control group. As
regards after 24 hours of treatment with and without S9, the chromosome aberration rate of CHL
cells was 0% in the vehicle control group, and 2%, 0% and 2% in the lycopene dose groups,

lycopene dose groups and vehicle control group. The chromosome aberration rate of CHL cells in
the positive control group (MMS) was 9%, which was significantly higher than that in the vehicle
control group. The findings from this study demonstrate that lycopene preparation does not cause
chromosome aberration in CHL cells under the test conditions.
6.2.2.2.3. In Vivo Mammalian Micronucleus Test of Lycopene Preparation
In a study in mice effects of lycopene preparation on micronucleation in immature
erythrocytes was investigated. The study was conducted as per National Standards of the People’s
Republic of China: GB 15193.5-2014 National Food Safety Standard, effects on incidence of
micronucleation in immature erythrocytes of mice. For this study, SPF Kunming mice (25/sex;
weighing 25-30 g) were used. For this study, three dose groups for treatment with lycopene
preparation were set, i.e., low dose (1250 mg/kg bw), intermediate dose (2500 mg/kg bw), and
high dose (5000 mg/kg bw). Animals in the positive control group were administered
cyclophosphamide by oral gavage at 40 mg/kg bw. The test article (lycopene preparation) was
administered via gavage twice within 30 hours, that is, a second dose was administered 24 hours
after the first dose by oral gavage.
Animals were observed once a day for changes in the skin, hair, eyes, mucous membranes,
respiratory system, circulatory system, nervous system, limb activities and behavior. For sampling,

the animals were euthanized by cervical dislocation 6 hours after the second dose. Once blood and
muscles were removed, the sternum was cut transversely to expose the medullary cavity. The
sternal bone marrow was squeezed out using a small hemostat, dropped onto the calf serum at one
end of the slide and mixed thoroughly. The smear was prepared using a push technique.
The smear was air dried after spreading, the slide specimen was fixed in methanol for 5 to
10 min and air dried, stained with Giemsa, and microscopically examined. Areas with intact,
evenly dispersed, and properly stained cells were selected under low magnification and then
observed under oil immersion microscopy. A total of 2,000 polychromatic erythrocytes (PCEs)

were counted per animal. The number of micronucleated PCEs was also counted to calculate the
incidence of micronucleation by the following formula: Incidence of micronucleation (‰) =
Number of micronucleated PCEs/total number of PCEs x 1000. The number of immature
erythrocytes among 200 erythrocytes (PCE+NCE) was counted for each animal to calculate the
percent of immature erythrocytes as follows: Percent of immature erythrocytes (%) =
PCE/(PCE+NCE) x100.
During the treatment period, no animal death or significant abnormal changes were
observed in the activities, feed intake, water intake, and defecation of animals in each group. The
percent of PCE in each dose group of the test article and the positive control group was not lower
than 20% of that in the solvent control group, and the difference was not statistically significant.
This suggest that the test article, lycopene preparation, has no inhibitory effect on bone marrow
cells of female and male Kunming mice.
The incidence rates of PCE micronuclei in the bone marrow of female and male mice in
the solvent control group were 1.3‰ o and 1.4‰, respectively. The incidence of PCE micronuclei

6.2.2.3. Summary of Specific Toxicity Studies of Lycopene Preparation
In summary, the product specific studies did not reveal any adverse effects of lycopene
preparation. In acute toxicity in rats, the LD of lycopene preparation was >10 g/kg bw indicating
50
that lycopene preparation is practically safe. In mutagenicity and genotoxicity studies as evaluated
by Ames assay, in vitro mammalian chromosomal assay and in vivo mammalian micronucleus
assay was negative. Although these studies are not yet published, the findings from all these studies
corroborate the safety of lycopene preparation, the subject of this GRAS determination.
6.2.3. Animal Toxicity Studies

In multiple animal toxicity studies, potential adverse effects of lycopene has been
investigated. An overview of the available animal toxicity studies of lycopene derived from
different sources is provided in Table 11. In an acute toxicity study, the oral LD value of lycopene
50
in mice was assessed to be higher than 3000 mg/kg bw (Milani et al., 1970). The source of lycopene
used in this study is not specified in the publication.
In a subchronic toxicity study, Jonker et al., (2003) investigated the toxicity of lycopene
derived from a fungal biomass (B. trispora). In this study, lycopene, as a suspension in sunflower
oil (20% w/w) was fed at dietary concentrations of 0, 0.25, 0.50, and 1.0% to groups of Wistar rats
(20/sex/group) for a period of 90 days. Lycopene intake was calculated to be 0, 145, 291, and 586
mg/kg bw/day in control through high-dose males and 0, 156, 312, and 616 mg/kg bw/day in
control through high-dose females. The results from this study do not provide any evidence of
toxicity of lycopene at dietary levels up to 1.0% as demonstrated by the findings of clinical

observations, neurobehavioral observations, motor activity assessment, body weight and food
consumption measurements, ophthalmoscopic examinations, hematology, clinical chemistry,
urinalysis, organ weights, gross pathology, or histopathology. The NOEL from this 90-day oral
toxicity study with lycopene extracted from B. trispora was determined as 1.0% in the diet (586
mg lycopene/kg bw/day in males and 616 mg lycopene/kg bw/day in female), the highest dietary
concentration tested.
In the published literature, multiple animal toxicity studies of lycopene have been reported
(Table 11). In these studies effects of lycopene derived from sources such as tomato, Blakeslea
trispora and synthetic have been used. These studies included short-term, subchronic, genotoxic
and reproductive toxicity of lycopene. In three subchronic toxicity studies, no significant
toxicological findings were reported in male and female rats following 13 weeks (Mellert et al.,
2002) 14 weeks (McClain and Bausch, 2003) following oral exposure to synthetic lycopene and
in male and female Sprague Dawley rats following 13 weeks exposure to tomato oleoresin extract
(East, 1995). In all these studies NOAEL corresponded to the highest dose tested i.e., 300 mg
lycopene/kg bw/day (Mellert et al., 2002), 500 mg/kg bw/day (McClain and Bausch, 2003) and
270 mg lycopene/kg bw/day (East, 1995).
In the thirteen-week studies by Mellert et al. (2002), effects of synthetic lycopene 10
CWDO and Lyco VitO 10% were investigated. Lycopene 10 CWDO was administered to male
and female Wistar rats (10 rats/sex/group) at doses of 0, 500, 1500, or 3000 mg/kg bw/day. Lyco
VitO was administered at doses of 0 or 3000 mg/kg bw/day. Red discoloration was seen in the
jejunum and cecum of the treatment groups, but there were no histopathological changes. The

NOAEL for both products was 3000 mg/kg bw/day, equivalent to 324 mg synthetic lycopene/kg
bw/day.
In several additional studies in mice, rats and dogs that lasted for 2 weeks to 10 months,
effects of oral exposure to lycopene (naturally occurring and synthetic) at doses up to 1000 mg/kg
bw/day were investigated. These studies are summarized in Table 11. Regardless the source of
lycopene, the totality of the evidence suggest that lycopene is well tolerated and there were no
adverse effects on mortality, body weight gains, food consumption or clinical observations. With
the exception of few studies where discolored tails in few animals was noted, no changes in coat
appearance was noted at doses of dietary exposure up to 60 mg lycopene/kg bw/day (Zhao et al.,
1998). In other studies, treatment related effects on major organs were limited to slight pigment
accumulations in the liver and kidney in small groups of rats fed 10 to 20 mg lycopene/kg bw/day
for 200 days and in one dog administered 100 mg lycopene/kg bw/day for 192 days (Zbinden and
Studer, 1958).
In a publication on safety of synthetic lycopene as a water-dispersible beadlet formulation
containing antioxidants, McClain and Bausch (2003) described acute and subchronic safety studies,
reproductive studies, genotoxicity studies, metabolic studies, and exploratory studies on the
hepatic uptake of lycopene. These investigators reported that lycopene has a low order of acute
toxicity and no significant toxicity has been observed in rats treated with lycopene beadlet
formulations in the diet at doses of up to 500 mg/kg bw/day for 14 weeks or 1000 mg/kg bw/day
for 4 weeks. No teratogenic effects were noted in a rat two-generation study (1000 ppm in the diet)
or in a teratology study in rats with 1000 mg/kg bw/day lycopene as beadlet formulations. It was
noted that lycopene accumulates in hepatocytes and to a lesser extent in spleen. In short-term
studies with synthetic lycopene, as a beadlet formulation, and natural source lycopene, as tomato
concentrate, the accumulation of lycopene in the liver and the presence of pigment deposits in the

6.2.4. Mutagenicity and Genotoxicity Studies
In an unpublished study described in GRN 173, potential genotoxic effects of lycopene
derived from B. trispora (20%) was investigated in bacterial (Salmonella typhimurium strains
TA1535, TA1537, TA98, TA100 and Escherichia coli strain WP2 uvrA) and mammalian (human
lymphocytes) test systems. In these studies no increase in revertant colony counts of any of the
strains, either in the presence of or absence of S9 mix was noted. Similarly no statistically
significant increase in the incidence of cells with chromosome was noted. These findings indicate
that lycopene 20% showed no evidence of genotoxicity. Additionally, naturally occurring and
synthetic formulations of lycopene were investigated in in vitro bacterial (Salmonella typhimurium
and E. coli strains) and mammalian (mouse lymphoma cells and human lymphocytes) test systems,
as well as in vivo with mice and rats. In the in vitro studies, consistently negative results were
reported (He and Campbell, 1990; Rauscher et al., 1998; Aizawa et al., 2000; McClain and Bausch,
2003).
The degradation products of crystalline lycopene, as a result of being exposed to light and
air, were shown to exhibit some mutagenic activity. Mutagenicity testing of formulated lycopene
using mouse lymphoma cells did not reveal increase in mutant frequency with lycopene (McClain
and Bausch, 2003). These investigators reported that unformulated pure crystalline lycopene and
lycopene as a 10% beadlet formulation are not genotoxic as determined in a comprehensive battery
of tests, however, improperly stored, unformulated crystalline lycopene can degrade to mutagenic
products if exposed to light and air. There was no evidence of clastogenicity or DNA damage in
mouse peripheral blood or rat hepatocytes, respectively following oral administration of synthetic
lycopene formulation (McClain and Bausch, 2003). Oral exposure to naturally occurring lycopene
Lycopene GRAS Page 31 of 46 Hesheng Technology
did not induce chromosomal damage in mouse bone marrow cells (Rauscher et al., 1998) or DNA
damage in human lymphocytes (Pool-Zobel et al., 1997; Collins et al., 1998; Riso et al., 1999).
6.2.5. Human Studies with Lycopene
In a systematic review and meta-analyses, Tierney et al. (2020) determined the effects of
consuming dietary and/or supplemental lycopene on cardiovascular risk factors. In this review and
analysis, 43 studies were included. Lycopene interventions were highly variable (supplement with

or without food, based as tomato juice/paste/raw product, or combined with olive oil), the dose
ranged from 1.44 to 75 mg lycopene/day and was not reported in 11 of 43 included studies. The
duration of effect studied was considerable and lasted from 30 min to 6 months. Studies reported
conflicting findings for the effect of lycopene on cardiovascular risk factors. This was supported
by meta-analyses where there were no significant differences between lycopene intervention and
control groups for blood pressure and lipids (total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol,
and triglycerides). This was observed for overall groups and in subgroup analyses for individuals
with elevated risk factor concentrations at baseline. Lycopene interventions for cardiovascular risk
factors were highly variable across studies in both the dosage provided and the mode of delivery
(supplement or food based). No adverse effects of lycopene were reported.
In another review, Shao and Hathcock (2006) reviewed the available human studies of
lycopene. For this risk assessment, the inclusion criteria were: study duration; at least 1 week,
lycopene dose; not less than 8 mg/day, and study design; only randomized, placebo-controlled
intervention trials (Table 12). Studies that were uncontrolled and unblinded and studies
investigating acute bioavailability, pharmacokinetics or post-prandial responses from single bolus
doses were excluded. Studies that did not quantify the administered dose of lycopene (such as
certain feeding studies) were also excluded. In total, 16 human safety studies were included, in
which the highest lycopene dose was 150 mg/day (for 7 days) and the longest study duration was
20 weeks (the lycopene dose was 13.3 mg/day). None of the clinical trials found an adverse effect
related to lycopene administration. Hence, no LOAEL or NOAEL could be established and Upper
Limit (UL) could not be set.

In GRN 173, several clinical studies of lycopene from different sources have been
evaluated. In 12 clinical trials, ranging from 1 to 16 weeks, effects of lycopene (natural and
synthetic) have been investigated. In these studies, anthropometric and biochemical measurements,
including body weight, full blood counts, and immune function and liver function tests, did not
reveal any abnormalities in subjects supplemented with lycopene capsules or lycopene rich foods
at levels ranging from 0.5 mg/day for 4 weeks to 75 mg/day for one week. The tolerance of
lycopene supplementation was investigated in healthy individuals as well as in prostate cancer
patients. Administration of lycopene at doses ranging from 12 to 75 mg/day (approximately 3 to
20 times normal dietary intake) were generally well tolerated.
6.2.5.1. Adverse Effects in Humans
There is not much information on the adverse effects of lycopene in humans. High intakes
of lycopene-containing foods has been reported to result in lycopenemia, characterized by an
orange discoloration of the skin. All cases of lycopenaemia reported in the literature followed
excessive ingestion of lycopene in foods. In a case report, a 61 year old woman who had consumed
about 2 L of tomato juice daily for several years reported the incidence of lycopenemia (Reich et
al., 1960). Although there was evidence of lycopene and fatty deposits in the liver, there was an
absence of measurable hepatic dysfunction. After 3 weeks of consuming a diet free of tomato juice,
the orange discoloration faded. Shaw and Koti (2009) reported another case of a 40 year old
woman presented with orange discoloration of both palms while the rest of her skin, her sclera and

other mucous membranes were normally colored. She consumed tomatoes and tomato-based
dishes roughly 5 times per week for 3 years, totaling on average 1.4-1.8 kg of tomatoes weekly.
The subject was advised to reduce her tomato intake to 0.5-0.9 kg per week. At a follow-up
examination 2 weeks later, the discoloration had faded, and by 4 weeks it had completely
disappeared.
Recently, Tanaka et al. (2022) reported a rare case of carotenoderma due to lycopenemia
caused by the excessive intake of lycopene-rich vegetables and fruits. These investigators
examined a hematoxylin-eosin-stained specimen from the patient and tape-stripped samples by
fluorescent microscopy with 488 nm wavelength emission and compared them with normal skin
samples. Notably, the patient's samples showed a weaker autofluorescence in the stratum corneum
and sweat glands. Furthermore, carotenoid concentrations in the patient's skin was measured
noninvasively and a higher score than the average of 24 healthy volunteers was noted. This case
further highlights that the excessive intake of lycopene causes carotenoderma and demonstrates
that carotenoid deposition is particularly pronounced in the stratum corneum of the skin.
6.2.6. Uses and Regulatory Status
Lycopene has been authorized by the EFSA (E 160d) as a food additive, with an acceptable
daily intake of 0.5 mg/kg bw/day, regardless of source (EFSA, 2008). FDA has also approved
lycopene use as a natural food and beverage colorant in concentrations within 5 and 70 mg/kg of
food (WHO, 2007). In addition, it is included in the Codex General Standard of Food Additives
(GSFA) and as such, it can be used in food products under conditions of good manufacturing
practices. As per the classification of the WHO for hazard compounds, lycopene belongs to the
compounds of “very low” toxicity. Because of the lack of adverse effect data for lycopene in

animals or healthy humans, the Institute of Medicine (IOM, 2000) did not set a tolerable upper
intake level for lycopene.
6.2.6.1. FDA Review of Lycopene GRAS Notices
As mentioned earlier, lycopene has been the subject of four GRAS determinations
evaluated by FDA and issued no question letters. In the first GRAS notice (GRN 119), BASF
Corporation determined that synthetic lycopene is GRAS, through scientific procedures, for use as
a direct food ingredient in breakfast cereals, drinks, instant soup, low fat dressings, meal
replacements, meatless meat products, nutrient bars, salty snacks, crackers and yogurt at levels
ranging from 5 to 70 mg/kg of food. BASF described synthetic lycopene as a crystalline material
derived from chemical synthesis and describes a three-stage process for this chemical synthesis.
Synthetic lycopene is stored under nitrogen or suspended in an aqueous solution containing
antioxidants to prevent oxidation and isomerization of lycopene. The commercial product is
prepared as Lycopene 10 Percent (powder spherical particles in a food starch coated matrix of
gelatin and sucrose), Lycopene 10 Cold Water Dispersion (CWD), and Lycopene Dispersion 20
Percent (lycopene in vegetable oil). Product specifications include 96% lycopene, limits on total
carotenoids, arsenic, lead, copper, zinc, and heavy metals, loss on drying and residue on ignition.

BASF estimates the 90th percentile intake of 11 mg/person/day from the proposed uses and is
comparable to the intake of lycopene from plant sources.
In the GRAS notice, BASF discusses published and unpublished studies related to the
potential toxicity of synthetic and natural lycopene. Based on findings from a 13 week published
study a published 13-week oral toxicity study in rats, the NOAEL for synthetic lycopene was
determined as 324 mg/kg bw/day. The NOAEL is approximately 4000-fold higher on a body
weight basis than the mean EDI of synthetic lycopene. Additionally, no adverse effects were
reported in a developmental toxicity study conducted in rats and rabbits fed lycopene products. No
mutagenic effects were observed in unpublished genotoxicity studies conducted with BASF's
lycopene products. Furthermore, no adverse effects were observed in several published clinical
studies conducted with either BASF's lycopene products or natural lycopene. BASF discussed
published human studies related to the bioavailability of natural lycopene and synthetic lycopene
products. Findings from these studies showed no adverse effects on the absorption of other
carotenoids. BASF noted that excessive intake of food or dietary supplements high in carotenoids
or lycopene has been associated with carotenodermia and lycopenodermia, respectively. Based on
the information provided by BASF, as well as other information available to FDA, the agency did
not question BASF’s conclusion that synthetic lycopene is GRAS under the intended conditions
of use.
In addition to the above mentioned first GRAS notice on synthetic lycopene, subsequently
FDA received three GRAS notices on lycopene derived from other sources. These included tomato
lycopene extract (GRN 156); lycopene from Blakeslea trispora (GRN 173); and concentrated
tomato lycopene extract (GRN 185). In these GRAS notices, product related information such as
description, specification, manufacturing, intended uses and resulting intake, and safety related

use of lycopene in food. All these GRAS notices received no question letter from FDA.
Concentrated tomato lycopene extract containing at least 90% lycopene was the subject of

principal carotenoid of the extract. Additionally, in GRN 185 published and unpublished acute and

6.2.7. Safety of Production Strain
S. cerevisiae has a safe history of use in food and belongs to a species that is known not to
produce toxins. S. cerevisiae is considered GRAS for use in brewing, baking and winemaking
industries (21 CFR §172.896). The genome of S. cerevisiae has been extensively studied and it has
been determined that the yeast is free of known pathogenicity traits. In addition, several genetically
modified S. cerevisiae strains for use in fermented beverages have received letters of no objection
from the US FDA (GRN 120, GRN 175, GRN 350, GRN 798 and GRN 841). The FDA has not
questioned the manufacturer's GRAS conclusion for the intended uses of the following enzyme
preparations produced by S. cerevisiae strains.
S. cerevisiae species has been included in the Environment Protection Agency (EPA) list
as a recipient microorganism that is eligible for exemptions from EPA review under the Toxic
Substances Control Act and/or expedited EPA review (40 CFR 725.420). This inclusion is based
upon the demonstrated lack of adverse effects for this species. It has been determined that the
introduction of genetic material in this species would not increase the potential for adverse effects,
provided that the genetic material is limited in size, well-characterized, free of certain sequences
and is poorly mobilizable. As per EFSA, yeasts used in food production, particularly
bakers/brewer's yeast, are considered among the safest of microorganisms. In Europe, S. cerevisiae
has been designated Qualified Presumption as Safe (QPS) status, indicating that no additional
safety assessment is needed according to the established guidelines. The JZL03 host strain belongs
to the S. cerevisiae species which has been used for over 7,000 years by humans in fermented
beverages. Given this background, it can be concluded that species will remain safe, even after
genetic transformation, as long as the transformation does not introduce new or changed
capabilities for harmful effects.
As discussed earlier, the subject of this GRAS lycopene is derived from recombinant S.
cerevisiae strain JZL03. This strain is constructed from S. cerevisiae HESHEHG001 and
incorporates 13 genes, including 8 target genes and 5 marker genes. As explained in Part 2.5, all
transferred gene DNA fragments from recombinant S. cerevisiae JZL03 in three batches of the
final product lycopene were below the limit of detection. Additionally, the residual protein levels
in three batches of the final product, was found to be below the quantitation limit of 17 mg/kg,
suggesting the absence of residual protein in the final product lycopene. In addition, Hesheng also
assessed the bioinformatics and potential allergenicity of all exogenous proteins:

FOREWORD
MoreMeat (Guangzhou) Biotech Co., Ltd. (“MoreMeat”) is dedicated to discovering and developing
strains of fungi capable of efficiently producing target proteins. Utilizing advanced microbial and
synthetic biology technology platforms, MoreMeat aims to meet the growing demand for alternative
proteins and health foods by producing fungal proteins and health foods at lower costs and with greater
sustainability. MoreMeat specializes in producing mycoprotein, which is the subject of this GRAS
notification. Mycoprotein can be used as an ingredient or macronutrient.
At MoreMeat's request, Anchor Center for Certification (ACC) convened an Expert Panel to complete
an independent safety evaluation of this mycoprotein preparation.
ACC primarily focused on composite safety information, i.e., scientific procedures with corroboration
from the history of use. The review covered the production strains and identity information,
safety/toxicity studies of mycoprotein, the history of use of mycoprotein, and compositional details,
specifications, and method of manufacture of MoreMeat mycoprotein. A thorough search of the
scientific and regulatory literature was conducted through February 8, 2025, with particular attention
paid to adverse effect reports and those that supported safety conclusions. Pertinent references from
this review are listed in Part 7. The integration of safety/toxicity studies, supported by the history of
use and dietary exposure information, ultimately forms the specific scientific basis for the GRAS
conclusion.

Part 2 IDENTITY, METHOD OF MANUFACTURE, SPECIFICATIONS, AND PHYSICAL
OR TECHNICAL EFFECT
This section reviews and cites publicly available information, alongside the information provided by

the manufacturer, MoreMeat (Guangzhou) Biotech Co., Ltd, pertaining to the composition,
manufacturing process, and specifications of this mycoprotein, which is the subject of this GRAS
determination.
2.1 Identity of Ingredient
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein ingredient is derived from submerged liquid aerobic fermentation of
Fusarium compactum. This mycoprotein consists of the mycelial network of the fungal microorganism
F. compactum MM-135. Under well-controlled cultivation conditions, F. compactum MM-135 grows
into a filamentous mat of mycelial biomass, referred to as a “biomat”, with a texture profile similar to
that of muscle fibers.
F.compactum MM-135 was isolated from soil of Shennongjia, Hubei Province, China and subsequent
identification was performed in-house by MoreMeat (as described further, below). Morphological
study shows that fungal cells are arranged in a filamentous pattern to form hyphae and that there are
separations between the cells. The average length of hyphae is 800~1500 μm, the hyphae are usually
branched, and the large conidia are sickle-shaped or long cylindrical, with more transverse septums.
The hyphae may cross and entangle to form a reticular structure (Figure 1).

Numerous molecular phylogenetic studies over the past two decades have indicated that morphological
species recognition frequently fails to distinguish many fusaria that have been discovered by
employing genealogical concordance phylogenetic species recognition (GCPSR sensu Taylor et al.
2000); therefore, MoreMeat has taken a polyphasic approach to further verify the strain through
sequence analysis of four Fusarium-ID genes. These four genes include internal transcribed spacer
region (ITS), translation elongation factor I (TEF1), RNA polymerase I (RPB1), and RNA polymerase
II (RPB2) genes (Geiser et al. 2004; Park et al. 2010; O’Donnell et al. 2010; O’Donnel et al., 2013).
MoreMeat employed the Polyphasic identification from the FUSARIOID-ID database to identify F.
compactum MM-135 using these four genes. Result of DNA sequence comparison from these four
genes shows that F. compactum MM-135 shares the greatest sequence homology with F. compactum
LLC 2178, with a similarity of 99.82%.
Furthermore, MoreMeat collected TEF1, RPB1, RPB2, and ITS sequences from all strains of multiple
subspecies in the FUSARIOID-ID database (www.fusarium.org) and analyzed the evolutionary
position of the F. compactum MM-135 by constructing a multigene phylogenetic tree. The subspecies
includes Fusarium incarnatum-equiseti species complex (FIESC, to which F. compactum belongs to),
Fusarium sambucinum species complex (FSAMSC, to which F. venenatum belongs to), and Fusarium
solani species complex (FSSC, to which F. strain. flavolapis belongs to). The steps for multigene
phylogenetic tree analysis are as follows: First, use MAFFT (version v7.310) to perform multiple
sequence alignment for each gene; then, use GBLOCKS (version 0.91b) to prune the multi-sequence

alignment result file; and finally use AliView to manually prune. After pruning, the sequences of the
four genes were concatenated. IQ-TREE (version 2.2.5) was used to construct a multigene
phylogenetic tree based on the concatenated sequences. The tree below (Figure 2) is drawn by ggtree.
As the closest species of MM-135 is Fusarium compactum, MoreMeat verifies and concludes that the
production organism indeed is Fusarium compactum.

Preparation of medium and raw materials
The raw materials used in mycoprotein fermentation are commonly used in the food, fermentation, and
enzyme production industries. All raw materials are of food-grade standards and the filters used are
food-contact safe and/or listed in 21 CFR as approved food-contact materials. None of the materials

This process is the first critical control point of the whole production process. All raw materials are
inspected batch by batch according to internal procedures and review of the corresponding certificate
of analysis provided by the supplier before release to production. Subsequently, raw materials are
filtered through a 60-mesh stainless steel sieve to remove impurities; this step prevents physical
hazards from raw materials entering the production process. After, the fermentation medium is either
sterilized at 115-121℃ for 20-30 minutes or filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane, which
prevents microbial contamination from raw materials entering the production process. Only the

Inoculation
The production strain master and working banks are prepared under sterile conditions (in the Biosafety
Anchor Center for Certification (ACC) Page 14 of 94
GRAS Notice –
Mycoprotein MoreMeat GRAS Submission Date: February 24, 2025
cabinet) and tested for microbial purity by plating and observing the morphology of the resulting
colonies. The production strain is inoculated into seed culture medium and enlarged by two runs of
seed culturing. The first run is conducted in a 50-mL bioreactor, and the second run is then conducted
in a 1000-mL bioreactor, respectively. The seed culture medium includes glucose as major carbon
source, yeast extract as major nitrogen source, as well as potassium dihydrogen phosphate, magnesium
sulfate, and calcium chloride. Strain purity is monitored by morphological tests on individual colonies
that have been picked from the seed cultures and grown on plates. The entire operation is carried out
using aseptic technology under sterile conditions.
Fermentation
Before fermentation begins, the pre-sterilized fermentation tank is configured with a temperature range
of 20–35°C, an agitation speed of 50–300 rpm, a ventilation rate of 0.5–2 VVM, and a pH range of
4.0–7.0. The whole fermentation process takes place in a closed system to prevent any cross-
contamination. Fermentation medium includes corn starch (10-100 g/L), citric acid (1-10 g/L),
ammonia (1-20 mL/L), ammonium sulfate (1-10 g/L), phosphoric acid (0.1-10 g/L), sodium hydroxide
(0.1-10g/L), α-amylase (1 g per 1 kg corn starch), glucoamylase (1 g per 1 kg corn starch), and vitamins
and minerals listed in Table 3.
Heat treatment
After fermentation, the fermentation broth is transferred to a heat treatment tank and is treated at 60-
90℃ for 10-30 minutes. The heat treatment inactivates the F. compactum and enzymes, if any, while
reducing the RNA content. The final product is tested for RNA content and microbial limits to ensure
no live F. compactum is present in the final product.
Heat treatment processing is the second critical control point. The production organism F. compactum
is inactivated in this process and, as a result, MoreMeat’s final product mycoprotein does not contain
live F. compactum or active enzymes. The control limits are the heat treatment’s temperature and time
parameter. If the production process deviates from the set parameters, all involved product will be
quarantined and evaluated by the quality management team.
Filtration and cooling
After heat treatment, the fermentation broth is filtered with a vacuum drum filter to remove excess
water and to cool the product. The vacuum drum filter has a pore size of 400 mesh and operates at
0.04-0.08 mPa pressure. The residues of the raw material are removed via the filtration process.
Packaging
The product is packaged in an aluminum foil bag and vacuum sealed, or other food-grade packaging
material provided the stability results meet the required standards.
Store in freezer at -18℃
The product is stored at -18℃ before shipping to customers.

Disposal of production wastes
Fusarium species are well researched with many published studies. It is of interest because numerous

species are important plant pathogens. (Balajee et al. 2009, Geiser et al. 2013, Nelson, 1981). For this
reason, MoreMeat implements stringent HACCP plan to control and screen mycotoxins in its
production process, as well as strict waste management to prevent environmental contamination. All
solid and liquid wastes contaminated with F. compactum are sterilized prior to disposal. All solid waste
from production is collected by qualified third-party contractors for disposal. Wastewater is collected
and sent to the local wastewater treatment facility for proper treatment as per the local regulations. The
release of treated wastewater complies with National Standard GB 18918 Discharge Standard of
Pollutants for Municipal Wastewater Treatment Plant.
MoreMeat manufactures mycoprotein using a non-genetically modified F. compactum. Furthermore,
the absence of production organism and control of RNA residue is verified in three non-consecutive
batches (See Table 5). These precautions taken are to ensure that the mycoprotein product is of the
highest quality and safe for human consumption.
2.3 Quality Control
2.3.1 In-process Quality Control
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is manufactured in compliance with Current Good Manufacturing Practices
(cGMP) and Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles. MoreMeat’s prerequisite
programs are written according to the cGMP components listed in US FDA 21 CFR Part 117 Subpart
B. These GMP programs establish conditions and practices that MoreMeat follows when producing
mycoprotein under sanitary conditions.
In addition, the food safety plan for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is developed in compliance with the
requirements defined in the US FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA). Potential hazards
arising from raw materials/processing aids and each manufacturing step are reviewed and evaluated.
Based on MoreMeat’s HACCP plan, there are two identified critical control points for the production
process. The first critical control point is the preparation of medium and raw materials. Materials are
either heat sterilized or undergo sterile filtration before going into production. The purpose of this
process is to make sure no contaminating microorganism enters the production system. The sterile
conditions during fermentation are tightly monitored by production operators and online quality
assurance personnel. The second critical control point is the heat treatment. During the heat treatment
process, the production organism F. compactum is inactivated and, as a result, MoreMeat’s final
product mycoprotein does not contain live F. compactum or active enzymes.
Allergen management and control procedures are implemented and executed at the warehouse,
production, and packaging areas. The quality system established at MoreMeat is certified by the
globally recognized food safety verification program Food Safety System Certification FSSC 22000.

do not impact product safety, and the additional test parameters help to ensure that potential
contaminants are characterized and controlled.

MoreMeat’s mycoprotein contains a high‐quality protein as indicated by an average Protein
Digestibility Adjusted Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS) of 1.00 out of 1.00. (See Appendix 4 for

recommended by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and World
Health Organisation (WHO) for evaluating protein quality.

Part 6 NARRATIVE
Extensive information relating to product identity, nutritional composition, digestibility, potential
contaminants and by‐products, allergenicity, and toxicology have been assessed to determine the safety
of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein and the basis for its GRAS status. Safety studies, including toxicology
studies commissioned by MoreMeat, as well as published literature on similar Fusarium‐derived
products, have indicated that there are no acute or chronic exposure concerns from the consumption of
mycoprotein. Additionally, the available literature provides evidence that compositionally similar
Fusarium‐derived products support normal growth and development in animals and humans. An
allergenicity evaluation was conducted through a literature search in concert with testing conducted by
MoreMeat, the results of which have been reviewed by an independent allergenicity expert. It has been
concluded that F. compactum does not present additional significant risk for allergenicity to foods
containing mycoproteins. Furthermore, there are no impurities or secondary metabolites that present a
safety concern from the consumption of mycoprotein, even at relatively high intake levels. The
culmination of these data supports the conclusion that MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is GRAS for use in
food, as detailed in the following sections.
6.1 Substantial Similarity of Mycoprotein to The Subject of GRN 000904 and GRN 000945
In exploring the potential use of fungal proteins in food ingredients, it is important to recognize the
significant impact of different production strains on product properties, nutritional content, and by-
products. The production microorganism F. compactum belongs to the same genus as the Fusarium
strain flavolapis (formerly known as F. novum. yellowstonensis) described in GRN 000904 and which
received a “no questions” letter from FDA in 2021, and the F. venenatum described in GRN 000945
and which received a “no questions” letter from FDA in 2022. For this reason, we compared the
similarity between the Fusarium-derived ingredients described in the two previous GRAS notifications
to MoreMeat’s F. compactum production organism in terms of strain, manufacturing process, and
product specifications. The safety studies of GRN 000904 and GRN 000945 can be used as pivotal
safety information for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.
6.1.1 DNA Sequencing Comparison
The phylogenetic tree described in Part 2 demonstrates that there are genetic similarities between F.
compactum MM-135, F. venenatum, and Fusarium strain flavolapis. F. compactum MM-135 is closer
in genetic similarity to F. venenatum (the production organism described in GRN 000091 and GRN
000945) than F. strain flavolapis (the production organism described in GRN 000904) is to F.
venenatum.

When comparing the production processes of these three fungal proteins, it was found that their
fermentation procedures, heat deactivation treatments, and storage environments are essentially the

6.2 Toxicology Studies Commissioned by MoreMeat
6.2.1 Genetic Toxicity Studies
As part of the safety evaluation for a new food ingredient, genotoxicity studies are performed to
determine if the ingredient has the potential to cause genetic damage. MoreMeat has assessed
mycoprotein for potential genotoxic effects using an AMES test, an in vivo Mammalian Erythrocyte
Micronucleus test, and an in vitro Mammalian Chromosome Aberration test. The three tests
unanimously concluded that MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is nongenotoxic under the tested conditions. In
addition to these tests, a review of the genotoxicity evaluations for other Fusarium‐derived products
also provides no evidence of genotoxic effects of mycoproteins.
6.2.1.1 Bacterial Reverse Mutation Test (Ames) of MoreMeat’s Mycoprotein
To assess the mutagenic potential of mycoprotein, an Ames assay was conducted at the GLP compliant
laboratory - Chemical Toxicity Testing Institute of the Shanghai Municipal Center for Disease Control
and Prevention. The study was conducted in accordance with the OECD Guideline for the Testing of
Chemicals No. 471. The assay utilized plate incorporation and pre-incubation methods to evaluate the
mutagenic potential of mycoprotein on Salmonella typhimurium strains TA97a, TA98, TA100, TA102,
and TA1535, all of which are histidine-dependent. The evaluation was conducted with and without
metabolic activation using a chemical-induced rat liver S9 mix. The test substance was formulated as
a solution in sterile water (0.0158, 0.05, 0.158, 0.5, 1.58, 5, 15.8 and 50 mg/mL) to provide
corresponding dose levels of up to 5000 μg/plate.
The pre-experiment with plate incorporation method was conducted with mycoprotein at dose levels
of 15.8, 50, 158, 500, 1580 and 5000 μg/plate, but serious precipitate occurred in the 5000 μg/plate.

Therefore, the initial test with the plate incorporation method was conducted with mycoprotein at dose
levels of 15.8, 50, 158, 500, and 1,580 μg/plate. For the confirmatory test, a preincubation modification
of the plate incorporation method was used. In this approach, the test or control substances were first

the mixture was combined with overlay agar and poured on minimal agar plates. The plates were
handled in the same manner as in the initial test, with incubation at approximately 37 °C until adequate

Five different concentrations were tested for all strains, thus adequately evaluating bacterial

6.2.1.2 In Vivo Mammalian Erythrocyte Micronucleus Test
The in vivo mammalian erythrocyte micronucleus test for mycoprotein derived from F. compactum
MM-135 was conducted according to the OECD Guideline for the Testing of Chemicals No. 474
Mammalian Erythrocyte Micronucleus Test (2016) by the GLP compliant laboratory - Shanghai
Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention. The in vivo micronucleus assay in mammals
was performed to assess the genotoxic potential of the mycoprotein from F. compactum MM-135 by
detecting any chromosome damage or effects on the mitotic apparatus. Mice were weighed and the
prepared test solutions of different concentrations and the positive control solution were
administered to each group of animals at a dose of 10 mL/kg body weight. Comparisons between
the micronucleated cell frequencies in the treated groups and the negative control revealed no
significant differences. Consequently, mycoprotein derived from F. compactum MM-135 yielded a
negative outcome in the mammalian erythrocyte micronucleus test, indicating no in vivo genotoxicity
under the conditions of the study. It is concluded that mycoprotein from F. compactum MM-135 does
not exhibit mutagenicity related to clastogenicity and/or aneugenicity based on the in vivo mammalian

Co., Ltd.) were randomly divided into four groups (5/sex/group) and fed diets containing 0, 50,000,
100,000, and 150,000 ppm of mycoprotein, i.e., 3866, 8343, and 12,150 mg/kg/day for males, and

conducted, with detailed clinical observations once daily. Rats were weighed on Days 3, 7, 10, 14, and
15 (pre-necropsy). Food consumption was measured daily, and food efficiency was calculated as Food
efficiency = (Mean Daily Body Weight Gain) / (Mean Daily Food consumption). Clinical pathology
