6.4 Overarching Basis for Comparing Toxicological Profiles
Based on generally recognized methods for evaluating toxicity in Fusarium, MoreMeat has determined
that F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum grown under controlled conditions possess
the same toxicological potential or lack thereof. This conclusion is based on an assessment of
similarities from a phylogenetic and compositional standpoint, as well as similarities and differences
in their potential and actual production of toxic secondary metabolites. This determination is consistent
with generally recognized methods for read-across of biological substances and is additionally based
on well-established literature and methods for evaluating the production of toxic secondary metabolites
in Fusarium as detailed below. MoreMeat’s determination can readily be verified by the scientific
community using generally recognized methods of toxicity assessment for Fusarium and mycotoxins,
as well as publicly available genetic data on F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum. This
conclusion is further corroborated by the results of unpublished studies on MoreMeat’s mycoprotein
derived from F. compactum, which include in vitro and in vivo genotoxicity studies and a 14-day in
vivo study.
6.4.1 Read-across Precedent
Within FDA GRAS precedent, there is a well-accepted practice of leveraging toxicological data from
a prior GRAS Notice whereas here -- there are clear compositional and phylogenetic similarities
between the notified substance and the subject of prior GRAS Notices. In fact, numerous successful
GRAS Notices have incorporated this approach to supporting their GRAS conclusions for novel
proteins and other complex biological substances, see e.g., GRN 000737, GRN 000811 and GRN
000904. Thus, it is MoreMeat’s view that our approach of referencing pivotal studies and data from
GRN 000091 and GRN 000904 to support a GRAS conclusion for F. compactum in our present GRAS
Notice aligns with FDA precedent.
Further, in recent successful instances of “read-across” in the GRAS context, FDA has accepted
reasoning based, in part, on the generally recognized methodology outlined by Pariza and Johnson
(2001). Although originally intended for assessing the safety of modified organisms for enzyme
production, the decision-tree approach advanced by Pariza and Johnson can effectively apply more
broadly to novel protein production, including the safety of secondary metabolites, as evidenced by
GRN 000737 for soy leghemoglobin protein derived from Pichia pastoris (Jin et al., 2018).
While the decision-tree methodology from 2001 has largely focused on modified strains of the same
species lineage, advancements in bioinformatics and “omics” that have occurred over the twenty years
since Pariza and Johnson’s publication now allow scientists to similarly assess distinct species for their
common lineages and shared evolutionary relationships to inform toxicology assessments (Pielaat et
al., 2013). Toxicology experts and regulatory agencies in the U.S. and other developed nations are
increasingly incorporating these modern approaches, particularly metabolomics (the systematic
identification and quantification of small molecule metabolic products in their safety assessments of

distinct species; Rivetti et al., 2019; Viant et al., 2019; Sauer et al., 2010).
As such, and consistent with methods outlined in the decision-tree approach and modern
bioinformatics, our assessment of the safety of F. compactum has focused on understanding its

phylogenetic and compositional relationship to F. strain flavolapis and F. venenatum, as well as a
comparison of the toxicological potential of F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum. The
evaluation described in further detail below is grounded in published data on: a) the genetic pathways
and regulation of toxic secondary metabolites in Fusarium, b) analytical methods for quantifying
mycotoxins, and c) established safe exposure limits to mycotoxins.
6.4.2 Overarching Similarity of F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum
Our multi-faceted comparison of F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum clearly indicate
strong similarities between the species pertinent to understanding their toxicological potentials and
supportive of “read-across” to pivotal toxicology studies on F. strain flavolapis and F. venenatum.
These similarities are summarized as follows:
 Phylogenetics: F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum are all Fusarium spp. and
members of closely related clades, as described in Section 2.1. and Section 6.1.1.
 Composition: Mycoprotein derived from F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum
have similar nutritional and protein profiles, as discussed in Table 33 Nutritional Profile
Comparison.
 Intended Use: The mycoprotein ingredients derived from Fusarium spp. are intended for use as a
replacement for animal-based and plant-based proteins in the human diet, as discussed in Section
Part 3 dietary exposure of this notification, though at different levels and different food categories.
 Toxicological Potential: Similarities and differences in the potential and actual production of toxic
secondary metabolites by F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum are well
understood through generally recognized methods of genetic analysis and analytical testing, as
discussed in further detail below.
 Toxic Effect: The assessment of toxicological potential is corroborated by a battery of in vitro and
in vivo toxicology studies, additionally discussed below.
6.4.3 Genetic and Analytical Basis of Similar Toxicological Profiles
As stated in GRN 000904’s response to FDA’s inquiry (Toxicology Question 1), GRN 000904 outlined
a well-established phylogenetic, genomic, and analytical approach to support the general recognition
of similar toxicological profiles between Fusarium species. MoreMeat has followed the same
approaches for determining that F. compactum has the same toxicological potential or lack thereof as

6.4.4 In vitro & in vivo Basis of Similar Toxicological Profiles
While there is no genetic or analytical evidence that F. compactum produces mycotoxins at levels of
concern for food safety when MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is consumed under the intended uses, there
also is strong evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies that further corroborate our conclusion that F.
compactum has a toxicological potential similar to or less than that of F. strain flavolapis and F.
venenatum.
In vitro Basis of Similar Toxicological Profiles
As described in the above section, MoreMeat’s mycoprotein has been tested using a battery of in vitro
toxicity assays that have been shown to be sufficient to detect carcinogens and in vitro toxicity in
rodents (Kirkland et al., 2011) and are used to support the safety of human consumption (FDA 2007).
These tests would be expected to detect harmful effects from potentially unknown secondary
metabolites commonly associated with filamentous fungi (Pariza and Johnson, 2001).
Testing found no significant increase in DNA mutation rate (Ames tests; OECD 471), similar to the
results from the Ames test on mycoprotein derived from F. strain flavolapis and F. venenatum which
showed non-mutagenicity (Furey, 2022; Miller, 2001), when both metabolically active and inactive
bacterial cells were treated with the highest recommended concentration of mycoprotein derived from
F. compactum (5 mg / plate). Additionally, no significant increase in cell death or increase in the
number of micronuclei were observed in a mammalian erythrocyte micronucleus study (OECD 474)
in which mammalian erythrocyte cells were treated with the highest concentration of mycoprotein

Together, results of the Ames test, chromosome aberration test, and micronucleus tests show that

In vivo Basis of Similar Toxicological Profiles
Finally, the published in vivo results for substantially similar mycoprotein ingredients, which indicate
a lack of acute and chronic adverse effects, are further corroborated by the 14-day in vivo oral toxicity
tests in rats fed with high amounts of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, as described in Section 6.2.2. The test
identified no physical or gross morphological differences between controls and rats fed MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein up to 12,150 mg/kg/day for males, and 12,499 mg/kg/day for females.
6.4.5 Conclusion of Similar Toxicological Profiles
Based on the foregoing similarities and assessment of the extensive published and peer-reviewed data

on Fusarium toxicity and F. compactum toxicity, as well as the data on F. strain flavolapis toxicity and
F. venenatum toxicity, we have determined that F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum
have the same toxicological potential or lack thereof, when grown under controlled conditions, and
that the read-across to pivotal data cited in GRN 000091 and GRN 000904 for F. venetanum and F.
strain flavolapis offers sound scientific support for our conclusion that the consumption of MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein under the proposed conditions of use is safe to a reasonable certainty.
6.5 Allergenicity
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is produced using F. compactum MM-135, a species of the Fusarium
incarnatum-equiseti species complex. To comprehensively evaluate its potential allergenic risk,
MoreMeat conducted a risk assessment, including:
a) A literature search to identify published evidence of allergy to food and environmental
protein sources of various Fusarium species, of IgE binding and allergy to specific proteins
from these sources, or of cross-reactivity to other sources with high sequence identity to
Fusarium proteins.
b) The stability of the proteins in the strains was tested in simulated gastric fluid (SGF) and
simulated intestinal fluid (SIF) assays.

c) MoreMeat conducted a genome sequence of their production organism, and the genome
sequence of this strain was evaluated to predict possible proteins and compared to
AllergenOnline.org version 22 to identify matches to allergen identities.
The purpose of this allergenicity assessment is to identify any potential additional food allergy risk
that may arise from consuming mycoprotein-containing foods that may be relevant to consumers who
are allergic to other protein sources. Obviously, most food sources present some food allergy risk, so
the results of this assessment are not expected to show that there is no risk of allergic reaction, but
rather to predict risks arising from the consumption of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.
The genome of the F. compactum MM-135 production strain was sequenced by MoreMeat using an
Illumina NextSeq 2000 Sequencer. The analysis indicated that the genome could express 12,548
proteins based on gene prediction and annotation of the DNA. In March 2024, we evaluated whether
the predicted amino acid coding regions matched allergen sequences listed in the
www.AllergenOnline.org database version 22 (AOLv22, sequences were collected from NCBI). We
compared the predicted protein sequences using FASTA-35.4.12 to provide matches of >35% identity
over 80 or more amino acids. We also compared the sequences to the NCBI non-redundant protein
database (NR) using BLAST+ version v2.13.0.
The Codex Alimentarius Commission Guidance (2003) is utilized to evaluate the potential risk of food
allergens, as well as to assess the toxicity and nutritional properties of genetically modified (GM) food
crops with the addition of one or more genes. It is important to note that while the Guidance was
followed in this risk assessment, it was not meant to assess a novel organism intended to be used as
food ingredients and the mycoprotein reviewed is not a GM food crop. MoreMeat has adhered to the
Codex Alimentarius process for assessment, consistent with the approach taken for other novel food
ingredients, such as GRN 000904 and GRN 000945.
Through this assessment, MoreMeat has verified that F. compactum MM-135-derived mycoprotein

demonstrates no high identity matches to proteins with very high identity matches to clinically severe
allergens from common allergenic sources (e.g. Ara h 1, Ara h 2, Ara h 3, or Ara h 6 from peanut;
tropomyosin from shrimp; or beta-lactoglobulin from milk). The Codex guidance also recommends
reviewing published scientific studies on the allergenic potential of the novel protein with peer-
reviewed published studies related to allergies and allergens. The highest identity matches identified

6.5.6 Summary of Allergenicity of Fusarium compactum MM-135
Bioinformatics analysis of the F. compactum MM-135 genome revealed that the potential allergenic
proteins identified are commonly found in other Fusarium species, while their sequence similarity to
proteins in non-fungal species is low. F. compactum MM-135 does not contain sequence-matching
proteins in common allergens such as peanuts, sesame, soybeans, and seafood. The potential allergens
are likely limited to fungi or Fusarium spp. Consumers who are allergic to these fungal sources will
likely have allergy risks if they consume MoreMeat’s mycoprotein. Therefore, products made with
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein should include appropriate food labels clearly indicating that they contain
proteins derived from Fusarium fungi.
A search of the literature for evidence of allergy to Fusarium proteins showed that some people do
develop allergic reactions to several proteins from this species when the fungus invades human tissues,
most commonly the lungs or sinuses. In addition, based on the evidence from QuornTM, a small number
of people may develop IgE-mediated allergic reactions to the ingestion of QuornTM proteins (derived
from F. venenatum), which is used in large amounts in foods as a source of protein. These reactions
are not surprising, as most foods containing large amounts of protein do cause allergies or adverse
reactions similar to allergies in some consumers. Some cross-reactions are possible, as consumers
become allergic to related proteins after inhaling homologous proteins from Aspergillus or Penicillium.
Four proteins have been identified as allergens from both Fusarium species and are recognized by the
WHO/IUIS Subcommittee on Allergen Nomenclature and are included in the AllergenOnline.org
database. However, three of them are marked as putative allergens based on IgE binding only. There
is also an additional protein identified from AllergensOnline, but not in WHO/IUIS databases, which
is also recognized as a putative allergen based on IgE binding.
An important feature of reactions to QuornTM is the rare case of overt IgE-mediated allergy. There is
evidence that two people may have died from consuming QuornTM: individuals who were previously
sensitized to the fungus and who ate a patty-sized meal of QuornTM (Jacobson and DePorter, 2018).
Based on the fragmentary information provided by Jacobson and DePorter and references therein, it is
uncertain whether their deaths were due to an IgE-mediated reaction to the QuornTM proteins. The

reaction could have also been due to other possible proteins in the food (e.g., from eggs, milk whey,
etc.) Additionally, some individuals have reported occasional symptoms of vomiting or diarrhea after
consuming Quorn™ products, which may be attributed to the ingestion of large quantities of food that
are difficult to digest due to its high chitin content (Chitin is an N-acetylglucosamine polymer, an

6.7 Mycotoxins
MoreMeat has reviewed the publicly available literature on mycotoxins for similar food products. To
obtain a current, thorough, and comprehensive understanding of publicly available studies that support
the safe use of mycoprotein, literature searches were conducted using both PubMed and GoogleScholar
to identify relevant mycotoxins. The search terms “mycoprotein AND mycotoxins”, “Fusarium species
AND mycotoxins” and “Fusarium compactum AND mycotoxins” were used to identify published
studies conducted with mycotoxin to February 8, 2025.
Mycotoxins, a type of secondary metabolite produced by fungi, have a wide range of toxicity. Once

these toxins enter the food chain in large quantities, they are known to cause serious harm to animals,
humans, and the entire biological environment. Therefore, the detection of mycotoxins is essential to
ensure food safety and human health.
More than 400 varieties of mycotoxins have been identified to date. However, according to a previous
work that shows the distribution of the varieties of mycotoxin production in Fusarium species, different
Fusarium species have various abilities to produce mycotoxins (Munkvold, 2021; Wu, 2013). The
three predominant classes of mycotoxins synthesized by Fusarium species are trichothecenes

cyclonerodiol, which were reported from Fusarium compactum. Moreover, a type of zearalenone
analog, deoxynivalenol, is consistently regarded as a significant concern in the realm of food safety
(Ekwomadu, 2021).
Fusarium spp. reported by O’Donnell et al. (2018), among others, varies in the particular subsets of
known mycotoxins that those closely-related strains produce. The potential and actual variation in the
coding for and production of toxic secondary metabolites in Fusarium can readily be evaluated based
on generally recognized bioinformatics and analytical methods, as has been conducted on F.
compactum. As such, these sources do not contradict our determination that F. compactum, F. strain
flavolapis and F. venenatum have the same toxicological potential or lack thereof. Rather, the
references cited are corroborative of the analysis as discussed in Section 6.4, and instead show that:
 Each biosynthetic gene complex (BGC) produces a different mycotoxin;
 New mycotoxins have historically evolved by duplication and divergence of known BGCs;
 Genetic variation within a BGC can cause differences in mycotoxin expression levels, loss of
mycotoxin production, or loss of certain decorations to the core chemical backbone (Proctor et al.,
2006; Suga et al., 2018; Sultana et al. 2019); and
 Genetic variation within a BGC does not demonstrate the production of novel mycotoxins outside
of those already discovered.
MoreMeat has conducted extensive analysis to determine if any mycotoxins are produced by F.
compactum MM-135 using both genetic sequencing and analytical testing of the finished product

6.7.2 Enniatins
Enniatins are emerging mycotoxins synthesized by toxigenic microfungi mainly belonging to the
Fusarium spp., but also other genera such as Alternaria, Halosarpheia, and Verticillium (Pallares,
2020). These filamentous fungi are widespread pathogens of crops and represent a critical concern for
food and feed safety worldwide. To date, 29 ENN analogs have been isolated and characterized, and,
among them, ENNs A, A1, B, and B1 are most frequently found in cereals with cyclic
hexadepsipeptides (Meca, 2012).
Studies on enniatins by Meca et al. (2012) used duodenal fluid from the simulated gastrointestinal
digestion of 3 g of wheat crispy bread spiked with enniatin A, A1, B, and B1 at 1.5 and 3.0 μMol/g to

evaluate the intestinal absorption (transport profile) and bioavailability of these mycotoxins using a
two-compartment Caco-2 cell system. However, generally, the calculated enniatins bioavailability
percentages were below or around 50%, thus, half of the amount of the enniatins digested was not
transported across the intestinal barrier (Gautier, 2020).
The enniatins have ionophore properties and their toxicity mechanism is related to their ability to
transport cations across the cell membrane. Enniatins are cytotoxic, as they decrease cell viability,
promote cell cycle arrest, and increase apoptosis and the generation of reactive oxygen species in
several cell lines. They also cause changes at the transcriptomic level and have immunomodulatory
effects in vitro and in vivo (Hasuda, 2024). Toxicokinetic findings are limited, and despite the

For enniatins, the results support a genotoxic effect in bone marrow and liver cells after acute treatment,
but not after repeated exposure. Immunotoxic enniatins effects were observed in both genders,
suggestive of a suppressive/inhibiting activity particularly evident in males. Based on the repeated-
dose enniatins study, the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) for females is 0.18 mg/kg bw/day
(histomorphometrical effects on thymus, uterus and spleen). In male mice, the NOAEL is 1.8 mg/kg
bw/day (enterocyte vacuolization in duodenum, increased Reactive Oxygen Species, and reduced
glutathione brain levels). The maternal NOAEL is 1.8 mg/kg bw/day (decreased white pulp area and
increased red/white pulp area ratio in spleen) and the developmental NOAEL is 18 mg/kg bw/day
(Maranghi, 2018). The average enniatins levels determined in three representative lots of MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein result in a calculated mean and 90th percentile EDI of 0.001 µg/kg bw/day and 0.003
µg/kg bw/day, respectively, which are well below NOAEL.
Additionally, the calculated dietary exposure to enniatins from consumption of MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein is much lower than the CONTAM Panel estimated total chronic and acute dietary
exposures to enniatins, with mean exposure ranged from 0.42 to 1.82 μg/kg bw/day and the 95th
percentile exposure ranged from 0.91 to 3.28 μg/kg bw/day. The highest acute exposure estimates of
enniatins were 4.67 μg/kg bw/day (mean) and 10.1 μg/kg bw/day (95th percentile) (EFSA, 2014).
Therefore, the safety margins currently in place are not significantly altered by MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein when compared to existing consumption levels.
In summary, enniatins were identified in MoreMeat’s mycoprotein ingredient and were previously
found to be toxic in in vitro assays. However, published data indicate that half of the amount of digested
enniatins are not transported across the intestinal barrier in the duodenal fluid from the simulated
gastrointestinal digestion. Importantly, the resulting dietary exposure amount of enniatins from

MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is at a low level compared to the CONTAM Panel exposure estimates.
Consequently, there is reasonable certainty of no safety risks from the consumption of mycoprotein
derived from F. compactum MM-135 in relation to any anticipated enniatins residues. Furthermore,
MoreMeat has established maximum specifications for enniatins to minimize the risk of increased
consumer exposure.

Beauvericin is a common mycotoxin produced by various Fusarium spp. and occurs naturally on corn
and corn‐based foods and feeds. Currently, the EFSA has issued relevant risk assessment reports on
the contamination of beauvericin in cereals and their products. However, no regulatory or expert
authority has established a specific threshold of safety concern for beauvericin.
An evaluation of beauvericin on oral toxicity was implemented by EFSA in 2018, and is composed of:

6.8 Nitrates
Ammonia is used as fermentation ingredient, that means nitrates maybe generated during the
fermentation process and are the only possible source of input identified in mycoprotein production.
Nitrogen is an essential building block for the natural synthesis of amino acids and proteins.
Concerns about the safety of nitrate exposure have resulted in reviews by several authoritative bodies,
including JECFA and FDA. The established stablished safety levels for nitrate exposure compared with

estimated nitrates exposures from MoreMeat’s mycoprotein under the proposed conditions of use are
not anticipated to present a safety risk.
JECFA evaluated the safety of nitrates in conjunction with the safety of nitrites and nitrosamines on
the basis that, although nitrate can generally be considered to be of relatively low toxicity, nitrate can
be metabolized in the human body to form nitrite and N‐nitroso compounds can also be formed from
nitrite and N‐nitrosatable compounds under certain conditions (JECFA, 1995). In its most recent
evaluation in 2002, JECFA retained the acceptable daily intake (ADI) for nitrate of 0‐3.7 mg nitrate
ion/kg bw/day, which was first established in 1995 (JECFA, 2002). This ADI specifically addressed
concerns about the potential conversion of nitrates to nitrates. A reevaluation conducted by the EFSA
in 2017 maintained the ADI for nitrate at 3.7 mg/kg bw/day10.
As calculated in Section 3.6, the exposure to nitrates from consumption of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein
is estimated to be 0.592 mg/person/day (mean) and 1.304 mg/person/day (90th percentile). This
exposure is more than 400‐fold below the upper‐bound ADI established by JECFA, giving a
reasonable certainty of no harm from nitrates from the consumption of mycoprotein derived from F.
compactum.
In addition to the JECFA review, FDA and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) have
established safety thresholds for the presence of nitrates in drinking water. The drinking water standard
is 10 mg/L, measured as nitrogen (21 CFR 165.110). The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering,
and Medicine has determined that an adequate daily fluid intake is about 15.5 cups (3.7 L) of fluids
for men and about 11.5 cups (2.7 L) of fluids per day for women, of which about 20% is absorbed from
food11.
Assuming a fluid intake entirely from the tap or bottled plain water, the daily consumption of nitrate‐
nitrogen for men would be 29.6 mg/person/day (equivalent to 130 mg nitrate ion/person/day, as 1 mg
nitrate‐nitrogen = 4.4 mg nitrate). The consumption of nitrates from MoreMeat’s mycoprotein under
the proposed uses (i.e., 90th percentile EDI of 1.304 mg/person/day nitrate) is well below this level.
EPA also has established an oral reference dose (RfD) for chronic exposures to nitrate‐nitrogen of 1.6

mg/kg bw/day, based on critical effects seen in infants (equivalent to about 7.0 mg nitrate ion/kg
bw/day) (Jonas, 2001). As noted in Section 3.6, the 90th percentile EDI for nitrates is estimated to be
0.019 mg/kg bw/day from consumption of MoreMeat mycoprotein under the proposed conditions of
use. On these bases, there is reasonable certainty of no harm from the calculated exposure to nitrates
from consumption of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.

6.9 Ribonucleic Acid (RNA)
Another important consideration in the production of any mycoprotein intended for human
consumption is the nucleic acid content of the final product. Upon ingestion, purinic nucleic acids are
ultimately metabolized to the relatively insoluble uric acid. If uric acid levels exceed the excretion
capacity of the kidneys, the excess acid crystallizes in joints and soft tissues, leading to gout and kidney
stones (Sinskey, 1975).
The production organism F. compactum was isolated from the soil as a wild strain, thus genetic
modification concerns need not be addressed. During its production, the biomass of F. compactum is
subjected to heat treatment. By rapidly heating the fungal biomass in the broth to temperatures of 70-
90°C, and maintaining it for 20–30 min, the RNA content of the mycoprotein is reduced to less than
2%. The thermal treatment acts by degrading the RNA into monomers that diffuse out of the cells
(Raats, 2007) and are regularly consumed as a significant component of the human diet.
Importantly, the analysis of the 3 representative batches demonstrates an average RNA level of 0.02%
(Table 5), which is much lower than the 2% specification limit, and at a level similar to the RNA
present in mycoprotein product described in GRN 000904 (page 48).
As a core component in the structure of DNA and RNA, nucleic acids are abundant in all living
organisms. Yeast (baking) has a relatively high nucleic acid content, of approximately 10% of the dry
weight (Kihlberg R, 1972). Commonly consumed pig and beef have nucleic acid content of around 1-
4% and 2-6% of the dry weight, respectively (GRN 000904, page 48). In addition, MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein has the same maximum limit of RNA compared with the mycoprotein ingredients
described in GRN 000904 and GRN 000945 (which received “no question” letters from FDA). The
level of RNA in MoreMeat’s mycoprotein product is similar to or lower than levels present in common
foods and reported in previous GRAS notifications; therefore, there is reasonable certainty of no harm
from dietary exposure to RNA from consumption of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.

Mycoprotein’s nutritional composition and structure were the basis of research projects investigating
the effect of mycoprotein on human health. With billions of mycoprotein-based products consumed
over a 30+ year period in numerous countries around the world, there are very few published cases of
intolerance. Four clinical cases have been reported, which all suggest that patients who are allergic to
mold might react adversely to mycoprotein due to cross-reactivity (Katona, 2002; Hoff, 2003c; Van

As noted on page 28 of GRN 000945 and a publication written by Finnigan et al. (2019), the
mycoprotein manufacturer’s database indicates that 92% of reported illnesses are associated with GI
symptoms. In 2011, an Expert Panel was convened by Marlow Foods to review adverse reactions
related to mycoprotein and potential causes. The Panel concluded that gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms
were likely to be related to the high fiber content of mycoprotein. The panel hypothesized that in certain
individuals or under certain conditions, consuming mycoprotein could speed up the normal transit of
foods from the small to the large intestine. This could, in turn, cause the fiber in mycoprotein to be
fermented very rapidly in the large intestine, leading to symptoms of gastrointestinal distress of the
type reported by some consumers. Those at risk from this type of gut response may have an imbalance
in their normal gut bacteria, an unusual dietary intake of fiber (too low or too high), or may suffer from

irritable bowel syndrome (York Health Economics Consortium, 2015).

consumption of mycoprotein were identified, only a small portion of consumers suffered from these

I have carefully reviewed the documents on MoreMeat's Mycoprotein product that were
provided to me by the Anchor Center for Certification (ACC) of Shanghai, China. That includes the
overall description in the GRAS dossier, as well as the In Vitro digestibility report, the literature
research associated with Fusarium sp. and Neospora crassa including reports and papers on
Quorn.
My professional experiences and knowledge about allergy began in 1980-1985 when I
worked at Hollister-Stier Laboratories in Spokane WA, USA describing and characterizing allergen
extracts for diagnosis. Then a PhD and postdoctoral studies in immunology. I worked at Monsanto
from 1997-2004 on the allergenicity evaluation of genetically modified crops. I represented
biotechnology companies as a non-governmental organization representative during the CODEX
Alimentarius Committee meeting in 2001 in Vancouver, Canada. In 2004 I accepted a faculty
position at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in the Food Allergy Research and Resource Program
in the Dept. of Food Science and Technology and managed the 'tl'l'-lW.Allfil.genQnline.org database
from 2004-2023. In this database we review peer reviewed publications demonstrating lgE binding
or more importantly allergic reactivity to allergenic sources and specifically to proteins in the

sources. The database includes FASTA amino acid sequence comparisons for potential risks of
cross-reactivity. We have included a celiac protein database of glutenins and gliadins for risks
assessment. I was the Chairman of the WHO/I UIS Allergen nomenclature subcommittee from
2014 to 2022 where short names are given to proteins from food, airway, dermal and injectable
proteins that submitters claim lgE antibody binding from subjects with suspected allergies. It is not
a risk assessment database. I am a Fellow in the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and
Immunology since 2002 and member of the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology.
My laboratory has performed bioinformatics analysis and literature searches on many Novel
Foods and GM Os. We have evaluated serum lgE antibody binding on proteins suspected of allergic
cross-reactivity and performed basophil histamine release to evaluate whether there are at least
two lgE epitopes on some proteins. We have also tested the stability of proteins in Simulated
Gastric Fluid and Simulated Intestinal Fluid models.
As discussed by MoreMeat, the genus Fusarium has many species and types, a few have
been associated with some allergies, mostly from humans with lung or airway infections of some
species of the genus. As shown by gene and protein comparisons, many proteins, usually including
house-keeping proteins that are enzymes or functional membrane bound proteins are highly
conserved in sequences of Fusarium sp., Aspergillus sp., Penicillium sp. and other fungi. Literature
searches did not identify clinical allergy from the related Fusarium grouped species. The long
history of the population in the United Kingdom consuming Quorn, for 30 years and in the United
States for more than 10years with only rare reports of symptoms that might be food allergy have not
been proven. Some proteins from these fungi have been reported to be targets of lgE binding in
some studies, but usually without inhibition assays or controls of whole material extracts leaves an
incomplete picture of allergy. There is some proof that these fungi can decorate some of their
proteins with complex carbohydrates that are listed as CCD, cross-reactive carbohydrates. Those
do not cause allergic reactions as binding to lgE on basophils and mast cells is really low affinity
and rare.
There are four Fusarium sp. proteins listed in the WHO/I UIS Allergen Nomenclature
database, but those are common housekeeping proteins. AllergenOnline lists the four from
WHO/I UIS plus the P2 acidic ribosomal protein as an apparent allergen from Quorn. This was
determined by lgE binding protein from serum of one subject with asthma reaction after
consumption of Quorn. Hoff et al. (2003) describes this protein as a common minor allergen of a
number of mold species including Fusarium culmorum protein, though Quorn is from Fusarium
venenatum. Symptoms from ingestion in the UK were reported as 1 in 370,000 and in Switzerland
as 1 in 80,000 subjects with symptoms of gastric cramping beginning one hour to four hours after
ingestion. Based on skin prick tests of weak reactions and low level RAST lgE binding, they found
apparent reactivity across a wide range of fungi. The one subject had a history of 30 years of
perennial asthma. They performed double blind food challenge with Quorn and also clear testing
with cloned Fus c 1 and with Quorn extract. The lgE binding was cross-reactive but not equal and
there is no connection with understanding clinical allergic risks. The low reactivity of Quorn which is
a high protein content mycoprotein food ingredient indicates little risk for the population.
The genome of the species is referenced but not in a way that allows it to be seen. The

description of FASTA results states that no matches were identified to clinically severe allergens
such as the 2S albumins of peanuts or tree nuts, tropomyosin of crustacean shellfish, parvalbumin
offish or beta-lactoglobulin of cow's milk. In addition, the only reference to a described allergen in
Fusarium is the acidic ribosomal protein P2. And the relevance of that protein causing clinical
allergic responses has not been verified. 12,548 proteins predicted from the genome were
compared to AlergenOnline.org version 22. Protein sequences of this species were obtained
computer predictions of DNA sequences. The predicted protein amino acid sequences were also
searched against the whole protein database using BLASTP, to evaluate similarity of the proteins to
housekeeping proteins that are shared by most fungi. Proteins that have high identity matches to
Quorn proteins should be safe as few people are allergic to Quorn and the causative allergen(s)
have not been identified. Only 33 proteins have less than 60% identity to Quorn proteins and those
have high identities to other proteins that are from housekeeping genes. BLASTP was also used to
compare proteins to human proteins (Homo sapiens). Some of the Fusarium proteins including Fus
p 4 had 61% identity to a human protein, and other proteins had modest identities to human
proteins. Those are not like to be significant allergens.
Tests of stability of the mycoproteins in SGF showed that most of the proteins were
digested in pepsin in relatively short times. While that does not guarantee safety from allergenicity,
it is a good indication that most of the proteins are relatively instable in conditions broadly
mimicking the stomach and are less likely to be available for absorption and allergy in the small
intestine. A similar assessment was tested using Simulated Intestinal Fluid, which also showed
good digestion. These tests indicate the proteins are relatively unstable under conditions that
mimic human food protein digestion.
My overall conclusion is that this mycoprotein does not represent a likely risk for food
allergy based on history from literature, and lack of high identity matches to abundant and potent
allergens.

Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) Panel Consensus on the Safety
and GRAS Status of MoreMeat’s Mycoprotein for Use as an Ingredient
in Foods
EXPERT PANEL STATEMENT
An independent panel of experts (GRAS Panel), qualified by scientific training and experience to
assess the safety of food and food ingredients, was convened by the Anchor Center for Certification
(ACC) on behalf of MoreMeat (Guangzhou) Biotech Co., Ltd (MoreMeat). The panel conducted
a critical and comprehensive evaluation of the available data and relevant information to determine

whether MoreMeat mycoprotein, when used in selected conventional human foods, is safe and
Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) under the conditions of its intended use. This determination
was made in accordance with scientific procedures outlined in the Federal Food, Drug, and
Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), as specified in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (21 CFR)
§170.30(b).
The GRAS Expert Panel convened on December 12, 2024, and unanimously concluded that
mycoprotein, as specified in the document "GRAS Determination for the Use of MoreMeat
Mycoprotein in Selected Conventional Foods," is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) based
on scientific procedures. This conclusion applies when mycoprotein is used as an ingredient in
conventional foods as a protein source and is manufactured in compliance with cGMP. A
summary of the basis for the GRAS Expert Panel’s conclusion is provided herein.
Summary and Basis for a GRAS Conclusion
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is produced by fermentation of Fusarium compactum MM-135. The
finished product contains ≥ 43% protein (on a dried basis). MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is intended
for use in processed food products (excluding infant formulas and meat or poultry products) as a
protein source, serving as a substitute for other animal- or plant-based proteins.
The GRAS Panel independently, collectively, and critically examined MoreMeat’s GRAS
dossier for mycoprotein as well as publicly available scientific information and data compiled
from the literature and other published sources and searches of published scientific literature
conducted through December 2024. The data evaluated by the GRAS Panel included information
pertaining to the methods of manufacturing and product specifications, analytical data, intended
use levels, consumption estimates, and comprehensive literature on the safety of mycoprotein.
Composition
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein derived from F. compactum is substantially similar to the mycoprotein
derived from Fusarium venenatum and Fusarium flavolapis, as described in GRN 91 and GRN
904. MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is a dietary source of protein, and its product specifications were
developed based on the monograph for mycoprotein derived from F. venenatum included in the
14th Edition of the Food and Chemical Codex (FCC 14th).
Analytical data provided in MoreMeat’s GRAS dossier for mycoprotein confirms three non-
consecutive batches meet or exceed the finished product specifications. In addition, MoreMeat
has established sufficient and appropriate maximum specification for potential contaminants,
including RNA, mycotoxins, heavy metals, and microbes.
The Expert Panel discussed the potential of the presence of diacetoxyscirpenol (DAS) in the
finished product. While DAS was not detected in representative batches, and while genome
sequencing does not indicate an increased likelihood of DAS formation, the Expert Panel notes
that MoreMeat plans to monitor DAS levels in their mycoprotein at least biannually and has a
response plan in place should detectable levels of DAS be found.
MoreMeat has also presented data on amino acid composition, nutrient composition, nitrate and
nitrite content, and protein quality in the GRAS dossier. The Expert Panel has reviewed the data
and concurs that MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is a dietary source of amino acids and nutrients,
and—based on the reported Protein Digestibility Adjusted Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS)—a
high-quality protein.
Additionally, the Expert Panel notes that while a 3-month accelerated stability study has
concluded, long-term stability testing for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is ongoing. The available
stability data presented in MoreMeat’s GRAS dossier indicate that the finished product is stable

under the recommended storage conditions (i.e., frozen). While MoreMeat has concluded that
these results support a 12-month shelf-life when stored in a vacuum-sealed aluminum bag at -
18°C, the Expert Panel notes that the shelf-life should be re-evaluated by MoreMeat as additional
long-term stability data becomes available.
Production Strain
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is manufactured from the fermentation of non-genetically modified F.
compactum MM-135, which is naturally found in soil. MoreMeat states that F. compactum is
non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic.
MoreMeat collected TEF1, RPB1, RPB2, and ITS sequences from all strains of multiple
subspecies in the FUSARIOID-ID database (www.fusarium.org) and analyzed the evolutionary
position of the F. compactum MM-135 by constructing a multigene phylogenetic tree. Results of
DNA sequence comparison shows that F. compactum MM-135 shares the greatest sequence
homology with F. compactum LLC 2178 with a similarity of 99.82%.
MoreMeat also performed a DNA sequence comparison between F. compactum MM-135, F.
venenatum (production organism described in GRN 945 and GRN 91), and Fusarium strain
flavolapis (production organism described in GRN 904), demonstrating that TEF1, RPB1, and
ITS genes of F. compactum MM-135 have a similarity greater than 80% to their counterparts in
F. venenatum and Fusarium strain flavolapis, respectively.
Manufacturing Process
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is manufactured under current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP)
with food grade raw materials and processing aids. MoreMeat states that none of the raw
materials used in the production process are derived from major allergens. Furthermore,
MoreMeat states that the mycoprotein is produced with aseptic technology under sterile
conditions.
As detailed in Table 3 of MoreMeat’s GRAS dossier, the production process consistently yields
a reproducible product. In addition, the mycoprotein has been extensively analyzed to ensure
compliance with MoreMeat’s established specifications, including protein content, moisture
level, total fiber, ash, heavy metals, RNA, and mycotoxins. Microbiological analyses include
total aerobic count, yeasts and molds, Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes,
Staphylococcus aureus, and viable fusarium.
Product Specifications
MoreMeat has established specifications for mycoprotein that are tailored to their finished
product while also analogous to the current industry standards for mycoprotein derived from F.
venenatum and Fusarium strain flavolapis (as outlined in FCC 14 in the monograph for
mycoprotein derived from F. venenatum, as well as GRNs 91, 904, and 945). The GRAS Panel
reviewed batch analysis results for 3 non-consecutive batches of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein as
presented in Table 5 of the GRAS dossier, and notes that the ingredient is well-characterized,
and that the analytical data obtained using internationally accepted methods and internally
validated methods (as outlined in Table 4) includes protein, moisture, total fiber, ash,
mycotoxins, microbiological, RNA, and heavy metal content.
Proposed Uses and Estimated Intake
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is intended for use as a food ingredient and macronutrient across a
variety of food categories. The range of intended incorporation rates for MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein in these foods is detailed in Table 13 of the GRAS dossier. Since MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein primarily consists of water (~75%), protein (~15%), and fiber (~10%), the intended

use levels are expressed on a wet weight basis, with the anticipated minimum and maximum
levels provided.
Among the total population (ages 2 years and older), the mean and 90th percentile consumer-
only intakes of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein were determined to be 94 g/day and 207 g/day,
respectively. Male teenagers (ages 12 to 19 years) were determined to have the greatest
consumer-only mean and 90th percentile intakes of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, at 105 g/day and
252 g/day, respectively. The lowest consumer-only mean and 90th percentile intakes were for
female adults (ages 20 years and older), at 88 g/day and 194 g/day, respectively.
Among the total population (ages 2 years and older) and on a body weight basis, the mean and
90th percentile intakes of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein were determined to be 1.5 g/kg bw/day and
3.4 g/kg bw/day, respectively. Children (ages 2-5 years) were determined to have the greatest
mean and 90th percentile consumer-only intakes at 5.3 g/kg bw/day and 11.9 g/kg bw/day,
respectively. The lowest mean and 90th percentile consumer-only intakes were for male adults
(ages 20 years and older), at 1.1 g/kg bw/day and 2.7 g/kg bw/day, and female adults (ages 20
years and older) at 1.2 g/kg bw/day and 2.6 g/kg bw/day, respectively. The Expert Panel concurs
with MoreMeat’s conclusion that these estimates are conservative, as it is unlikely that
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein will be incorporated into every product in the marketplace at the
maximum proposed uses levels.
MoreMeat also calculated the estimated daily intake of protein from its mycoprotein from the
conservative 90th percentile consumer-only estimate of the daily consumption of MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein from the proposed uses is 207 g/day for the total population (2 years and older).
Assuming a maximum protein content of 15% for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, the conservative
90th percentile consumer-only estimate of the daily consumption of protein from the proposed
uses of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is 31 g/day for the total population (ages 2 years and older).
This estimated 90th percentile consumer-only intake of protein from all proposed uses for the
total population is lower than or within the range of the recommended and/or background intake
levels of protein in the diet.
To further evaluate the quality of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, a protein digestibility-corrected
amino acid score (PDCAAS) test report was included in Appendix 5 of the GRAS dossier. The
Expert Panel notes that the PDCAAS for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is 1.0 for children (ages 3 to
10 years old) and adults (ages 18 years and older). The highest possible PDCAAS score is 1.0,
which indicates that MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is a source of quality protein.
The estimated daily intake for fiber was also calculated for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein contains ~10% dietary fiber; therefore, the conservative consumer-
only mean and 90th percentile estimate of the daily consumption of dietary fiber from
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is ~9 g/day and 21 g/day, respectively, for the total population (2 years
and older). This estimated 90th percentile consumer-only intake of dietary fiber from all
proposed uses for the total population is lower than or within the range of the recommended
and/or background intake levels of dietary fiber in the diet.

To further evaluate the safety of dietary exposure of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, the estimated
dietary exposure to mycotoxins and nitrates are presented in the GRAS dossier. MoreMeat has
identified DAS, enniatin, and beauvericin as potential mycotoxins in mycoprotein. Enniatins and
beauvericin were identified and quantified in analyses of three non-consecutive batches of
mycoprotein. MoreMeat has established maximum specifications for enniatin and beauvericin,
thereby ensuring that consumer exposure remains consistently within safe levels. The Expert
Panel notes that DAS was not detected in the three non-consecutive representative batches of
mycoprotein. As previously noted herein, the Expert Panel discussed the potential of the
presence of DAS in MoreMeat’s mycoprotein. While DAS was not detected in the representative
batches, and while genome sequencing does not indicate an increased likelihood of DAS
formation, the Expert Panel notes that MoreMeat intends to monitor DAS levels in their
mycoprotein at least biannually and have a response plan in place should detectable levels of
DAS be found.
The EDIs for nitrates was also calculated for MoreMeat’s mycoprotein using a mean nitrates
residue of 6.3 mg/kg (wet weight) and the mean and 90th percentile intakes for mycoprotein of 94
and 207 g/day, respectively. Thus, the mean and 90th percentile intakes for nitrates were
determined to be 0.324 mg/person/day and 0.714 mg/person/day, respectively, or 0.005 mg/kg
bw/day and 0.010 mg/kg bw/day, respectfully, for a 70-kg individual. The EDIs for nitrates are
lower than or within the range of the recommended and/or background intake levels of nitrates in
the diet.
Pivotal Safety Data
Limited toxicological and safety studies are available for mycoprotein derived from F.
compactum. However, as demonstrated in the data presented in the GRAS dossier, MoreMeat’s
mycoprotein derived from F. compactum is substantially equivalent to the mycoprotein derived
from F. venenatum (as described in GRN 945 and GRN 91) and F. strain flavolapis (as described
in GRN 904).
MoreMeat summarized and compared the DNA sequencing, manufacturing process, and product
specifications of the three mycoproteins, and concluded that its mycoprotein is quantitatively and
qualitatively equivalent to the subject ingredients of GRN 904 and GRN 945, respectively.
Furthermore, based on the precedence of read-across approach to support GRAS conclusions for
novel proteins and other complex biological substances, MoreMeat applied the same approach of
referencing pivotal studies and data from GRN 91 and GRN 904 to support a GRAS conclusion
for F. compactum. Based upon published and peer-reviewed data on Fusarium toxicity and F.
compactum toxicity, as well as the published data on F. venenatum and F. strain flavolapis
toxicity, MoreMeat has determined that F. compactum, F. venenatum, and F. strain flavolapis
have the same toxicological potential or lack thereof, when grown under controlled conditions,
and that the read-across to pivotal data cited in GRN 91 for F. compactum and GRN 904 for F.
strain flavolapis offers sound scientific support for MoreMeat’s conclusion that the consumption
of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is safe under the proposed uses.
The published toxicology studies performed with mycoprotein derived from F. venenatum and F.

strain flavolapis include: a bacterial reverse mutation test; an in vivo mammalian erythrocyte
test; an in vitro mammalian chromosome aberration test; a 14-day oral range-finding study in
rats; an estrogenic potential study on mouse and non-RNA reduced mycoprotein study on
Landrace pig; a 22-week oral feeding study in rats; a 13‐week oral feeding study in rats; a 13-
week oral feeding study in baboons; two 90-day oral feeding studies in rats; a 1-year oral feeding
study in dogs; a 2-year carcinogenicity study in rats; a 2-generation reproductive and
developmental toxicity study in rats; and teratogenicity studies in rats and rabbits. These
published toxicology studies were previously reviewed in GRN 91 and GRN 904, and
demonstrate that mycoprotein derived from Fusarium spp. is not genotoxic and does not result in
adverse effects at high intake levels.
In addition, unpublished toxicology studies commissioned by MoreMeat provide corroborative
evidence for establishing the safety of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein. MoreMeat has assessed their
mycoprotein for potential genotoxic effects using an AMES test, an in vivo Mammalian
Erythrocyte Micronucleus study, and an in vitro Mammalian Chromosome Aberration test.
Based upon the results presented in the GRAS dossier, the Expert Panel concurs with
MoreMeat’s conclusion that their mycoprotein is non-genotoxic and non-mutagenic under the
tested conditions.
In addition, MoreMeat conducted a 14-days range finding toxicity study on their mycoprotein
preparation. While the study is unpublished, the Expert Panel notes that it was completed in a
GLP compliant lab and follows OECD guideline No. 407. Furthermore, the results presented in
the GRAS dossier indicate that there are no toxicological concerns related to mycoprotein
administration under the study conditions.
The Expert Panel has reviewed the totality of toxicity data, both published and corroborative, and
concur with MoreMeat’s conclusion that consumption of mycoprotein is reasonably expected to
be safe under the proposed conditions outlined in the GRAS dossier.
MoreMeat conducted an allergenicity evaluation of its mycoprotein and also contracted
immunologist Dr. Rick Goodman to conduct an independent allergenicity evaluation. Following
a thorough evaluation of the product information, the in vitro digestibility report, the published
literature regarding Fusarium sp. – including reports and papers on mycoprotein derived from F.
venenatum— both MoreMeat and Dr. Goodman concluded that MoreMeat’s mycoprotein does
not represent a likely risk for food allergy. The Expert Panel reviewed the information provided
in MoreMeat’s GRAS dossier in concert with Dr. Goodman’s evaluation report (available as
Appendix 3 in the GRAS dossier), and concur with the conclusion that there is no expectation of
increased risk for food allergy from the consumption of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein.
The Expert Panel reviewed the safety aspects of nutrition and digestibility, mycotoxins, nitrates,
ribonucleic acid (RNA), and reported adverse effects. The digestibility test conducted by
MoreMeat indicated that over 94% of the proteins are digested by pepsin in relatively short
times. Thus, MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is expected to have good digestion following
consumption and it is very unlikely that usual intakes of mycoprotein from the proposed uses
would result in either adverse gastrointestinal or physiological effects. MoreMeat states that the
only mycotoxins for which there is the potential for dietary exposure from consuming
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein are enniatins and beauvericin; however, the Expert Panel notes that

DAS must also be considered and should be monitored on at least a biannual bases.
We, the GRAS Panel, unanimously conclude that the proposed use of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein
as an ingredient in conventional foods, at levels specified herein, up to consumer-only mean and
90th percentile intakes of 94 g/day and 207 g/day, respectively, for the total population (ages 2
years and older), is safe and GRAS based on scientific procedures and supported by a history of
safe use.
We, the undersigned independent GRAS Panel, have critically evaluated the safety of
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, a non-animal and non-plant mycoprotein, and unanimously conclude
that the scientific data, information, and methods described herein establish that the ingredient,
when produced in accordance with current Good Manufacturing Practice and meeting the
specifications outlined in the supporting dossier, meets the standard of reasonable certainty of no
harm and is Generally Recognized As Safe under 21 CFR.
In accordance with Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 170, Subpart E on
Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) Notices, we, the Expert Panel, have evaluated the
scientific evidence and agree with MoreMeat (Guangzhou) Biotech Co., Ltd’s conclusion that
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is GRAS for use as an ingredient in foods at the levels specified
herein. In our opinion, other experts qualified to assess the safety of food ingredients would
concur with this conclusion. Therefore, MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is excluded from the definition
of a food additive and may be used in the U.S. without requiring the promulgation of a food
additive regulation by the FDA under 21 CFR.

Biographical Sketch of the Panelists
Margitta Dziwenka, DVM, DABT
Dr. Dziwenka holds a Doctor of Veterinary Medicine degree from the University of Saskatchewan
and is a Diplomat with the American Board of Toxicology. She has over 27 years of experience as
a practicing veterinarian and laboratory animal research experience. Dr. Dziwenka has worked in
research, preclinical regulatory toxicology, safety evaluation of human food and animal feed
additives, GRAS dossier, and other regulatory filing dossier preparation for those 27 years. Dr.
Dziwenka also has extensive experience as an Expert Panelist. She has experience in the
management of preclinical contract research organizations and in the role of Study Director and
Study Monitor for GLP-compliant preclinical studies and has assisted in the design of
numerous preclinical studies. Dr. Dziwenka is experienced in the writing of position papers,
safety opinions for a variety of products, manuscripts for publication and critical review of
study results used to support regulatory submissions and safety conclusions.
Katrina Emmel, Ph.D.
Dr. Katrina Emmel is the founder and president of KemmelCal Inc. With an MS in Biochemistry
(WPI) and a Ph.D. in Chemistry (Northern Illinois University), Dr. Emmel started her career as an
analytical chemist, performing routine LC-MS analysis in a clinical laboratory, and then developing
analytical methods for a dietary supplement and food manufacturer. She was involved in preparing
the first Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) Notification for Enzyme Modified Steviol
Glycosides on behalf of NOW Foods. As an independent consultant since 2013, Dr. Emmel has
been involved in a number of GRAS evaluations as a chemist, technical writer, project manager,
Expert Panelist, and as Chair of the Expert Panel. She has also served as an Expert Witness to
support patent litigation activities for food ingredients.
Jianjun (Gene) Yang, Ph.D.
Dr. Yang has led a distinguished career in food ingredients innovation. He obtained his Ph.D. from
University of Kentucky, and then completed his NIH fellowship at Cornell University. He had
worked for almost 20 years at the DuPont Central Research and Development as Principal Research
Scientist, leading the DuPont Biotech Lab in many innovation projects for food ingredients and
industrial materials. He had also worked as the leader and advisor in other SynBio and
pharmaceutical companies. Dr. Yang has many U.S. and international patents, patent applications,

L-Ergothioneine is a metabolite of histidine, specifically a thiolhistidine derivative, that occurs
naturally in a number of common foods, including mushrooms, offal, cereals, and some varieties of

and mycobacteria and captured in the plant roots. It was first isolated from rye ergot (Claviceps
purpurea) in 1909 (EFSA, 2016). The structure of L-Ergothioneine is shown in Figure 1.

2.2.1. Host Strain
The host strain is E. coli K-12 MG1655, with its development history detailed in Browning et al. (2023).
E. coli K-12 MG1655 has been used in the manufacturing of L-Ergothioneine, as documented in GRAS
Notice (GRN) 000734, which received a “no questions” letter from the FDA. The strain is classified
by the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) as a Bio-Safety Level 13 organism (ATCC 47076
and 700926, for frozen and freeze-dried forms, respectively) and has also been used as the production
organism in GRNs 000749, 000897, 000951, and 001075, all of which received “no questions” letters
from the FDA.
2.2.2. Construction of the Production Strain
Three genes were optimized and expressed in E. coli K-12 MG1655 using plasmid pMUT1, as
described by Kan et al. (2021). This plasmid, available in the National Center for Biotechnology
Information (NCBI) database under accession number A84793, functions as a vector for expressing
the egt1 gene from Neurospora crassa (ATCC 24698) and the egtD and egtE genes from
Mycolicibacterium smegmatis MC2 155 (ATCC 700084).
The egt1 gene encodes the ergothioneine biosynthesis enzyme (Egt1), which catalyzes the S-adenosyl-
L-methionine (SAM)-dependent triple methylation of histidine’s alpha-amino group to form hercynine,
followed by conjugation with cysteine and oxygen to form hercynylcysteine sulfoxide. The egtD gene
encodes L-histidine N(alpha)-methyltransferase (EgtD), which also catalyzes the SAM-dependent
methylation of histidine to form hercynine. The egtE gene encodes hercynylcysteine sulfoxide lyase

(EgtE), a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of hercynylcysteine

2.2.3. Stability of Production Strain
The stability of genetically modified E. coli K-12 MG1655 was evaluated over five consecutive
subcultures (~210 generations) based on growth rate, genetic stability, and ergothioneine production.
Growth rate was assessed using turbimetry, with consistent growth curves observed across generations,
indicating stable growth.
Genetic stability was examined through PCR and sequencing analysis. PCR amplification confirmed
the presence of egt1, egtD, and egtE across generations with consistent band sizes. Sequencing results
further verified that the target gene sequences remained unchanged, demonstrating genetic stability.
Ergothioneine production was evaluated in shake-flask fermentation. Synthesis was detected in all
tested generations, with stable yields observed, confirming consistent production capability.

2.3.2. Production of L-Ergothioneine
Gene III’s L-Ergothioneine is manufactured in compliance with cGMP, with relevant documentation
provided in Appendix 3. Production is conducted in a sterile, contained environment. In-process
controls include media sterilization, macromolecular filtration, and resin column filtration. The
manufacturing process is summarized in Figure 4 and further described in the following sections.
The production water meets the national drinking water standard GB5749-2022, consistent with those
set by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA), except for per- and poly-
fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The purification process includes sequential steps such as filtration,
sand filtration, activated carbon filtration, softening, reverse osmosis with electrodeionization, and
ultraviolet (UV) sterilization. Both activated carbon filtration and reverse osmosis effectively remove
PFAS (U.S. EPA, 2018). Along with the national standard, this purification process ensures the
production water complies with U.S. EPA drinking water standards.
Solid waste is periodically collected and disposed of by a third-party waste management service.
Wastewater undergoes initial on-site treatment in accordance with national discharge standards before
being transferred to a third-party treatment facility.
2.3.2.1. Inoculation and Seed Culture
The glycerol stocks of the modified E. coli strain are stored at -70 ± 5°C and thawed at room
temperature prior to use. The seed culture medium, composed of yeast peptone, yeast extract, and
sodium chloride, is sterilized at 120–123°C for 25–30 minutes before inoculation. The inoculated seed
culture (1% stock) is incubated at 37 ± 2°C for 15–17 hours with shaking at 220 ± 20 rpm. Once the
culture transitions from clear to turbid, it proceeds to the fermentation stage.
2.3.2.2. Fermentation
A basal culture medium is prepared using yeast extract, potassium dihydrogen phosphate, ammonium
sulfate, dextrose, magnesium sulfate, defoamer, and potable water. The pH is adjusted to 6.5–7.3 with
ammonia water, and the medium is sterilized in a fermentation tank at 119–123°C for 30 minutes.
Supplement 1, composed of dextrose, magnesium sulfate, and potable water, is sterilized under
pressure at 118–121°C for 20 minutes in an auxiliary tank. Supplement 2, containing L-methionine, L-
histidine, L-cysteine, and potable water, undergoes high-pressure sterilization at 118–121°C for 20
minutes in a separate auxiliary tank.
The seed culture is inoculated into the fermentation tank containing the basal culture medium at
0.04%–1% of the initial fermentation volume. During fermentation, Supplements 1 and 2 are added
stepwise in multiple batches over time. The fermentation temperature is controlled at 33–37°C for the
first 8–10 hours and then maintained at 20–24°C until the end of the process. The pH of the medium
is maintained at 6.8–6.9 throughout the fermentation process. Ventilation is maintained at 600–1200

m³/h, and the agitator speed is controlled at 80–165 rpm. Fermentation is carried out for 90–96 hours

and is terminated by sterilization at 95°C for 25–30 minutes once the L-Ergothioneine concentration
reaches ≥6000 mg/L.
2.3.2.3. Filtration
Bacterial cells are removed by plate-and-frame pressure filtration, followed by removal of
macromolecular impurities using an ultrafiltration membrane. The collected supernatant is
preliminarily concentrated by nanofiltration before prior to purification.
2.3.2.4. Purification
The supernatant undergoes decolorization and impurity removal using macroporous adsorption resin.
The resulting flow-through is subjected to cation exchange chromatography, where it is washed with
primary reverse osmosis water and eluted with 0.3–0.5% ammonia water.
2.3.2.5. Concentration
The eluent (purity >95%) is transferred to a concentration unit to be concentrated, where the
temperature is controlled at ≤60°C and the vacuum pressure at ≤-0.08 MPa.
2.3.2.6. Decolorization
The concentrated solution is decolorized and purified by removing insoluble substances using activated
carbon. Activated carbon (0.2%–0.5%) is added and stirred for 30–35 minutes.
2.3.2.7. Filtration, Crystallization, and Centrifugation
The solution is filtered using a plate-and-frame system and transferred to a crystallization tank. Ethanol
is added, and the mixture is stirred for 0.5–1.5 hours. Crystals are collected using a tray centrifuge
operated at high speed.
2.3.2.8. Drying, Sieving, and Iron Removal
The obtained crystals are placed in a vacuum drying oven, where the vacuum pressure is maintained
at ≤-0.08 MPa and the hot water temperature at 60–65°C. After drying for 6–8 hours, the product is
sieved through a 40-mesh oscillating sieve and undergoes iron removal using a high-intensity magnetic
separator, yielding the final L-Ergothioneine product.
2.3.2.9. Packaging
The final L-ergothioneine powder is packed in vacuum-heat-sealed polyethylene bags. The sealed
product is then packed and sealed into a light-shielding aluminum composite bag and stored at room
temperature.

2.6. Stability
2.6.1. General Stability Data for L-Ergothioneine
Based on a six-month accelerated stability study (40±2°C, 75±5% relative humidity) and a 12-month
intermediate stability study (30±2°C, 65±5% relative humidity), Tetrahedron reported that its L-
Ergothioneine material is expected to remain stable for one year (EFSA, 2016).
In GRN 000734, Blue California reported the initial results of a planned 36-month shelf-stability study
for its L-Ergothioneine. Samples stored under ambient conditions and tested at 6 months and 12 months
showed no changes (FDA, 2018b).
2.6.2. Stability Data of Gene III’s L-Ergothioneine
Gene III conducted two stability studies on L-Ergothioneine under different conditions. All samples
were vacuum-heat sealed in polyethylene bags and then packed in light-shielding aluminum composite
bags. Samples were taken from individual sealed bags at each time point.
The long-term stability study is conducted at 25±2ºC for 24 months, with sampling at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18,
and 24 months. The currently available results (Table 5) indicate that product quality remained stable
under the specified conditions for up to 18 months. Further evaluations are ongoing, with updates to
be provided as additional data becomes available.
The accelerated stability study is conducted at 40±2ºC and 75±5% relative humidity for 6 months, with

sampling at 1, 2, 3, and 6 months. Results from the accelerated stability study (Table 6) demonstrate
that L-Ergothioneine remained stable throughout the study period.
The accelerated stability data support a two-year shelf life for L-Ergothioneine when stored at room
temperature in its intended commercial packaging, which is vacuum-heat sealed polyethylene bags
enclosed within light-shielding aluminum composite bags.

Part 3. DIETARY EXPOSURE
3.1. Background Exposure
As part of their evaluation of synthetic L-Ergothioneine manufactured by Tetrahedron, the European
Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Panel reviewed a published intake assessment by Ramirez-Martinez et
al. (2016) that discussed the estimated daily intakes of ergothioneine in the European population. The
EFSA Panel noted that the mean chronic dietary intake of ergothioneine in several European countries
ranged from 0.051 to 0.255 mg/kg body weight/day and from 0.306 to 0.409 mg/kg bw/day for adult
and adolescent consumers, respectively.
Ramirez-Martinez et al. (2016) also estimated the dietary intake of ergothioneine in US consumers
using probabilistic estimates considering the consumption of the main dietary sources of ergothioneine
(i.e., mushrooms, beans, meat organs, and oatmeal). In the US, the mean chronic background dietary
intake of ergothioneine was estimated to be 0.153 mg/kg bw/day and 0.299 mg/kg bw/day for adult
and adolescent consumers, respectively. As compared with European populations, US consumers were
estimated to have a lower overall consumption of ergothioneine in their diet.
The L-Ergothioneine reviewed by EFSA had an intended use level of up to 5 mg per serving in a
limited number of conventional foods, including alcohol-free beverages, cereal bars, milk, fresh dairy
products, and chocolates, and dietary supplements at 30 mg per day for adults and 20 mg per day for
children (EFSA, 2016).
In GRN 000734, submitted by Blue California, the estimated 90th percentile daily intake (calculated
as mean intake × 2) of ergothioneine from the intended uses was reported to be 0.48 mg/kg bw/day for
adults, 1.55 mg/kg bw/day for children aged 3 to 10 years, 0.8 mg/kg bw/day for children aged 10 to
14 years, and 0.56 mg/kg bw/day for children aged 14 to 18 years. Combining the GRN 000734
proposed intake estimate with the background intake reported by Ramirez-Martinez et al. (2016)
results in the highest cumulative intake estimates of 0.633 mg/kg bw/day for adults and 1.85 mg/kg

bw/day for children aged 3 to 10 years.

Part 6. NARRATIVE
The purpose of this section is to provide information relevant to the safety of L-Ergothioneine. A
review of the historical, scientific, and regulatory literature related to the safety of L-Ergothioneine
was conducted through April 14, 2025. For this purpose, PubMed was searched for information without
limits on publication date and the search terms/string included (ergothioneine or L-Ergothioneine) and
(safe or safety or adverse). Various government databases were also used to identify regulations across
jurisdictions.
The safety of L-ergothioneine has been evaluated by the FDA in GRN 000734, which received a “no
questions” letter. In addition, the EFSA assessed L-ergothioneine as a novel food and concluded that
it is safe for the general population under the proposed conditions of use. As part of its assessment,
EFSA identified a no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) of 800 mg/kg bw/day, based on the
subchronic toxicity study by Marone et al. (2016). Given that Gene III’s L-ergothioneine is
substantially equivalent to the subject evaluated by EFSA (Table 3), the NOAEL of 800 mg/kg bw/day
is pivotal to this GRAS determination. The safety of L-Ergothioneine is further supported by a
consistent body of toxicological evidence indicating that L-ergothioneine is non-genotoxic and does
not exhibit reproductive or developmental toxicity. Clinical studies have also shown that L-
Ergothioneine is well tolerated in humans at intake levels up to 25 mg/day.
6.1. History of Safe Consumption
L-Ergothioneine is a naturally occurring amino acid which is present primarily in mushrooms (Kushairi
et al., 2020). It can only be synthesized by a limited number of microorganisms including
cyanobacteria, mycobacteria, and non-yeast fungi, and is only present in human tissues via the diet
(Kushairi et al., 2020). L-Ergothioneine is naturally occurring in a number of foods that are part of the
typical American diet, including mushrooms, grains and grain products, beans and some vegetables,
eggs, animal products (including meat, organ meat, and offal), and beer (EFSA, 2016; Ey et al., 2007).
Ramirez-Martinez et al. (2016) estimated the dietary intake of L-Ergothioneine in U.S. and European
consumers (France, Italy, Ireland, Finland, and Belgium) using the consumption of the main dietary
sources of L-Ergothioneine (i.e., mushrooms, beans, meat organs, and oatmeal) and applying a
probabilistic model. The mean chronic background intake of L-Ergothioneine was estimated at 0.153
mg/kg bw/day for adults and 0.299 mg/kg bw/day for adolescents in the U.S. In European countries,
the mean intake ranged from 0.051 to 0.255 mg/kg bw/day for adults and 0.306 to 0.409 mg/kg bw/day
for adolescents. Overall, U.S. consumers were estimated to have a lower overall consumption of L-
Ergothioneine in their diet than European consumers.

6.3. Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism & Excretion (ADME) Studies
Orally administered L-Ergothioneine is transported into cells and tissues by the Organic Cation
Transporter Novel Type 1 (OCTN1), also referred to as the Ergothioneine Transporter (ETT) due to its
high level of selectivity for L-Ergothioneine over other substrates such as L-carnitine (Liu et al., 2023).
ETT is expressed in several different tissues throughout the body, facilitating cellular uptake due to the
hydrophilicity of L-Ergothioneine, meaning it is not passively absorbed (Zalachoras et al., 2020). ETT
mRNA expression in rats indicates that L-Ergothioneine can be distributed to the liver, kidney, brain,

heart, and placenta (Wu et al., 2000). However, despite the potential for placental distribution, L-
Ergothioneine has not been shown to induce reproductive or developmental toxicity in rats (Forster et
al., 2015; Guijarro et al., 2002). L-Ergothioneine is not rapidly metabolized or excreted — it is retained
in tissues such as the liver or in circulation stored in red blood cells and is reabsorbed in the kidney
(Halliwell et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018). Details on the specific elimination pathways for L-
Ergothioneine have not been identified and limited study data with purified L-Ergothioneine is
available.
Pharmacokinetic (PK) studies indicate that there is limited urinary excretion of L-Ergothioneine after
oral administration in healthy males. Cheah et al. (2016) investigated the pharmacokinetics of L-
Ergothioneine after oral administration in healthy adult males. The participants were randomly
assigned to receive placebo, 5 mg, or 25 mg of L-Ergothioneine daily for 7 days (n = 15/group). Blood
and urine samples were collected on Days 1, 3, 5, 8, 14, 21, 28, and 35, and participants were asked to
refrain from ergothioneine-rich foods during the study. The plasma concentration of L- Ergothioneine
increased in a dose-dependent manner from Days 1 to 8, then gradually declined until Day 35. However,

6.4.2. Subacute and Subchronic Toxicity Studies
The subacute and subchronic oral toxicity of L-Ergothioneine have been evaluated in 14-, 28-, and 90-

For the 14-day study conducted by Forster et al. (2015), L-Ergothioneine was given to male and female
rats (numbers /group not stated) in the diet at 0, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.9%. The animals were checked twice
daily for mortality and morbidity and observed once a day for clinical signs (cage-side observations).
Body weight was recorded before allocation, on Day 1 and then twice a week, and food consumption
was recorded twice a week. A complete macroscopic post-mortem examination was performed on all

animals at termination. There were no signs of toxicity at concentrations up to and including 0.9%,
which was equivalent to 662 ± 82.5 mg/kg bw/day in males and 721 ± 57.6 mg/kg bw/day for females.
Marone et al. (2016) evaluated the safety of L-Ergothioneine in a 28-day repeat dose toxicity study in

ergothioneine (Miranova Labs, >98% purity) or vehicle (distilled water) for 28 days. None of the

compared to controls that was accompanied by an increase in food intake. This finding did not exhibit
dose-dependency and was deemed unrelated to treatment by the authors. Based on these results, the
authors determined that rats could tolerate L-Ergothioneine at doses ≥500 mg/kg bw/day. This
conclusion guided their dose selection for a 90-day study.

6.4.6. Clinical Studies
The safety of oral ergothioneine in humans has been evaluated in several studies. In particular, EFSA
(2016) reviewed the existing human studies as part of their review of ergothioneine as a novel food.
EFSA addressed potential concerns about the effects of ergothioneine on glucose homeostasis (Salt,
1931; Fraser & Jegard, 1950, as cited in EFSA, 2016; Epand, 1982; Epand et al., 1988), Crohn’s disease
(Peltekova et al., 2004; Taubert et al., 2005, 2009; Leung et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2010; Huff et al.,
2011), and rheumatoid arthritis (Reglinski et al., 1991; Tokuhiro et al., 2003; Taubert et al., 2006, as
cited in EFSA, 2016). The EFSA panel concluded that no relationship could be determined between
dietary or supplemental ergothioneine and the development of these conditions. This conclusion was
based on the observational nature of the studies, which assessed ergothioneine levels in the study
populations rather than through controlled intervention trials. Regarding direct human exposure to
ergothioneine, only one short-term oral intake study was reviewed by EFSA. Based on the study by
Cheah et al. (2016), the panel determined that no safety concerns were associated with short-term oral
