6.5. Safety of Production Organism
The production strain used for L-ergothioneine manufacturing is a genetically modified E. coli K-12
MG1655, engineered to express three biosynthetic enzymes that catalyze the conversion of histidine
to L-ergothioneine. The safety of the production strain is assessed based on the established safety
profile of the host strain, the safety of the inserted genes, and the genetic modification process. The
decision tree by Pariza and Johnson (2001) was also used to determine the safety of the production
organism.
Additionally, the manufacturing process includes a pasteurization step designed to eliminate
production strain. To confirm the absence of the production organism, E. coli testing is included in the
product specifications. Batch analyses of five non-consecutive batches (Table 4) demonstrated that E.
coli was not detected per 1 g of the final product. Gene III also tested three non-consecutive batches
for residual DNA, and the results demonstrated that residual DNA was not detected in the final product
(Appendix 6). Thus, there is reasonable certainty that the production organism does not pose safety

concerns to the consumer.
6.5.1. Safety of Host Strain
The host strain, E. coli K-12 MG1655, is classified as a Biosafety Level 1 microorganism by the ATCC.
E. coli K-12 has been widely used as a laboratory organism for over 50 years and is among the most
extensively characterized microorganisms (Bachmann, 1972; Jensen, 1993). The complete genome of
E. coli K-12 has been sequenced, confirming the absence of toxigenic potential (Blattner et al., 1997;
Hayashi et al., 2006). It is classified as a Risk Group 1 organism under the National Institutes of Health
(NIH) Guidelines, indicating that it is not associated with disease in healthy adult humans (NIH, 2024).
Beyond laboratory research, E. coli K-12 has a well-documented history of safe use in the food and
pharmaceutical industries. Both E. coli K-12 and its derivatives have been utilized in the production
of specialty chemicals and pharmaceuticals and were exempted from review under the Toxic
Substances Control Act (TSCA) by the U.S. EPA (U.S. EPA, 1997). The FDA affirmed the GRAS
status of chymosin, a food enzyme preparation derived from a genetically modified E. coli K-12 strain,
in 1990 (21 CFR §184.1685) (Flamm, 1991; Olempska-Beer et al., 2006). In addition, E. coli K-12
and its derivatives have been used as production organisms in multiple GRAS notices (e.g., GRN
000624, GRN 000659, GRN 000735, GRN 000745, GRN 001010, and GRN 001106), all of which

1997). It is frequently used as a reference strain for studying the virulence factors of pathogenic E. coli,

as it is non-pathogenic (Blanc-Potard et al., 2002; Kaper et al., 2004). E. coli K-12 and its derivatives
do not colonize the mammalian gastrointestinal tract, produce toxins such as Shiga toxin, or persist in
soil and water (U.S. EPA, 1997).
In summary, E. coli K-12 is a non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic microorganism that has been used as
a production organism for food ingredients, which have either received a "no questions" letter from
the FDA or been deemed safe by EFSA.
6.5.2. Safety of Inserted Genes
The three inserted genes—egt1, egtE, and egtD—are sourced from N. crassa and M. smegmatis MC²
155. The egt1 gene is derived from N. crassa, a non-pathogenic filamentous fungus (Santos et al.,
2018). N. crassa is non-toxic and has a well-documented history of human consumption (Havlik et al.,
2017; Bartholomai et al., 2022). It has traditionally been used in East Asia for fermenting soybean
byproducts in China, producing oncom in Indonesia, and in traditional foods in Brazil and Borneo
(Bartholomai et al., 2022). No evidence of pathogenicity or toxigenicity has been reported in either its
long history of food use or laboratory studies (Perkins & Davis, 2000).
The egtD and egtE genes originate from M. smegmatis MC² 155, a bacterium classified as a Biosafety
Level 1 organism by ATCC. M. smegmatis is a saprophytic bacterium commonly found in soil, water,
and seborrheic secretions (Czubat et al., 2020). It is widely recognized as non-pathogenic (Warner et
al., 2005; Czubat et al., 2020; Sparks et al., 2023). A PubMed search found no evidence suggesting
that M. smegmatis poses a risk of toxigenicity.

6.5.2.1. Potential Allergenicity
The potential allergenicity of the inserted genes was assessed using the AllergenOnline and Allergome
databases. A multi-tiered approach was applied in AllergenOnline, incorporating (1) direct sequence
comparison using FASTA alignment to known allergens with >35% sequence identity and an E-value
<1, (2) an 80-amino-acid sliding window search, and (3) identification of contiguous 8-mer sequence
matches with known allergens. The analysis was further supplemented by cross-reactivity evaluations
using the Allergome database.
For egt1, AllergenOnline identified a FASTA alignment match with Proj1 (Group 2468), showing 26.3%
identity over a 99-amino-acid alignment, with an E-value of 0.9. No matches exceeding the 35%
identity threshold were found in the sliding window analysis, and no 8-mer matches were detected.
The Allergome analysis identified potential cross-reactivity with Cav p 4.0101, Fel d 2, and Alta 3.0101,
exhibiting sequence identities of 55%, 51%, and 58%, respectively. These matches involved short
sequences (<80 amino acids) associated with structural motifs (e.g., β-sheets and α-helices) rather than

immune recognition sites. These findings suggest a low direct allergenicity risk and a low-to-moderate
potential for cross-reactivity based on sequence similarities within conserved structural motifs.
For egtD, AllergenOnline did not identify any significant matches using FASTA alignment. The sliding
window search confirmed the absence of relevant alignments, and no 8-mer matches were detected.
The Allergome analysis indicated weak sequence similarities with the apple allergen Mal d 1 (42%
identity over 76 amino acids) and the dust mite allergen Der p 1 (39% identity over 68 amino acids).
These alignments were localized to β-sheet-rich conserved domains and signal peptide regions, which
are not associated with IgE-binding epitopes. Collectively, the data indicate a low direct allergenicity
risk and a low likelihood of cross-reactivity.
For egtE, no significant matches were identified in AllergenOnline using FASTA alignment. The
sliding window analysis found no alignments exceeding the identity threshold, and no 8-mer sequence
matches were detected. The Allergome analysis yielded results consistent with those for egtD, showing
sequence similarities with Mal d 1 (42% identity over 76 amino acids) and Der p 1 (39% identity over
68 amino acids). These matches were confined to short sequence segments and structural regions with
minimal potential for immune recognition. The overall assessment indicates negligible direct
allergenicity risk and a low potential for cross-reactivity.
In conclusion, the inserted genes egtD, egt1, and egtE present a low risk of direct allergenicity.
AllergenOnline did not identify any sequence alignments exceeding established thresholds for
allergenic potential. While sequence similarities with known allergens were observed in Allergome,
these involved short structural motifs with limited relevance to immune recognition. Overall, the
findings support the conclusion that the inserted genes pose no significant allergenic risk.

6.5.2.2. Potential Toxigenicity
The toxigenicity of the inserted genes was evaluated using ToxinPred2 and the T3DB database.
ToxinPred2 predictions were conducted using a hybrid algorithm (RF+BLAST+MERCI) with a
classification cutoff of 0.6 and an E-value threshold of ≤10⁻6. Additionally, sequences were aligned
against known toxin sequences in T3DB using FASTA alignment, with a homology threshold set at E
≤ 1 × 10⁻5.
ToxinPred2 classified all tested sequences (egt1, egtD, and egtE) as non-toxic, with toxicity scores
ranging from 0.08 to 0.15 and confidence levels of 93–96%. No N-terminal signal peptides or toxin
domains were detected. Similarly, T3DB analysis did not identify significant homology between the
inserted genes and known toxins.
In conclusion, the absence of toxin domains, low toxicity scores, and lack of homology with known
toxins collectively indicate that these genes do not pose a significant toxicity risk.
Collectively, the non-toxigenic and non-pathogenic nature of the source organisms, along with in silico
evaluation results indicating no allergenic or toxigenic risk for the inserted genes, supports the
conclusion that the insertion of these genes encoding enzymes involved in L-Ergothioneine
biosynthesis does not pose a safety concern in food production.

6.6. GRAS Criteria
FDA defines “safe” or “safety” as it applies to food ingredients as:
“…reasonably certainty in the minds of competent scientists that the substance is not harmful
under the intended conditions of use.”7
Amplification is provided in that the conclusion of safety is to include probable consumption of the
substance in question, the cumulative effect of the substance and appropriate safety factors. It is the
FDA’s operational definition of safety that serves as the framework against which this evaluation is
provided.
Furthermore, in discussing GRAS criteria, FDA notes that:
“…General recognition of safety requires common knowledge, throughout the expert scientific
community knowledgeable about the safety of substances directly or indirectly added to food, that

there is reasonable certainty that the substance is harmful under the conditions of its intended use.”
“Common knowledge can be based on either “scientific procedures” or on experience based on
common use of a substance in food prior to January 1, 1958.”
FDA discusses in more detail what is meant by the requirement of general knowledge and acceptance
of pertinent information within the scientific community, i.e., the so-called “common knowledge
element”, in terms of the two following component elements:
• Data and information relied upon to establish safety must be generally available, and this is
most commonly established by utilizing published, peer-reviewed scientific journals; and
• There must be a basis to conclude that there is consensus (but not unanimity) among qualified
scientists about the safety of the substance for its intended use, and this is established by relying
upon secondary scientific literature such as published review articles, textbooks, or compendia,
or by obtaining opinions of experts or opinions from authoritative bodies, such as JECFA and
the National Academy of Sciences.
General recognition of safety based upon scientific procedures requires the same quantity and quality
of scientific evidence as is required to obtain approval of a food additive. General recognition of safety
through scientific procedures shall be based upon the application of generally available and accepted
scientific data, information, or methods, which ordinarily are published, as well as the application of
scientific principles, and may be corroborated by the application of unpublished scientific data,
information, or methods.
The apparent imprecision of the terms “appreciable”, “at the time” and “reasonably certainty”
demonstrates that the FDA recognized the impossibility of providing absolute safety in this or any
other area (Lu, 1988; Renwick, 1990; Rulis and Levitt, 2009).
As noted below, this safety assessment to ascertain GRAS status for L-Ergothioneine for the specified
food uses meets FDA criteria for reasonable certainty of no harm by considering both the technical and
common knowledge elements.

Dear Dr Deng:
Per your request, Anchor Center for Certification (ACC), acting as the agent for MoreMeat

1. In Table 3, ammonium sulfate is listed as a nitrogen source in the fermentation media, with 21
CFR 184.1143 cited for its regulatory status. However, the regulatory status for ammonium
sulfate under 21 CFR 184.1143 applies specifically to its use as a dough strengthener, firming
agent, and processing aid in baked goods, gelatins, and puddings. Please provide the correct
regulation for your intended use of ammonium sulfate. In addition, please confirm that all raw
materials and processing aids used in the production of mycelial biomass of F. compactum “MM-
135” are food grade and are used in accordance with an appropriate U.S. regulation, are GRAS
for their intended use, or are the subject of an effective food contact notification.
MoreMeat’s response:
Ammonium sulfate is used as a nitrogen source in the fermentation medium to support microbial growth
and metabolite production (Akpoghelie et al., 2024; Yalçın & Özbaş, 2007). While 21 CFR 184.1143
designates ammonium sulfate as a direct food additive for specific functions (dough strengthener,
firming agent, processing aid), MoreMeat uses ammonium sulfate as an in-process fermentation
nutrient, not as a direct ingredient in the final product.
In fermentation media, ammonium sulfate’s function is to supply bioavailable nitrogen to the
production microorganism. Its use in microbial fermentation is well-established in food biotechnology,
and it is not expected to be present in the final purified ingredient, thereby aligning with the definition
of a processing aid under FDA guidance (e.g., 21 CFR 170.3(o)(24)). Therefore, while the cited CFR
section covers direct food use, the use of ammonium sulfate in More Meat’s process is functionally and
scientifically justified, and consistent with recognized fermentation practices and precedented use in
food biotechnology (Papagianni et al., 2005).
Furthermore, there is a prior precedent for the use of ammonium sulfate as a nutrient source in
fermentation media used for the production of GRAS ingredients. For example, on November 22, 2024,
FDA responded with a “no questions” letter to GRN 001183 for Monellin preparation produced by
Komagataella phaffii P-MON-40 expressing a gene encoding for a modified monellin, where
ammonium sulfate, anhydrous is listed in Table 2 of the GRAS dossier as a “Raw material/processing
aid” with the “function/purpose” of “nutrient source.”
MoreMeat hereby confirms that that all raw materials, processing aids, and food contact substances
used in the production of mycelial biomass of F. compactum MM-135 are food grade and are used in

accordance with an appropriate U.S. regulation, are GRAS for their intended use, or are the subject of
an effective food contact notification.

5. We noticed discrepancies between Table 13 in GRN 001255 and its Appendix 3 regarding the
food categories and use levels for mycelial biomass of F. compactum “MM-135”. For example,
your uses include processed fruit and fruit juices, but only the food code for orange juice
(92550350) is used while there are more than 7 food codes for orange juice in the National
Health and Examination Survey (NHANES). We also note that food codes for apple and
vegetable juices were omitted. Please clarify these differences, explaining any variations in the
food categories between your intended uses and those used in your dietary exposure estimate.
Additionally, please address why specific foods were omitted from the dietary exposure
assessment when those foods were listed as intended food categories in Table 13.
MoreMeat’s response:
The GRAS substance mycelial biomass of Fusarium compactum MM-135, manufactured by
MoreMeat, is intended solely for use in “high-protein juice” products within the categories of Processed
Fruits and Fruit Juices and Processed Vegetables and Vegetable Juices, as indicated in Table 13 in the
notification. These intended uses do not include 100% fruit or vegetable juices, such as 100% orange
juice or 100% apple juice, which would not be expected to contain added protein. Accordingly, product
codes representing pure juice products—such as Orange Juice, 100%, NFS (61210000)—have been
intentionally omitted from the intake assessment. Instead, the assessment includes product codes most
likely to represent high-protein juice formulations, such as 92550360 (Apple juice beverage), along
with various vegetable juice blends (e.g., 92550400, 92550405, 75132000, etc.), which more closely
align with the intended application of the ingredient.
6. We noted that several sections of your notice contain significant amounts of text copied from
GRN 904 and GRN 945. Be aware of the rules to avoid plagiarism; there are guidance
documents available, including those provided by the US Government, National Institutes of
Health, etc. It is important to note that using quotes and ascribing a source is not enough to avoid
plagiarism when the section being copied is long. There is discussion regarding how to discuss
data and information incorporated into a GRAS notice on page 54988 of the GRAS Final Rule
(62 FR 54988, August 17, 2016).
MoreMeat’s response:
MoreMeat acknowledges FDA’s observation regarding the textual similarities between our GRAS
notice and portions of GRN 000904 and GRN 000945. In preparing our submission, our intent was to
accurately convey well-established scientific principles and regulatory concepts relevant to our
ingredient, some of which have been previously articulated in publicly available GRAS notices.
Thank you for your suggestion to review the guidance on how to incorporate data and information from
previous GRAS notices into our own GRAS submission. We note that Comment 48 and Response 48
in the 62 FR 54988, Aug 17th, 2016 stated that we must have sufficient knowledge of data and
information submitted by another party, and to identify the specific source of data and information to
be incorporated into our own GRAS submission, and to ensure the information incorporated must be
public and not confidential and need to be obtained through FOIA.
We affirm that our GRAS assessment reflects our independent review, and we would like to revise
section 6.4 to demonstrate our original scientific evaluation, in alignment with the principles outlined
on page 54988 of the GRAS Final Rule (81 FR 54988; August 17, 2016).
“6.4 Read-Across Rationale and Supporting Evidence
Based on established scientific principles for evaluating the safety of Fusarium species, MoreMeat has

independently determined that F. compactum, F. strain flavolapis, and F. venenatum, when cultivated
under controlled fermentation conditions, demonstrate equivalent toxicological profiles. This
conclusion is supported by an integrated assessment of phylogenetic relationships, compositional data,
genetic determinants of secondary metabolite production, and analytical testing results. In addition, our
conclusion is substantiated by in vitro and in vivo safety studies specific to MoreMeat’s F. compactum-
derived mycoprotein.
This “read-across” approach is consistent with scientific principles recognized by the GRAS
community, including the use of phylogenetic and compositional comparators to infer toxicological
equivalence. Our evaluation aligns with longstanding practices in toxicological risk assessment of
biological substances and applies current methodologies in genomics and metabolomics to substantiate
the absence of safety concerns.
6.4.1 Scientific Basis for Comparative Evaluation
The application of comparative safety assessments has precedent in GRAS determinations involving
closely related microbial species. Numerous GRAS notices—such as GRNs 000737, 000811, and
000904—have employed this approach to establish safety based on demonstrable similarities in
taxonomy, metabolic activity, and intended use. Although our safety assessment references select data
from prior notices, we have conducted an independent and comprehensive evaluation of F. compactum
using current data and methods.
We also consider the framework described by Pariza and Johnson (2001) relevant to our assessment.
While originally proposed for genetically modified production strains, the broader principles outlined—
namely, evaluating an organism’s history of safe use, taxonomic relatedness, and potential for toxin
production—remain applicable. With the advancement of high-resolution sequencing and metabolomic
profiling, these tools now enable a rigorous comparison across Fusarium species.
6.4.2 Comparative Toxicological Potential of Key Fusarium Species
The toxicological potential of F. compactum was assessed relative to F. strain flavolapis and F.
venenatum based on the following key domains:
 Phylogenetics: All three species are members of the Fusarium genus and fall within closely
related clades, indicating high genetic similarity.
 Composition: Their respective mycoproteins share similar nutritional, protein, and fiber
profiles.
 Intended Use: All are intended for use as alternative dietary proteins in similar food
applications.
 Secondary Metabolites: The profile of mycotoxin-related gene clusters and their expression
under controlled growth conditions is consistent across the three strains.
 Toxicological Data: All are associated with a low likelihood of mycotoxin production under
food-relevant fermentation conditions, supported by targeted analytical testing and toxicology
data.
6.4.3 Genetic and Analytical Evaluation
Our investigation of F. compactum included genomic screening of biosynthetic gene clusters associated
with key Fusarium mycotoxins (e.g., trichothecenes, enniatins, and beauvericin). The structure and
functionality of these gene clusters in F. compactum were evaluated in context with homologous
sequences in F. strain flavolapis and F. venenatum, revealing no evidence of increased mycotoxin-
producing potential.
These findings were confirmed through targeted analytical testing of fermentation samples, which
demonstrated non-detectable or minimal levels of known Fusarium-associated mycotoxins under
standard production conditions.
6.4.4 In Vitro and In Vivo Safety Studies
To further support the conclusion of safety, MoreMeat conducted a battery of in vitro genotoxicity
assays (Ames test, micronucleus test, and chromosome aberration test), none of which indicated
mutagenic or clastogenic activity. These assays are conducted as per internationally recognized

standards (e.g., OECD Test Guidelines) and have been used to assess other Fusarium-based
mycoproteins.
Additionally, a 14-day oral toxicity study in rats demonstrated no adverse effects at high doses of
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein. These results are consistent with published data on F. venenatum- and F.
strain flavolapis-derived mycoproteins.
6.4.5 Conclusion
The combined genetic, compositional, analytical, and toxicological evidence provides a robust basis
to conclude that F. compactum poses no greater toxicological risk than F. strain flavolapis or F.
venenatum when grown under controlled production conditions. This conclusion reflects an
independent scientific evaluation using contemporary methodologies and is consistent with FDA’s
expectations for a scientifically grounded and transparent GRAS notice, as outlined in the GRAS
Final Rule (81 FR 54988).”

9. On page 71, you discuss consumption of a similar product and the resulting reactions, including
vomiting and diarrhea, which could be attributed to the high chitin content. There is no mention
of chitin levels in your ingredient or a safety discussion of chitin. Please discuss the chitin
content in your ingredient and why this does not pose a safety concern for consumers.
MoreMeat’s response:
As noted on page 71 of the GRAS notice, gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting or diarrhea have
been reported in isolated cases following consumption of certain fungal-based mycoproteins. These
effects have been hypothesized to result, in part, from the relatively high content of chitin, a naturally
occurring polysaccharide found in the cell walls of filamentous fungi.
Chitin Content in MoreMeat’s Mycoprotein
Chitin is an insoluble dietary fiber that is widely recognized as a structural component of fungal cell
walls. While chitin is not measured directly in MoreMeat’s mycoprotein specification, it contributes
significantly to the total dietary fiber content of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein, which approximately 10%
on a wet weight basis (Table 33 page 74 in the GRAS notification).
It was noted in an EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) panel review in 2022, there is currently no
nationally or internationally recognized reference method for the analytical determination of chitin
levels (EFSA NDA Panel, 2022).
Safety of Chitin at Reported Levels
Chitin is classified as a non-digestible carbohydrate and is generally recognized as safe when consumed

in moderate amounts. It is not absorbed in the human gastrointestinal tract and functions similarly to
other insoluble fibers. Several GRAS notices (e.g., GRNs 000091, and page 4 of appendix 5 from
000904) have concluded that chitin at levels typical for fungal mycoproteins does not pose a safety
concern for the general population.
Currently, there is no officially established tolerable upper intake level (UL) for chitin in humans set
by major regulatory agencies such as the U.S. FDA, EFSA, or JECFA (Joint FAO/WHO Expert
Committee on Food Additives). However, its safety and functional role as insoluble dietary fiber are
well recognized, particularly when it is part of the fungal biomass or mycoprotein-based foods
(Derbyshire et al., 2023).
Furthermore, human tolerance studies of fungal-derived mycoproteins have not identified chitin as a
causative factor for adverse effects at typical intake levels. The total fiber content—including chitin—
of MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is similar to that found in mycoproteins already present in the food supply
with a history of safe use.
Consideration of Gastrointestinal Symptoms
The mild gastrointestinal symptoms occasionally reported for fungal proteins have generally been
associated with very high intake levels or sudden introduction of high-fiber foods in sensitive
individuals (Jacobson & DePorter, 2018). These effects are not unique to chitin and can occur with
other high-fiber foods such as legumes, psyllium, or whole grains. The levels of chitin present in
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein are not expected to result in adverse effects when consumed under normal
dietary patterns.
In conclusion, the chitin content in MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is consistent with that of other fungal
mycoproteins with established safety records. Given its classification as a dietary fiber, its known
physiological effects, and the absence of evidence of toxicity at the levels consumed, chitin present in
MoreMeat’s mycoprotein is concluded to not pose a safety concern under the intended conditions of
use. MoreMeat’s conclusion is consistent with the broader scientific understanding of chitin safety and
its role as a naturally occurring fiber in fungal-derived ingredients.

13. A preliminary 14-day toxicity study discussed in Section 6.2.2 appears to have been published in
May 2025 (Xian et al., 2025) after submission of the GRAS notice. The published study states
there are ongoing 90-day studies. Toxicological studies are pivotal in determining the safety of
consumption of food ingredients, including the maximum safe level of exposure. Such pivotal

safety of the ingredient. Data or information presented in a GRAS submission should be publicly

Introduction
MoreMeat (Guangzhou) Biotech Co.,Ltd. has developed a novel food product
based on a new Fusarium species (Fusarium compactum, MM-135), which is
obtained through a strict fermentation process. The company is currently declaring a
new food ingredient to the regulatory authorities and requires a safety evaluation of
thenew ingredient, with protein allergenicity being a key assessment.
The Codex Alimentarius Commission guidelines for assessing the allergenicity

of novel foods (2003) recommends assessing the novel food ingredient for stability in
pepsin at acidic pH using standard conditions as an assay to help evaluate whether the
novel ingredient is likely to increase the rate of sensitization or increase the likelihood
of eliciting an allergic response in consumers. In addition, the stability of mycoprotein
was tested using simulated intestinal fluid digestion experiments, which the Codex
Alimentarius Commission recognizes as a useful method to consider potential allergic
risks when conducting safety assessments of foods with new protein sources. In vitro
digestion provides a simple reference basis to assess protein digestion rates and the
potential increase in food allergy risks. Pepsin has optimal activity between pH 1.2
and 2.0, but its activity significantly decreases at pH 3.5 and becomes irreversibly
denatured at pH 7.0. Thomas et al. (2004) found that protein digestion at pH 2.0
compared to pH 1.2 results in slightly slower degradation of full-length proteins and
protein fragments, without changing the overall sensitivity of proteins to digestion.
Therefore, in this study we only assessed the stability of the test protein in simulated
gastric fluid at pH 2.0, with auxiliary assessments in simulated intestinal fluid at pH
7.5.

3．Results
3.1Limit ofDetection.
Figure 1. illustrates that all protein (different molecular weight) bands could be
shown on the gel when the protein loaded amount was ≥4 μg/well (lanes P and 1-6),
while the largest molecular weight protein band (~120 kDa) could no longer be
displayed in lane 7 (<4 μg). Therefore, we concluded that the minimum amount of

protein that was reliably detected (limit of detection) was 4 μg sample protein, which
ensure that all bands could be shown in the gel. Based on these data, the limit of
detection was approximately 20% (1/5) of the sample protein loaded in digestion
samples, 20μg/well was taken as 100%ofloading digestion samples.
The protein loading mentioned here refers to the loading of total proteins, which
contains a wide range of proteins, especially the relatively low proportion of high
molecular weight proteins. The initial protein concentration of sample extract was
13.25 mg/mL based on BCA method. If we set the digestion endpoint at 10% protein
residue, 1/10 sample dilution and other reaction solutions adding would result in
lower concentration of total protein. Further dilution may cause the total proteins
bands could not be fully shown in the gel, especially high molecular weight protein
(like120kDa).
Based on the result, we set the end of simulated gastric digestion at 20% protein
residue (1/5 of sample protein). The P1/5 protein solution was seen as the end
reference forevaluating digestion stability inSGF.

Conclusion
The mycoprotein of Fusarium compactum produced by MoreMeat (Guangzhou)
Biotech Co.,Ltd. via fermentation method could be rapidly digested by simulated
gastricdigestion, and the wholeproteins doappear to berapidly digested bysimulated
intestinal digestion. The results indicate that proteins from Fusarium compactum are
relatively labile to enzymes from the human digestive tract. Therefore, it is less likely
to cause allergic reactions in humans. Since some people may likely have allergies to
the Fusarium compactum protein, digestion of the proteins is unlikely to alleviate all

2.1. Identity of the notified substance
The subject of this notification is an industrial brewing Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain called
BY-927. BY-927 is intended for use in brewing to improve beer quality by keeping diacetyl, an
off-flavor compound produced by yeast with a buttery, butterscotch-like flavor, below sensory
threshold levels. This strain contains a gene from Acetobacter aceti that encodes an
α-acetolactate decarboxylase enzyme (ALDC) that converts the diacetyl precursor,
α-acetolactate, directly into acetoin.
2.2. Intended use of BY-927
Berkeley Fermentation Science Inc. has proposed the use of BY-927 in brewing to prevent the
formation of the vicinal diketone diacetyl (IUPAC name butane-2,3-dione). Diacetyl is a small
molecule produced as a byproduct of yeast metabolism during beer fermentation1–3. If present at
concentrations above the threshold of human detection, diacetyl will impart an undesirable
buttery flavor. The biochemical pathway that leads to diacetyl production during beer
fermentation is outlined in Figure 1.
The chemical precursor of diacetyl is α-acetolactate, which is produced by actively fermenting
yeasts as a metabolic intermediate in the valine biosynthesis pathway. A proportion of the
α-acetolactate produced is excreted from the cell, where it is spontaneously decarboxylated to
produce diacetyl4. Due to the relatively low flavor detection threshold for diacetyl, even small
quantities that are produced by this process can negatively impact the flavor and aroma of
beer5.
The detrimental impact of diacetyl on beer flavor has motivated the brewing community to
develop strategies to minimize its concentration in beer prior to packaging5. Two predominant
strategies exist for this. The first is to perform a ‘diacetyl rest’, in which brewers leave the yeast
and beer in the fermenter for 1-30 days after fermentation. During this period of days or weeks,

the yeast will slowly uptake diacetyl from the beer and reduce it first to acetoin, then again to
butane-2,3-diol. A diacetyl rest leads to a gradual elimination of diacetyl from the beer, and the
diacetyl concentration will eventually fall below the flavor detection threshold, at which point the
beer can be packaged. Butane-2,3-diol has a relatively high flavor detection threshold and does
not impact the final aroma or taste of the beer. As the yeast are no longer vigorously fermenting
during this period, very little additional diacetyl is produced. However, the yeast may not be
active enough to metabolize all diacetyl present, and any remaining α-acetolactate still has the
potential to become diacetyl after the beer is packaged. In addition, the added time increases
the cost of brewing.
5
A second commonly employed method that brewers use to manage diacetyl is to add an
α-acetolactate decarboxylase (ALDC) enzyme to their beer fermentations6,7. ALDC directly
converts α-acetolactate to acetoin8, thereby circumventing diacetyl formation entirely (Figure 1).
Several purified ALDC enzymes derived from food-grade bacteria are commercially available for
this purpose9,10. However, due to its unpredictable performance, most breweries do not
supplement their fermentations with ALDC, or do so in concert with a diacetyl rest. Additionally,
if the enzyme degrades before α-acetolactate has been secreted out of the cell, then diacetyl
may still form in packaged beer.

formed naturally during the brewing process. Fermentable sugars are consumed by yeast through
glycolysis, and pyruvate is converted to α-acetolactate, a metabolic intermediate in the valine

The practice of dry hopping - adding flavoring hops directly to beer in the fermentation tank -
also has a significant impact on the production of diacetyl in beer. The hop cones used for dry
hopping contain amylase enzymes that hydrolyze oligosaccharides to release shorter, more
readily fermentable sugars. When added to beer fermentations, these amylases hydrolyze
non-fermentable oligosaccharides in the wort and release shorter chain sugars that yeast can
readily ferment. This release of short-chain sugars re-initiates yeast fermentation, leading to the
production of additional diacetyl. Dry hopping thus creates an additional challenge for brewers
6
concerned with diacetyl production, and it can further extend brewing timelines by forcing an
even longer diacetyl rest11,12. Addition of purified ALDC at the same time as dry hopping can
help minimize this hop-catalyzed diacetyl release, but as mentioned above, the efficacy of ALDC

addition is highly variable across different fermentations.
Because neither method is completely effective, significant efforts have been made to
genetically engineer brewers yeast strains that either produce less diacetyl, or remove diacetyl
by converting it to butane-2,3-diol. A variety of genetic strategies towards these ends have been
explored. These include: 1) lowering the activity of genes that produce alpha-acetolactate13–16,
2) increasing the activity of genes that convert alpha-acetolactate to subsequent metabolites in
the valine biosynthesis pathway13, 3) increasing the activity of genes that convert diacetyl to
acetoin and butane-2,3-diol13, and 4) heterologous expression of ALDC in yeast17,18. Of these,
ALDC expression in yeast has most consistently been shown to reduce the concentration of
diacetyl in beer17,19–26.
To create an ALDC-expressing brewer's yeast strain that would shorten the brewing timeline
and obviate the need for purified ALDC, we engineered BY-927 to express the ALDC from
Acetobacter aceti. Production of the ALDC enzyme inside the cell is a reliable method that is
robust to process variation, resulting in a yeast strain that does not accumulate α-acetolactate
and finished beer with diacetyl below sensory threshold levels.
BY-927 is used as any other commercial yeast would be used in the beer manufacturing
process.
2.3. Host microorganism
2.3.1. History of use
Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been used in food and beverage production for thousands of
years. The first evidence of beer production comes from ancient Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, although
spontaneous fermentations resulting in beer were likely happening far earlier than that, as wild
yeasts in the air will ferment most grain left unattended27. Similarly, archaeological evidence of
wine production dates to 5400 BC Iran28, but spontaneous fermentations of grapes into wine by
wild yeasts were likely happening even earlier. Ancient peoples utilized yeast in the production
of other fermented foods and baked goods29. Today yeast is an integral component in many
industries, and millions of tons are produced commercially each year. The food and beverage
applications of S. cerevisiae range from alcoholic beverages to bread, coffee, and chocolate, to
name a few. S. cerevisiae has also served as a model organism in scientific research and was
the first eukaryote to have its genome completely sequenced.
The parent yeast strain from which BY-927 was derived is an industrial brewing strain of
Saccharomyces cerevisiae that has been used extensively in commercial beer production for
decades. Like many industrial brewing strains, the parent yeast strain is tetraploid.
7
2.3.2. Taxonomy
The parent strain is classified as belonging to the Saccharomyces cerevisiae species. A
considerable amount of genetic diversity exists within the species S. cerevisiae, and genome
sequencing efforts have covered thousands of individuals30. The strains used for various
industrial food and beverage manufacturing processes have evolved considerably from their
wild ancestors, which likely inhabited primeval forests31. These industrial strains have been
categorized into distinct clades: one containing sake yeasts, one containing wine yeasts, a
mixed clade containing bread yeasts, and two separate beer yeast clades30.
2.4. Donor organisms
2.4.1. Taxonomy
The following organisms contributed DNA to BY-927:
Acetobacter aceti
BY-927 contains a gene that encodes an ALDC derived from Acetobacter aceti, a gram-negative
bacterium belonging to the acetic acid bacteria family and a food microorganism used in

commercial vinegar production32. Acetobacter species oxidize ethanol to form acetic acid, the
main chemical component of vinegar. A. aceti has a long history of safe use in the production of
vinegar, which dates back more than 5,000 years.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
BY-927 contains promoter and terminator DNA sequences derived from the S. cerevisiae strain
S288C. The history of use of this species is given in Section 2.2.1. The S288C strain, a widely
used lab strain, was isolated through genetic crosses for biochemical studies by Robert
Mortimer33 and serves as the reference genome sequence in the Saccharomyces Genome
Database. S288C is mainly derived from a wild yeast strain that was isolated from figs; minor
portions of its genetic material are derived from baking yeasts and other yeasts isolated from
fruit. In addition, the sequences isolated from S288C are 99% identical to the sequences found
in the parent strain.
2.4.2. Genetic material from donor organisms
The ALDC gene sequence
The ALDC gene sequence encodes a decarboxylase that converts α-acetolactate to acetoin34–36.
Yeast biosynthesizes α-acetolactate as an intermediate in the valine biosynthesis pathway.
During fermentation, excess α-acetolactate is secreted into the wort, where it is spontaneously
decarboxylated to produce diacetyl4, which imparts an undesirable butter-like flavor to finished
beer. ALDC converts α-acetolactate directly into acetoin, thereby preventing diacetyl formation
8
and ensuring that excess α-acetolactate does not accumulate and form diacetyl in packaged
beer.
The A. aceti ALDC gene was previously shown to reduce diacetyl production when expressed in
brewer’s yeast23–25. BY-927 expresses a truncated variant of the originally identified A. aceti
ALDC gene, as this variant has been found to possess greater activity than the original
sequence23.

The promoter sequence
The promoter sequence (i.e. the genetic element immediately 5’ of the integrated gene) is
derived from S. cerevisiae strain S288C. Promoter sequences define where transcription of a
gene by RNA polymerase begins. The promoter used in this strain consists of a 800 bp
fragment ending at the base pair immediately preceding the ATG start codon of its associated
gene.
The terminator sequence
9
The terminator sequence (i.e. the genetic element immediately 3’ of the integrated gene) is
derived from S. cerevisiae strain S288C. Terminator sequences provide a signal that triggers the
release of mRNA from the transcription complex during gene expression. The terminator used in
this strain consists of a 225 bp fragment starting immediately after the stop codon of its
associated gene.
2.5. The modified microorganism
2.5.1. General construction strategy
The strain was constructed with a single genomic integration. The molecular tools and practices

used during the construction of BY-927 are standard to the field of molecular biology and yeast
genetics.
2.5.1.1. Integration of the ALDC insert
First, we generated the construct containing the genetic material described in Section 2.4.2
using standard methods of genetic cloning as follows: the gene coding for the ALDC enzyme
was synthesized by oligonucleotide assembly and inserted into a cloning vector, which was then
sequenced. The promoter and terminator sequences were amplified by PCR from S. cerevisiae
strain S288C genomic DNA and inserted into cloning vectors, which were then sequenced.
After each plasmid was sequenced, further cloning to generate the insert was performed by
Golden Gate Assembly, a restriction enzyme-based cloning method that avoids mutations
introduced by PCR-based methods37. The promoter, gene, and terminator plasmids were
assembled into a single plasmid using Golden Gate Assembly. The resulting plasmid was
sequenced to confirm that it contained all three genetic elements and then linearized using a
restriction enzyme.
The resulting DNA fragment containing the ALDC gene under the regulation of a native S.
cerevisiae promoter and terminator, was directly integrated into the genome of the parent strain
at a single locus.
In addition to the linear fragment, transformation of the parent strain also used an integration aid
plasmid. This plasmid encodes the tools for genetic incision, including an endonuclease that
specifically cuts the target locus. The plasmid also encodes an antibiotic resistance gene that
confers resistance to G418, which allows the cell to maintain the plasmid through selection by
growth on G418-containing medium. This plasmid was used only as a co-transformation aid and
none of its genetic material was integrated into the cell. Following confirmation of the
integration, the plasmid was removed by passaging on YPD medium.
2.5.2. Screening method for transformants
10
The transformed strain was plated onto G418-containing medium in order to select transformed
cells. Confirmation of the integration event at the single locus across four homologous
chromosomes was conducted by diagnostic PCR (Figure 3).
The presence of the insert was confirmed using two sets of primer pairs, targeting the 5' end
and the 3' end of the insert (Figure 3b). Each primer pair contains one primer that binds inside
the insert and one primer that binds outside the insert. The intended integration results in PCR
bands with both primer pairs, whereas the non-engineered parental control does not produce
bands. Homozygosity was confirmed using an additional pair of primers that flanks the insert at
the engineered locus. Integration across four homologous chromosomes results in a single
band, and the engineered strain produces a larger band compared to the non-engineered
parental control due to the presence of the insert. Incomplete integration, where the insert is not
integrated at all four chromosomes, results in both bands.

2.5.3. Genetic characterization of the modified microorganism
2.5.3.1. The loss of the plasmid containing the antibiotic resistance gene
Following confirmation of the integration event, the integration aid plasmid was removed from
the engineered strain by passaging on YPD medium. Loss of the plasmid was confirmed by
testing for growth on YPD medium containing the antibiotic G418 and confirming sensitivity.
BY-927 is unable to grow on a G418-containing medium, like the non-engineered parent strain.
Therefore, any antibiotic resistance genes were removed from the final strain and no antibiotic
resistance is conferred to BY-927.
2.5.3.2. Genetic stability of the modifications
The inserted DNA is integrated into the S. cerevisiae genome at the target locus across four
homologous chromosomes. In previous research, we have demonstrated that homozygosity is
critically important for integration stability38. If engineering results in heterozygosity, the
modifications are highly unstable, often reverting to the parental allele within only a few
generations. On the other hand, integration across four homologous chromosomes is stable
over hundreds of generations.
We confirmed the genetic stability of the strain over 100 generations by serially passaging
BY-927 on YPD medium. After passaging, the presence of the inserted DNA was re-confirmed
by diagnostic PCR using the parent strain as a control.
2.5.3.3. The introduced DNA is the expected sequence
To confirm that the correct sequence was inserted, we used PCR to amplify the locus containing
the ALDC insert with primers that bind outside the engineered region (represented by primers 1
and 4 in Figure 3b). The resulting DNA amplicon was sequenced and compared to an expected
reference sequence of the engineered region. The actual DNA sequence and the intended
reference sequence matched exactly, thus confirming that the engineering work produced the
expected outcome.
2.5.4. BY-927 and its parent strain are highly genetically similar
The genome of all S. cerevisiae strains contain long terminal repeat sequences known as δ
elements. These δ elements are the remnants of Ty1 and Ty2 transposon integration events39.
The number and location of these δ elements are strain-specific and serve as an effective
means of distinguishing between strains of S. cerevisiae40. We verified the genetic relationship
between the parent strain and the engineered strain by amplifying these δ sequences by PCR
with primers 5’-GTGGATTTTTATTCCAAC-3’ and 5’-TCAACAATGGAATCCCAAC-3’
(delta2/delta12 primer pair), a technique called interdelta analysis. PCR amplification resulted in
identical banding patterns from both strains. We therefore conclude that the engineered strain
and its parent strain are highly genetically similar.
12
2.6. Method of manufacture of BY-927
2.6.1. Overview of manufacturing method
BY-927 is manufactured in accordance with Good Manufacturing Practices. Production is
conducted at a fermentation facility with established procedures and equipment suitable for
large-scale contained production of S. cerevisiae. At all steps, appropriate analyses are
conducted to ensure that the yeast meets the finished product specifications.
BY-927 is started from frozen glycerol stocks by streaking directly onto YPD agar plates, grown
in liquid medium in increasing volumes, and inoculated into a propagation vessel with aeration.
Quality control specifications are measured throughout the process; if a lot does not meet target

specifications, then the batch is rejected. When the culture has depleted all fermentable sugar,
the yeast cell mass is collected as a concentrated liquid slurry.
2.6.2. Raw materials
All raw materials and processing aids used in the manufacture of BY-927 are used in
accordance with U.S. regulations, are the subject of an effective food contact notification, or are
concluded to be GRAS for the intended use. The raw materials are standard food-grade
ingredients used in traditional yeast production and include malt extract or molasses (the carbon
source) and other essential nutrients. The only other material used is a food-safe, 100%
vegetable oil-based defoamer, which is commonly used in commercial beer production. None of
the components used in the manufacturing process or in the final ingredient include or are
derived from one of the nine major food allergens (milk, eggs, fish, Crustacean shellfish, tree
nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, or sesame).
2.6.3. Lab stage
The manufacturing process begins with a series of carefully controlled serial steps with cultures
being used to inoculate successively larger volumes. Fermentation is performed under
controlled conditions. A brief overview of these steps is listed below.
1. Master stock cultures of yeast strains are stored in cryogenic conditions at -80°C in
glycerol.
2. Propagation begins by inoculating BY-927 onto a YPD (Yeast extract, Peptone,
Dextrose) agar plate from frozen master stocks with a single-use sterile loop.
3. After growth, colonies are transferred into 40 mL YPD liquid medium and grown for 24
hours.
4. The 40 mL pre-culture is sequentially transferred into increasing volumes in propagation
medium (1L, 20 L; see Section 2.6.4 for a description of the ingredients).
5. Microbial QC is performed on the final starter culture.
2.6.4. Propagation and recovery
13
The yeast from the lab is inoculated into propagation vessels, grown until it reaches peak cell
count, and harvested. A brief overview of these steps is listed below.
1. To prepare the propagation medium, malt extract or molasses is mixed with water and
essential nutrients, brought to a boil, and sterilized in a large steam-heated vessel.
Propagation media is transferred to cylindroconical propagation vessels (fermenters) and
diluted to target density with sterile water.
2. The starter culture is added to the propagation medium.
3. The propagation is conducted at 24°C. Fermenters are aerated throughout propagation
using sterile air.
4. Sugar consumption and pH are monitored throughout the growth cycle. When the culture
has depleted all fermentable sugar, the temperature is lowered to 4°C and the cells are
separated through natural processes of flocculation and settling. The yeast cell mass is
collected as a concentrated liquid slurry.
5. Cell counts, viability measurements, and microbial QC are performed on all vessels.
6. Yeast is packaged in FDA-approved, sterilized HDPE containers and stored at 4°C until
used to inoculate a beer fermentation. Containers are shipped overnight in an insulated
box with ice packs.
To prevent contamination, the propagation medium is sterilized and all equipment is carefully
cleaned and sanitized. Fermenters are cleaned in place with base and rinsed to neutral pH, then
heat sanitized prior to filling with sterile propagation medium. Transfer lines are heat sanitized.
Fermenters are sampled at many points throughout the process for quality control.
2.7. Product specifications
The specifications for liquid yeast are measured for every batch. All analytical methods used are
validated for their intended use. If a lot of finished, food-grade liquid yeast slurry does not meet

the quality control specifications, then the batch is rejected.
Viability is determined with an automated cell counter using AOPI fluorescence and with a
hemocytometer using methylene blue staining. pH measurements are taken using a benchtop
pH meter. Contaminating microorganisms are detected by swabbing to identify the presence of
ATP and by plating samples on microbiological growth mediums, including non-differential
medium (MYPG) and differential media (MYPG plus cycloheximide, MYPG plus copper, WLD,
MRS). Lead levels are quantified using ICP-MS. Product specifications are listed in Table 1.

PART 3:
DIETARY EXPOSURE
3.1. Intended use of BY-927
Berkeley Fermentation Science Inc. has proposed the use of BY-927 in brewing to reduce
diacetyl production below sensory threshold levels (see Section 2.2). Diacetyl is a compound
with a buttery, butterscotch-like flavor that has a detrimental impact on beer flavor and can be
difficult and time-consuming to remove from beer. The yeast can be used as a drop-in
replacement for other commercial yeasts in the beer manufacturing process.
3.2. Levels of use of the substance
BY-927 is used as any other commercial yeast would be used in the beer manufacturing
process and is substitutional for any other S. cerevisiae strain currently used in beer
fermentation. We recommend that BY-927 be inoculated at a pitch rate of 7.50E+05 – 1.50E+06
cells per mL per degree Plato of wort, as is standard industrial practice. Its use is not expected
to increase dietary exposure to S. cerevisiae.
3.3. Dietary exposure
3.3.1. History of consumption
Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been used in food production for thousands of years, as
discussed above in Section 2.3.1.
ALDC is widespread among acetic acid and lactic acid producing bacteria, including those used
in food production (vinegar, yogurt, cheese, kombucha, beer, wine, cocoa processing), and may

therefore be found in various food products. Purified ALDC enzyme is also commonly used as a
processing aid in the brewing process to prevent diacetyl formation. TTB has formally approved
an ALDC enzyme preparation produced by Bacillus licheniformis containing an ALDC gene from
Bacillus brevis for use as a processing aid in the production of beer41. This enzyme is also the
subject of a GRAS Notice (GRN No. 587) that received a "No Questions" letter from the
FDA42,43.
Diacetyl and its associated metabolites (acetoin and butane-2,3-diol) occur naturally in many
foods and beverages common to the human diet44–46. All three can be found in a variety of
fermented products, including beer47,48, wine49, and cheese50. Diacetyl and acetoin are also
major contributors to the flavor and aroma profile of butter and are added to butter substitutes
and various other foods to impart a characteristic butter flavor51,52.
3.3.2. Estimated consumption
Exposure to the engineered yeast in finished beer will be extremely limited because yeast is
removed from beer as part of the standard brewing process. Removing yeast from finished beer
16
is intrinsic to the brewing process: standard industrial brewer’s yeast exhibit a strong propensity
to sediment at the bottom of the fermentation vessel as fermentable sugars are exhausted. In a
typical brewing process, the yeast is added to the wort and allowed to ferment at 64–74°C until
fermentable sugars are fully consumed and standard gravity has stabilized. Once stabilized, the
fermentation vessel is cooled to 0°C to promote sedimentation. After sedimentation is complete,
the sedimented yeast is removed from the finished beer by racking the yeast from the bottom of
the vessel. Using this method, only trace levels of yeast will remain in the finished beer. It is
worth noting the common misconception that the haze in the hazy IPA beer style is due to
unsedimented yeast; however, the haze is actually derived from high molecular weight
complexes between proline-rich proteins and hop-derived polyphenols53–55. Indeed, finished
beer that contains residual yeast is considered a strong character flaw and a source of
off-flavors. Additional methods of clarification include centrifugation and filtration56,57, which
remove all yeast that may be present. In light of this, it is extremely unlikely that beer made with
BY-927 would contain a significant amount of yeast in solution.
When purified ALDC is added during the brewing process, it is not specifically removed from the
final product. BY-927, however, produces the ALDC enzyme within the cell, and is removed from
the final beer. Therefore, consumption of ALDC from beer produced with BY-927 will be
negligible compared with beer made with purified ALDC, which is a standard brewing ingredient.
It is also worth noting that the only full-length yeast-derived proteins documented in finished
beer are those that are cell-wall associated58–60. In addition, glycolytic enzymes represent
30-60% of the total yeast proteome61 and ribosomal proteins represent another 30%62,63, so
proteins involved in other cellular functions are expressed at lower levels. Because the ALDC
protein is not cell-wall associated, glycolytic, or ribosomal and is contained within the BY-927
cell cytoplasm, and because yeast is removed from beer before consumption, it is extremely
unlikely that ALDC will be present in appreciable amounts in finished beer. Therefore,
consumption of ALDC from beer produced with BY-927 will be negligible.
The modification to BY-927 results in lower diacetyl and lower diacetyl potential (the potential for
excess α-acetolactate to form diacetyl after packaging). It does not result in the production of

new compounds or increased concentrations of existing compounds. Similar to non-engineered
strains, BY-927 reduces acetoin to butane-2,3-diol. The only difference is the time it takes to
reach that endpoint, since non-engineered strains must first import diacetyl and reduce it to
acetoin.
Beer produced with BY-927 will contain these compounds at concentrations that are similar to
what is already present in consumed beer and similar to or lower than what is present in other
foods and beverages, and therefore within levels safe for consumption. In order to quantify
these compounds in beer made with BY-927, brewing trials were conducted at commercial scale
and the beers were subject to analysis by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS)
and gas chromatography mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The concentrations are listed in Table 3,

3.3.3. Toxicology and comparison data
Acetoin is a synthetic flavoring substance and adjuvant that is generally recognized as safe
(GRAS) for its intended use by the FDA (21 CFR 182.60). Diacetyl is a substance permitted for
direct addition to human food that is affirmed as GRAS (21 CFR 184.1278). Independent
reviews conducted by both FEMA and the FAO/WHO determined that there is no safety concern
regarding the use and consumption of these compounds based on current levels of intake. The
judgment of the FEMA expert panel was that these substances are GRAS77.
JECFA evaluated diacetyl and acetoin at its fifty-first meeting78; the report states that although
intake exceeds the threshold for Class II (540 µg/person/day), diacetyl and acetoin occur
endogenously in humans and are metabolized to innocuous products. In addition, the intake of
acetoin as a natural component of food is greater than that from its use as a flavoring agent.
The report concluded that a NOAEL was not required for evaluation, and that both diacetyl and
acetoin are of no safety concern based on current intake.
Butane-2,3-diol is not typically used as a flavoring agent and no repeated dose toxicity data is

available. However, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) reported that no toxic effects were
observed from a 2-year study in rats for the structural analogue butane-1,3-diol (NOAEL of 5000
mg/kg bw/d)79. In addition, butane-2,3-diol is present as a natural component of beer and other
18
foods and beverages. JECFA also discussed butane-2,3-diol at its fifty-first meeting as a
metabolic product of diacetyl and acetoin metabolism; the report states that all substances
evaluated are metabolized to innocuous products and that these products, including
butane-2,3-diol, are not of concern.
The concentrations of diacetyl, acetoin, and butane-2,3-diol in beer produced with BY-927 will
be similar to or less than the levels in commercial beers, which are currently consumed (see
Table 3 for a comparison). Therefore, we expect that any exposure to these compounds from
beer made with BY-927 is substitutional. Based on this, we can conclude that exposure to these
compounds is unlikely to cause a safety concern.
19
PART 4:
SELF-LIMITING LEVELS OF USE
There are no proposed restrictions on the use of BY-927.
Use of BY-927 requires no alterations to the standard pitch rate - the amount of yeast added to
wort to start a fermentation. Regardless of pitch rate, the quantity of yeast cells present at the
end of the fermentation should not be significantly different. In addition, yeast is removed from
finished beer prior to packaging, leaving only trace levels in the finished product.

PART 6:
NARRATIVE
6.1. Overview of safety assessment
In this section, we present evidence that the modified S. cerevisiae strain, BY-927, is safe for
use in industrial brewing. BY-927 produces cleaner tasting beer by preventing the formation of
the common off-flavor diacetyl. Diacetyl concentrations are kept below sensory threshold
throughout fermentation and after packaging. We detail the safety of the host and donor strains,
the ALDC enzyme, the gene regulatory regions, and the small molecule composition of beer
made with BY-927, using both targeted and untargeted methods.
6.2. Safety assessment of the host strain
The host is an industrial brewing strain of S. cerevisiae that has been used extensively in
commercial beer production for decades. S. cerevisiae has an extensive history of safe use; it
has been used for more than 7,000 years by humans in fermentation processes, such as bread
leavening and beer and wine production. Fermentation products of this yeast are not associated
with adverse effects in humans (when consumed in recommended quantities for alcohol intake).
S. cerevisiae is considered GRAS through its use in the brewing, baking, and winemaking
industries. In the 27th report of The Scientific Committee for Human Food of the European
Community, the authors state that Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a safe history of use in food
and does not produce toxins.
6.3. Safety assessment of the donor strains
Donor strain Acetobacter aceti is a benign, gram-negative bacterium that has an extensive
history of safe use. Acetic acid bacteria, including Acetobacter aceti, have been used in vinegar
production for thousands of years. The first recorded evidence of vinegar production dates to
around 3000 B.C. from the Ancient Babylonians although spontaneous fermentations (including
the souring of wine) were likely happening far earlier. Members of the Acetobacter genus,

including A. aceti, are still used in commercial vinegar production today. A. aceti is on the FDA's
list of GRAS microorganisms; the EPA has included it as exempt from review under certain use
conditions in the Toxic Substances Control Act given its long history of safe use and its
classification as a low risk organism (CFR 725.420). There are no reports suggesting that A.
aceti is pathogenic to humans or animals, despite it often coming into contact with humans. It
does not produce toxins, enzymes, or virulence factors associated with pathogenicity or
allergenicity.
The safety assessment of donor strain S. cerevisiae has been previously established.
22
6.4. Safety assessment of the ALDC enzyme
Source: Acetobacter aceti
Enzyme name: α-Acetolactate decarboxylase
Reaction: α-acetolactate → acetoin + CO
2
ALDC catalyzes the conversion of α-acetolactate to acetoin, thereby circumventing diacetyl
formation and removing excess α-acetolactate which has the potential to form diacetyl after
packaging. The ALDC from A. aceti is well characterized and has previously been shown to
catalyze this reaction; it does not encode some other activity35.
This enzyme is widespread among acetic acid and lactic acid bacteria, several species of which
are used in food production. Purified ALDC enzyme is also commonly used as a processing aid
in the production of beer, and several enzyme preparations derived from food-grade bacteria
are commercially available for this purpose80. One of these, derived from Bacillus brevis, is the
subject of a GRAS Notice (GRN No. 587) that received a "No Questions" letter from the FDA.
6.4.1. Allergenic/Toxigenic potential of the ALDC enzyme
It is extremely unlikely that intracellular ALDC could cause a food allergy. This is based on the
following considerations:
1. The vast majority of enzymes present in the natural world are not allergens, and a wide
variety of enzyme classes and structures are naturally present in plant and animal based
foods.
2. The concentration of ALDC in finished beer is anticipated to be nominal (see Section
3.3.2). The total amount of ALDC protein is a small fraction of the total yeast protein and
because the ALDC is expressed inside the cell, and because the yeast is removed from
beer before consumption, only trace levels of ALDC protein or peptide fragments will be
found in finished beer.
3. This enzyme is derived from a microorganism that has been used in food production for
centuries. In addition, the ALDC gene is widespread among acetic acid and lactic acid
bacteria18, so ALDC may be found in food products such as vinegar, yogurt, and cheese.
Therefore, the enzyme already has a history of safe consumption.
4. Purified ALDC is used in commercial beer production. Therefore, the enzyme already
has a history of safe consumption and is already present in the brewing process.
In order to further evaluate the possibility that the ALDC enzyme will induce a reaction in an
already sensitized individual, amino acid sequence similarity to known allergens was assessed.
Following the guidelines developed by FAO/WHO, 200181, 82 and modified by Codex
Alimentarius Commission, 200983, the ALDC amino acid sequence was compared to allergens
23
from the Food Allergy Research and Resource Program (FARRP) allergen protein database
(http://allergenonline.org) as follows:
We conducted an alignment of the expressed protein to each of the allergens in the FARRP.
E-values < 0.05 were considered significant. No significant similarity was found between the

ALDC amino acid sequence and any of the allergens from the FARRP database. This was
repeated using a sliding window of 80 amino acid segments of the ALDC amino acid sequence;
no matches with more than 35% identity were found. In addition, a search for 100% identity
over 8 contiguous amino acids was completed; no matches were found.
We next set out to determine whether the expressed enzyme is similar to known toxins,
venoms, or virulence factors. We extracted all peptide sequences in the UniProt and Virulence
Factor databases described in Table 5, then queried these sequences with the expressed
ALDC protein using the BLASTP algorithm and default parameter settings84. In total, this
queried more than 142,000 sequences. E-values < 0.05 were considered significant. All hits
obtained during this search had E-values > 0.05, indicating that the alignments were due to
short random sequence identities and that ALDC is not homologous to any of the annotated
toxins, venoms, or virulence factors in these databases.
In addition to the assessments based on sequence alignment, we also analyzed the ALDC
protein using ToxinPred285,86, a web-based prediction tool for protein toxicity, set to default
parameter settings. This tool uses a hybrid approach combining a similarity-based approach
using BLAST, a motif-based approach using MERCI, and a machine learning approach to
predict protein toxicity. Based on the overall score, which is computed by integrating the three
different methods, the protein is categorized as toxic or nontoxic. The prediction was that ALDC
is nontoxic.
On the basis of the available evidence, we concluded that the ALDC protein does not pose any
food allergenic or toxigenic concerns.

6.5. Safety assessment of the promoter and terminator sequences
The promoter and terminator sequences were isolated from S. cerevisiae. The safety
assessment of S. cerevisiae has already been established and since the regulatory sequences
do not code for proteins, the source of this material does not raise a safety concern.
6.6. Presence of unintended gene products
As an additional measure, we tested whether the insert contained open reading frames (ORFs)
beyond the one that was intentionally introduced. We searched for ORFs of more than 100
codons using the NCBI ORF Finder (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/orffinder/). Analysis using the
NCBI ORF Finder shows that the integrated region contains one putative ORF. However, it is
contained within the promoter and therefore corresponds to a sequence already present in S.
cerevisiae. In the unlikely event that this ORF is translated into a protein, it would be found in
both BY-927 and the parent strain. As the parent strain has never been shown to release

unwanted products corresponding to this sequence, neither should BY-927.
6.7. Safety assessment of BY-927
6.7.1. Safety of BY-927
BY-927 is classified as S. cerevisiae, a species that is known to be non-pathogenic and safe for
use in industrial food and beverage processes. BY-927 is non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic. No
genes encoding for virulence factors, protein toxins, or enzymes involved in the synthesis of
toxins, allergens, or other undesirable substances are expected based on our knowledge of the
strain, the gene sequences, and the promoters and terminators.
6.7.2. Changes in brewing procedures or beer composition as a consequence of BY-927
fermentation
The use of BY-927 does not require changes to brewing procedures. BY-927 functions as a
drop-in replacement for beer created with any industrial brewing strain, in that a fermentation
performed with BY-927 will be substantially equivalent to a standard fermentation.
The only difference between BY-927 and a non-engineered strain is the diacetyl profile during
fermentation. BY-927 consistently keeps diacetyl levels low (and well below the flavor threshold)
throughout fermentation, while non-engineered strains produce a spike in diacetyl levels at the
25
start of fermentation. By the end of primary fermentation, though, diacetyl levels are similar. If
purified ALDC is added at the start, the diacetyl profile during primary fermentation will be
similar to that of BY-927. However, a significant difference is noticeable after dry hopping: while
BY-927 maintains diacetyl levels below the flavor threshold, non-engineered strains produce a
secondary increase in diacetyl, prolonging the brewing process as brewers wait for levels to
decrease.

10X phosphate buffered saline at pH 7.4 and 50 mg/L 3,4-diaminopyridine, which acted as a
derivatizing agent. The samples were incubated at 60°C for 1 hour, then extracted with ethyl
acetate. The resulting ethyl acetate was dried under vacuum, then subsequently dissolved in

Metabolites were separated using a linear gradient of 3-10% acetonitrile supplemented with

Diacetyl was detected by mass spectrometry with selected ion monitoring (SIM) at specific m/z
values. We confirmed the chemical identity of diacetyl based on the injection of an authentic
standard, which matched perfectly in retention time and in mass spectrum. Quantification was
accomplished by comparing peak areas to standard curves generated by spiking known
concentrations of isotopically labeled diacetyl (diacetyl-d6) into a beer matrix, then following the

standard curves generated by spiking known concentrations of target compounds into a beer
matrix, then following the same extraction protocol (Figure 6).

6.7.4. Untargeted metabolomic profiling of BY-927
The modifications resulted, as expected, in reduced diacetyl. However, unexpected effects are
also possible. In order to evaluate whether the genetic modification introduced unexpected
small molecule production that might pose a risk for consumption, un-targeted metabolomics
was performed on beer produced with BY-927, its non-engineered parent strain, and three other
commonly-used industrial brewing strains. We analyzed these samples by gas chromatography
mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to measure volatile molecules and by electrospray ionization liquid
chromatography mass spectrometry (ESI-LC-MS) in positive ion detection mode to measure
non-volatile molecules.
To perform the GC-MS analysis, quadruplicate cultures of the strains listed above were
inoculated into 80 mL of malt extract. Anaerobic fermentation then proceeded over 5 days at
20°C. The additional non-engineered yeast strains were included in this study to help
benchmark the variation in small molecule concentrations without genetic engineering. Upon
completion of fermentation, the yeast-free beer-like samples were pH adjusted, dosed with
2-octanol and 12-[[(cyclohexylamino)carbonyl]amino]-dodecanoic acid as analytical internal
standards, then extracted with ethyl acetate. The resulting ethyl acetate was treated with
sodium sulfate to remove excess water, then injected onto an Agilent 6890 GC fitted with a
high-polarity, ultra-inert column (Agilent G3903-63008) and coupled to an Agilent 5973N
single-quadrupole mass analyzer. Each sample was resolved over a temperature ramp from
40°C to 250°C over 26.25 min, with a total per-sample run time of 35.25 min including low and
high temperature holding time. The mass detector collected signals ranging from 30 to 300 m/z.
Raw signal was normalized to the intensity of the 2-octanol internal standard before further
processing. Figure 7 shows the total ion chromatograms of a representative sample from each
of BY-927 and its non-engineered parent, showing that the two ferments are highly similar.
For more comprehensive data analysis the raw GC-MS data files were uploaded onto the
XCMSOnline server (https://xcmsonline.scripps.edu/landing_page.php?pgcontent=mainPage)87,
which automates retention time alignment, peak alignment, intensity normalization, and then
identifies statistically significant, intensity-differentiated mass features. The preset “GC-MS /
single quad” parameter was selected for data processing, which yielded 127 mass features

among the five yeast strains upon multigroup analysis. We then searched for differentially
increased molecules in BY-927 compared to its parent in paired analysis while applying three
selection filters: (1) q-value less than 0.05, (2) peak intensity fold change less than 3, and (3)
fold-change over the non-engineered parent greater than two times the maximum intensity
difference among any pair of non-engineered yeast strains. This third filter is designed to
30
eliminate features that may seem differentially increased in BY-927 but are not biologically
significant when considering existing variation among non-engineered strains. Note, however,
that for this dataset, the third filter was not necessary because there were no features remaining
after filters 1 and 2 were applied. We did not detect any statistically and biologically significant
mass features increased in BY-927 compared to its parent. We concluded that GC-MS analysis
did not find molecules that warranted further safety assessment.
To perform the ESI-LC-MS analysis, fermented samples created in the same method as above
were processed through C solid phase extraction columns (Waters Sep-Pak WAT020515).
18
Columns were equilibrated with deionized water, then loaded with 5 mL of sample. After the
samples were pulled through by vacuum, the columns were rinsed with 5 mL deionized water
and eluted with 3 mL methanol. The eluate was dried overnight under vacuum to leave behind a
dark yellow film, then subsequently dissolved in 5% acetonitrile. 5 μL of this solution was
injected onto the Agilent 1290 Infinity II LC equipped with a C column (Agilent 959757-902)
18
coupled to a C guard column (Agilent 821725-901). The mobile phase was dosed with 0.1%
18
formic acid and ramped from 5% acetonitrile in water to 30% acetonitrile over 30 min, with a
total per-sample run time of 45 min including holding time. The Agilent 6130 single-quadrupole
mass detector collected signals ranging from 100 to 1,000 m/z. All sample vials were held at
4°C in the autosampler throughout the duration of the queue. Figure 8 shows the total ion
chromatograms of a representative sample from each of BY-927 and its parent, showing that the
two ferments are highly similar. This result is expected because features derived from wort
which are not altered by yeast fermentation contribute a larger percentage of the signal in
LC-MS data.
For data analysis, the raw LC-MS data was uploaded onto the XCMS online server and
underwent the same pre-processing steps as listed above for the GC-MS data, using the preset
“HPLC / single quad” parameter. Among the five yeast strains, there were 837 mass features
detected. Here a mass feature is defined as a unique [m/z, retention time] pair. After applying
the same statistical and biological thresholds as above, we did not detect significantly increased
features in BY-927 compared to its parent. We concluded that the LC-MS analysis did not find
molecules that warranted further safety assessment.
