6.2. Molecular Confirmation of the Lack Hazards That May Pose Food Consumption Risks
As context for the molecular characterization of POMM, this section provides some underlying
information on the life cycle of P. pulmonarius, with particular emphasis on morphology and karyology,
and the expected, but small differences between the fruiting body and mycelia characterized by Joh et al.
(2007) and Wang et al. (2017). In order to demonstrate that any potential toxin or allergens would not
be present in POMM, Mushlabs fully characterized the genome of POMM, completed a transcriptomic
analysis, and concluded with a proteomic analysis. The results of these studies demonstrated that there

were no proteins in POMM that could be linked to potential allergenicity or toxicity, and that the
molecular analyses support the conclusions of information provided herein that POMM does not pose a
food safety concern.
6.2.1 Differences Between Fungi and Plants
Plants and fungi constitute two distinct biological kingdoms of eukaryotes, each of which has evolved a
distinct biology. Although historical and superficial structural analogies once led to the classification of
fungi within the plant kingdom (e.g., stationary nature and presence of cell walls), key advancements in
understanding their structures, functions, and genetics have shown that fungi differ fundamentally from
plants in several respects. Key distinguishing traits include karyology, heterotrophic nutrition (obtaining
nutrients by digesting and absorbing organic material), the absence of chlorophyll, a chitinous cell wall as
opposed to the cellulosic cell walls, relatively undifferentiated cellular structure in the form of hyphae,
and very different modes of reproduction. This contrasts with plants, which have well developed distinct
cellular structures comprising different tissues of the plant (e.g., roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and their
component parts) that have specific functions. These different structures may have significant differences
in composition as well; for example, rhubarb leaves are toxic, but stems are edible. In contrast,
basidiomycetes produce dikaryotic hyphae that form a continuum over the organism, except for the
haploid spores (see Figure 6.1). These considerations led to the introduction of a new system (Whittaker
1969; Hagen et al. 2012) in which fungi are classified as a separate kingdom based on their unique
characteristics. As a result, biology would dictate that care should be taken when attempting to draw
conclusions from observations in one kingdom to another, including from the plant kingdom to the fungal
kingdom.
49
As an example, the historical nomenclature referring to the reproductive form of the mushroom as the
“fruiting body” appears to be derived from an analogy to the more commonly perceived “fruit” of a plant
that houses the seeds and may have occurred at a time when the differences between the fungal and
plant kingdoms were not fully articulated. The net result is often a confusion among non-mycologists who
may improperly characterize the “fruiting body” as a “fruit” that harbors “mushroom seeds”. The only
analogy of the haploid precursors to plant seeds is the formation of haploid nuclei that become
basidiospores; these are dispersed in nature where they germinate as monokaryotic mycelium again and
the life cycle repeats. Although these may be analogous to true seeds in plants, they have no homology
to them (Martinez-Carrera 1998).
6.2.2 The Life Cycle of P. pulmonarius in Nature
The following section provides a brief overview of the life cycle of Basidiomycetes, including P.
pulmonarius, in nature. It is provided as background to provide context for the similarities, and perhaps
more importantly, the lack of food-safety related differences between the edible, and therefore safe,
fruiting body of P. pulmonarius and POMM propagated by Mushlabs using submerged fermentation, both
being dikaryotic mycelial forms of the Phoenix oyster mushroom.
6.2.3 Life Phases and Karyology of P. pulmonarius
The genus Pleurotus, including P. pulmonarius, has two distinct “life phases”. These differ from those
exhibited by more differentiated eukaryotes such as most edible plants and non-colonial animals in which
gametogenesis is limited to a few highly specialized structures that produce haploid gametes, usually

within the greater part of the organism that is diploid. Basidiomycetes, particularly Pleurotus spp.,
alternate between monokaryotic phases (one nucleus or haploid) and dikaryotic or pseudo-diploid states,
which arise following the fusion of two monokaryons (mating). This is depicted in Figure 6.1.
Figure 6.1 Mushroom Life Cycle derived from https://quizlet.com/291268807/life-cycle-of-a-mushroom-
diagram/
50
The monokaryon results from the maturation of a basidiospore, which develops into a haploid mycelium
composed of hyphae as their simplest building unit. When compatible monokaryotic mycelia encounter
each other in the soil, they are able to “mate” by fusing hyphae in a process referred to as “plasmogamy.”
The resulting hyphae become binucleate, containing two genetically different nuclei in each hyphal
compartment of the mycelium and are therefrom described as dikaryotic (Martinez-Carrera 1998). Under
specific conditions, the dikaryotic mycelium can morphose into basidiocarp, a structure colloquially
referred to as the fruiting body.
As seen below in Figure 6.2, morphological mycelium (dikaryotic hyphae) is often found (and therefore
consumed) as “hairy” structures on the caps of oyster mushroom fruiting bodies at the market level.
Figure 6.2 Presence of white mycelium on the cap of consumed oyster mushrooms (outlined in red)83
6.2.4 Fruiting Body and Mycelial Structure of P. pulmonarius
The form of P. pulmonarius commonly available to consumers is the dikaryotic fruiting body. The basic
structural unit of the dikaryotic fruiting body is referred to as a hypha (pl. hyphae), which is also the basic
structural unit of the mycelium. What is now known as the hyphal systems of mushrooms i.e., how the
hyphae within the fruiting bodies ensure its shape and structure, was first described in 1932 and then
later reprised by Van der Westhuizen (1971), Pegler (1996), and Porter and Naleway (2022). The British
Mycological Society summarizes this as “The main body of the fungus is made up of fine threads (hyphae)
that group together to make a mycelium….the fine threads that make up the mycelium that lies hidden
from view can also form the fruit body of the fungus that we see."51
The hyphal system of oyster mushrooms is described as “monomitic” or having only one type of hypha.
Hence, all dikaryotic hyphae in P. pulmonarius are considered to be “generative” (i.e., totipotent) and
structurally similar. These generative (dikaryotic) hyphae can be assembled into threads, which can then
be referred to as dikaryotic generative mycelium or fruiting bodies, depending on their structural forms.
This means that fruiting bodies of P. pulmonarius are solely composed of a bundle of dikaryotic generative
hyphae (except for the spore) and “unidimensional” dikaryotic mycelia is also observed at market level as
a fluffy white layer expending on the cap of oyster mushrooms during their storage and sale (Figure 6.2).
51 https://www.britmycolsoc.org.uk/mycokids/mycokids-how-are-fruit-bodies-made last accessed 6 September
2024

51
POMM originates from dikaryotic generative hyphae directly isolated from the fruiting body of P.
pulmonarius and is propagated through submerged fermentation (as described in Section 2.2.1). Hence,
it also consists of dikaryotic hyphae assembled as dikaryotic mycelia, just as are the widely consumed
fruiting bodies (Ginterova and Janotkova 1975; Eger 1979; Zervakis and Balis 1996; Petersen and Hughes
1997; Bao et al. 2004; Li et al. 2019; Porter and Naleway 2022).
6.2.5 Gene Expression in P. pulmonarius
Little information is available on the specific patterns of gene expression in P. pulmonarius (or any
mushroom) found at the retail level. Once identified as being “edible”, with the exception of microbial
degradation or exposure to inappropriate storage conditions, these mushrooms are generally considered
safe to eat.52 Thus, specific differences in gene expression related to different growth conditions do not
affect the safety of oyster mushrooms currently available on the markets and consumed worldwide. In
fact, multiple vendors sell oyster mushroom growing kits to the general public53 on the assumption that
the resulting mushrooms (and attached white fluffy mycelia) will be safe to eat, regardless of changes in
gene expression that may occur as the result of different growth media or substrates.
Phenotypes of any living organism intrinsically rely on changing gene expression, which in turn reflect the
internal and external factors such as development phase, age, and environmental stimuli encountered
throughout the growth of these mushrooms. In particular, different gene expression patterns are
expected from oyster mushrooms grown on different substrates or under different conditions. As
previously stated in Section 2.2.1, Mushlabs controls the growth of POMM stringently to avoid any
differentiation of the mycelia into the fruiting body stage.
The effects on gene expression that may be attributed to internal and external factors have been
described in literature:
• Wu et al. (2021) demonstrated that the protein and metabolite profiles of consumed fruiting
bodies is not constant during their storage after harvest but instead constantly evolve over time.
• Wang et al. (2020) and Yu et al. (2023) showed that even within the same fruiting body, the
different parts (pileus, stem and gills) have different nutritional, transcriptome and proteome
profiles.
• Xiao et al. (2017), Angelini et al. (2021), Zeng et al. (2022), and Lee et al. (2023) highlight that
fruiting bodies obtained from different growth substrates show very different profiles and levels
of metabolites and proteins.
52 A key exception is the morel mushroom, and the “false morel” with which it is often confused. Morels may
contain the highly toxic hydrazine and must be cooked thoroughly prior to eating.

As a result, there is no “reference” mushroom fruiting body gene expression library that can serve as a
comparator for food safety assessment. Nonetheless, as previously indicated, fruiting bodies of Pleurotus
spp. are considered “edible mushrooms” and have been consumed safely regardless of any differences in
gene expression, which may manifest as changes in shape, maturity, composition, or proteome and
metabolite profiles.
As previously discussed in Section 2.2, Mushlabs stringently controls the growth of POMM in its
fermenters to favor the propagation of dikaryotic mycelia as threads and avoid transition to the fruiting
body phenotype and the potential for spore formation. Wang et al. (2017) reported that the mature
fruiting body of P. pulmonarius is always the developmental stage with the highest variation of expressed
proteins (+50%), while little to no protein is differentially expressed in the mycelium of P. pulmonarius.
Gene expression must differ among the different morphologies and developmental phases of all living
organisms. Joh et al. (2007) identified genes expressed uniquely at different developmental stages of P.
ostreatus and found that under his experimental conditions, among 4,060 genes, only eight (0.2%),
thirteen (0.3%) and two (0.05%) were expressed only in mycelia, fruiting body, and basidiospore,
respectively. The remaining genes are expressed in all stages although their expression may differ under
different growth conditions, age, specific portion of the fruiting body (stem or cap), and, most importantly,
how their sources of nutrition and environmental conditions may vary (e.g., substrate, temperature, light,
humidity; Sales-Campos et al. 2011; Wang et al. 2020; Berger and Ersoy 2022; Xu et al. 2022; Lee et al.
2021). Wang et al. (2017) specifically investigated the proteome of different morphological forms of P.
pulmonarius and came to similar conclusions, showing that among 1698 detected proteins only 11 (0.6%)
were solely expressed in mycelium and these were mainly belonging to known central metabolic pathways
(carbohydrate, lipid and ATP synthesis).
A review by Berger and Ersoy (2022), described studies of gene expression in three edible mushroom
species, Agaricus bisporus, Pleurotus ostreatus, and Lentinus edodes. They noted that all three species
exhibited differences in levels of gene expression at different stages of the fungal life cycle. Ye et al. (2021)
reported a detailed analysis of differential expression in vegetative mycelia and primordia (developing
fruiting bodies) in a closely related species P. eryngii. A number of genes related to cellular functions such
as transcription, carbohydrate utilization, and increased chitin production for the energy-consuming
process of building the fruiting body were up- or down-regulated. Several genes related to trehalose
metabolism were also identified as being up-regulated; trehalose is a stress protectant for cells. Virtually
all the differences identified were in the expression of enzymes generally attributed to typical
housekeeping functions present in all life stages, although their levels may differ.
Differences identified in the literature were related to changes in levels of expression rather than in the
presence of additional proteins in the vegetative mycelia compared to the fruiting body. Wang et al.
(2017) has demonstrated that approximately 65% of the proteins (and their isoforms) expressed across

the different life stages of P. pulmonarius likely have housekeeping functions
In summary, the gene expression differences noted in mycelia compared to fruiting bodies are likely
responsible for the differences in assembly and relative compositions of the major life forms of P.
pulmonarius. Gene expression changes are necessary for the efficient function of any organism. Edible
mushrooms have been consumed safely without consideration (or knowledge) of such differences in
levels of gene expression and changes in protein structure; we have simply referred to them as “oyster
mushrooms”.
53
As discussed here, the actual results from Mushlabs’ molecular analyses of POMM genomes and gene
expression levels are consistent with the published literature and provide specific instances of differential
gene expression. The conclusions of these analyses for food safety are discussed in Section 6.3. As
elaborated more fully in the following section, Mushlabs has reviewed differences in gene expression
between POMM and P. pulmonarius fruiting bodies that hypothetically may have an impact on food safety
at the molecular level. No genes with potential food safety concerns have been identified that could affect
the food safety of POMM.
6.2.6. Mushlabs Molecular Analyses with POMM
As discussed earlier in this section, P. pulmonarius has been reported to contain the dimer-forming
proteins (ostreolysin A and pleurotolysin B) in the early germinating tissue. These proteins, when present
together, can form a pore-forming complex that can lyse cells. Berne et al. (2005) have demonstrated by
immunofluorescence that these proteins are present in the early germinal tissue of the fruiting body, but
not in the mycelia. The latter finding, the absence of lytic proteins in mycelia of Pleurotus spp. was
confirmed by Vidic et al. (2005). In order to determine whether POMM contained this or any potential
toxic proteins, Mushlabs conducted a comprehensive series of molecular analyses. The analysis
specifically addressed the Pleurotus toxin genes that encode the proteins ostreolysin A and pleurotolysin
B54, as well as detailed comparisons of the molecular data from POMM to determine whether any other
potential known toxins from other fungi or allergens were present.
Mushlabs undertook a three-pronged approach to demonstrate that ostreolysin-related proteins, or other
proteins with toxic properties were not found in POMM
1. Whole Genome Sequence (WGS) analysis using DIAMOND BLASTX conducted by Charles River
Laboratories (CRL)55
2. Transcriptomic Analysis conducted by Novogene56
3. Sequence specific analysis of the proteome of POMM conducted by the University of
Griefswald (located in Griefswald, Germany)
These analyses were performed by laboratories with the specific expertise needed and were selected by
Mushlabs based on their qualifications and experience in molecular analyses of genomes and proteomes
in biological materials, with particular emphasis on food safety. The results of these molecular studies are
internally consistent: none of the studies were able to predict or discern the presence of any of the
hemolysin proteins or any other known mushroom toxin in POMM, as described in more detail in the
following sections.
6.2.6.1. Genomic Analyses
Charles River Laboratories (CRL) performed two analyses of the genome of POMM. Because of the
literature identifying ostreolysin and related hemolysins as potential toxins in Pleurotus mushrooms, the
emphasis was put on ostreolysin A and the two known isoforms of pleurotolysin (pleurotolysin A and

pleurotolysin B). It is important to remember that because the source of POMM was dikaryotic hyphae

the widely consumed fruiting body of P. pulmonarius. That genome has the ability to produce different
transcripts and their resulting translation products depending on the environmental conditions to which
they are exposed and will determine the morphology they assume. As Mushlabs isolated its POMM

grown under very diverse conditions (e.g. substrate, temperature, etc).
Database for comparison/annotation
CRL first performed a thorough search from GenBank for all fungal peptides that are closely or distantly
related to “toxins” and “defensins”. Defensins are frequently short peptides that are not well conserved
and are used to protect the organism from bacterial and eukaryote attack. They are often overlooked with
standard annotation pipelines because they are typically only 18-45 amino acids in length.
After building this library, CRL used the DIAMOND BLASTX (Diamond) method to analyze and query the
POMM genome. This approach uses the same NCBI public database (NR and NT) as the commonly used
BlastX. Diamond is routinely used by CRL and other laboratories because it utilizes a more efficient
algorithm to allow for a more rapid analysis with a comparable detection sensitivity to NCBI BlastX
(Buchfink et al. 2015). Potential loci of interest were annotated using Diamond match to non-redundant
peptides and fungal toxins previously identified during the construction of the toxin and defensin library.
Each of these loci were examined individually including referring to the original fungal toxin entry in
Genbank. In some cases, NCBI web blast was also used to identify conserved domains and match these
peptides with their function.
Stringency Cutoffs
One concern regarding genomic matches is that of stringency, often expressed as “expect values”, i.e., the
number of “hits” one could expect to see by chance for a search of a database of some finite size; these
are often expressed as “e-values or e-value thresholds”. CRL noted that with the standard/default online
e-value threshold used by NIH of 0.05 (5e-2), a larger list with more low-scoring (sensitive, not specific)
hits can be reported. This is often thought of as a convenient significant threshold for reporting results.
Nonetheless, CRL routinely employs the more stringent 1e-10 as the best trade-off for general users in
that it provides some sensitivity while winnowing out many, but not all, false positives. CRL notes that the
usual practice in the literature is 1e-3 or smaller, which removes most false positives.
To help ensure that conservative (i.e., health protective) concerns are met, CRL first employed a cut-off of
1e-10 to remove rare false positives that can occur from repetitive sequence matches. Then, to
demonstrate that lower stringency searches would not yield more relevant information for food safety,
CRL re-ran its genomic analysis for potential sequences in the genome that would possibly code for known

toxins (and/or allergens) using the far less stringent cut-off of 1e-2.

Overall, seven loci were identified with an 80% match to loci for known Pleurotus hemolysins,

proteins potentially involved in known fungal toxin biosynthetic pathways.
The first seven loci that matched the loci from known Pleurotus hemolysins Pleurotolysin B and
Ostreolysin A6 with high identity (>80%) were deemed not of safety concern as both of these genes are
also found in other edible Pleurotus species regularly consumed worldwide.
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has addressed this topic in its
consensus document on oyster mushrooms (OECD 2006). They concluded that:
“there is no data on the toxicity of P. ostreatus hemolysins in oyster mushroom consumers. Oyster
mushroom is considered a non-toxic mushroom and the presence of hemolysins does not influence
this conclusion. Hemolysins are thermo-labile, and potential toxicity would be considered only for
raw mushrooms. Furthermore, proteins are usually degraded in the gastrointestinal tract when
ingested. Administration of aqueous extracts of P. ostreatus to mice demonstrated no acute
56
effects and repeated oral feeding of the mushroom to rodents revealed no histopathological
changes of cardiac or hepatic tissue”.
More importantly, the presence of hemolysin protein dimers in the biomass of P. pulmonarius was later

excluded after review of the transcriptomic and proteomic data for POMM. The protein known as
Pleurotolysin B was not found in either dataset; the simultaneous presence of both Pleurotolysin B and
Ostreolysin A6 is required for an active hemolysin dimer to form. Thus, the presence of just one is not
indicative of a potential food consumption risk.
With respect to the remaining 26 loci initially identified by CRL in POMM, the loci overlapped with genes
encoding the eight peptides listed in Table 6.7. Each of these peptides was reviewed further by CRL, who
concluded that the proteins encoded by the identified sequences pose no food safety concern: they are
not allergens or toxin themselves, but are only distantly related to one step of an incomplete toxin
pathway, while having other key functions in the central metabolism of Pleurotus spp. For instance, the
first entry (VWO98972.1) encodes an RNA-helicase, an enzyme involved in 40S ribosomal subunit
biogenesis, while the fourth entry (VWO96292.1) encodes a glucose-6-isomerase, a central enzyme
involved in energy generation in the glycolysis pathway and in converting glucose-6-phosophate to
fructose-6-phospate as precursors of fungal cell wall biosynthesis.
Although some of the peptides in Table 6.7 are somewhat similar to enzymes involved in the cercosporin
pathway, CRL has determined that this pathway is incomplete in P. pulmonarius as several key enzymes
are absent from the POMM genome, transcriptome and/or proteome. For example, peptide VWO97386.1
Cercosporin MFS transporter encodes one protein on the biosynthetic pathway for cercosporin; other
proteins are missing. This is illustrated in Figure 6.3, which shows the key biosynthetic steps in the

cercosporin, thus highlighting again that the presence of this pathway in Pleurotus spp. is rather unlikely
(Caesar-Thonthat et al. 2009; US Patent No. 6,872,388).

6.3 Overall Conclusions Regarding POMM Food Safety
Sections 6.1 and 6.2 provide a detailed discussion of the information and data that support the finding
that when used as a food ingredient at the incorporation levels indicated in Table 1.1, POMM is safe to
eat. The key issues and information described in the notice are summarized below.
1. Confirmation of Identity: Mushlabs has thoroughly described the provenance of the species of
P. pulmonarius from which POMM is derived, i.e., it is cultured from a dikaryotic fruiting body to
yield dikaryotic mycelia (typical fruiting body tissue).
2. Highly Controlled Manufacturing: All manufacture of POMM is conducted under food GLP
conditions consistent with US Good Manufacturing Practices for foods. POMM is produced by
submerged fermentation that precludes the further differentiation of the dikaryotic mycelia into
fruiting bodies. POMM is manufactured. Further, given the tightly controlled conditions employed
by Mushlabs when producing POMM compared to the less prescribed conditions for the
cultivation of mushroom fruiting bodies on various lignocellulosic substrates in traditional
mushroom farming, POMM would be less likely to contain substances that could be injurious to
health that may be produced in response to changes to the environment of the fruiting body.
3. Establishment of Acceptance Criteria and Specifications: Mushlabs has established acceptance

criteria based on multiple production batches. Data from three non-consecutive batches are
provided herein. Acceptance criteria and specifications have been established for protein levels
in POMM as well as levels of heavy metals and microbes. Any batches that do not meet the
stringent acceptance criteria will be discarded. The data from the POMM batches analyzed show
that Mushlabs can reliably produce POMM that meets both the acceptance criteria and the
specifications.
4. Characterization of Growth Media: The medium in which POMM is produced is composed of
simple ingredients, does not contain any of the 9 major allergens, and none of the components
are derived from the nine allergens listed by FDA.
5. Description of Intended Uses of POMM and the Conditions of Its Use: POMM is intended to be
an ingredient in food that is incorporated as an alternative source of protein, and not to comprise
100% of any food. POMM is intended to be cooked prior to consumption.
6. Residual Nucleic Acids in POMM: Nucleic acid levels in POMM are below 2% as recommended by
FAO.
61
7. Completion of Dietary Exposure Assessment: Mushlabs performed a POMM-specific dietary
exposure assessment based on use of the most recent US data (NHANES data). Daily intakes of
POMM for eaters-only over two years of age were estimated to be 30.4 g/day (mean intake) and
64.3 g/day (90th percentile intake).
8. Safety Narrative:
a. A safety assessment conducted using more traditional methods did not indicate the
presence of any toxins, allergens, or other substances that could pose food safety
concerns.
b. To confirm that there are no substances in POMM that could be toxic or allergenic,
Mushlabs conducted a series of comprehensive analyses of the genome, transcriptome,
and proteome of POMM. There is no evidence that POMM contains any hazards that
could pose a food safety concern.
Based on a weight-of-the-evidence of the data and information, as well as the intended uses of POMM,
Mushlabs has concluded that POMM is generally recognized as safe by scientific methods when present
as an ingredient in food at the maximum levels indicated in Table 1.1.

PART 2. §170.230 IDENTITY, METHOD OF MANUFACTURE, SPECIFICATIONS, AND PHYSICAL
OR TECHNICAL EFFECT OF THE NOTIFIED SUBSTANCE
2.1. Product identity
β -casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 is a recombinant version of the naturally occurring protein β
-casein, which is present in bovine milk. β-casein is one of four primary casein proteins found in milk,
alongside αS1-casein, αS2-casein, and κ-casein (Fox and Mulvihill, 1990). Fermify’s β-casein is based
on the sequence of one of the two major subvariants of this protein, the A2 genetic variant. This variant
differs from the other major subvariant (A1) by one amino acid at position 67. The A1 genetic variant
has a histidine amino acid at this position, while the A2 genetic variant contains proline at position 67
(Poulsen et al., 2017).
The common name of the notified substance is β-casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139. The notified
substance is also referred to as β-casein produced by E. coli DSM 35048, in which the strain name
refers to the deposit number in the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms
(Section 2.2.1).
The product is produced by fermentation using the bioengineered strain E. coli stF_24_139. The product
is a liquid product, containing min. 2% protein in buffer solution. The protein fraction of the product
consists of min. 75% β-casein, the remaining proteins present in the product originate from the host

strain. The recombinant β-casein is dissolved in a sodium phosphate buffer and has a pH between 6.5
and 7.5.
Throughout this GRAS Determination, the product is referred to as “β-casein produced by E. coli
stF_24_139” (which consists of the recombinant β-casein dissolved in the sodium phosphate buffer),
and “Fermify’s recombinant β-casein” refers solely to recombinant
β-casein protein.
2.1.1. β-casein
β-casein is a protein that is naturally present in bovine milk and is the subject of this GRAS
Determination. The amino acid sequence of Fermify’s recombinant β-casein is based on the sequence
of the A2 genetic variant of bovine β-casein. The amino acid sequence is listed in the UniProt database
under Accession No. P02666.
Native bovine β-casein consists of 209 amino acids and has a molecular mass of 23.59 kDa for the
primary structure prior to post-translational phosphorylation, and a molecular mass of 23.98 kDa
following phosphorylation of 5 serine residues, i.e., Ser15, Ser17, Ser18, Ser19, and Ser35 (Farrell et
al., 2004) (Figure 1). The A2 variant of native bovine β-casein does not contain any other post-
translational modifications (Farrell et al., 2004).

Figure 1. Amino acid sequence of native bovine β-casein. The phosphorylation sites are indicated at Ser15,
Ser17, Ser18, Ser19, and Ser35. Figure based on Farrell et al. (2004).
In addition to the native sequence of bovine β-casein, Fermify’s recombinant β-casein contains an
additional methionine at the N-terminal end of the amino acid sequence, as a consequence of
expressing the protein in E. coli. In bacterial systems, protein expression typically begins with
methionine due to the start codon (AUG), and this methionine is typically not removed from the N-
terminus, which leads to Fermify’s recombinant β-casein consisting of 210 amino acids.
Substantial equivalence to native bovine β-casein
Fermify conducted a comprehensive assessment of its recombinant β-casein and concluded that it is
substantially equivalent to the native bovine β-casein, based on:

Construction of the production strain
DNA constructs (plasmids) were created using standard molecular biology methods, mainly via
modified Gibson assembly (Zhang et al., 2012). DNA insertion into the bacterial genome was performed
using the Red recombination system of bacteriophage λ (Jensen et al., 2015).
E. coli stF_24_139 was built based on the BL21(DE3)-pET expression system. Briefly, E. coli
BL21(DE3) expresses a high throughput T7 RNA polymerase which can transcribe genes downstream
of the T7 promoter. Additionally, the T7 promoter contains a binding site for lac operon inhibitor lacI,
which makes the system inducible by lactose or its synthetic analog – isopropyl-β-D-
thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). The coding sequence for β-casein was de novo synthesized prior to
insertion downstream of the T7 promoter in the pET29b(+) plasmid. The nucleotide sequence of the β-
casein gene was specifically optimized for expression in E. coli, however, it encodes for an amino acid
sequence identical to the bovine β-casein protein (A2 variant). The expression of the protein can be
controlled by the addition of IPTG. A specific transcription terminator sequence was also included
downstream of the coding sequence to avoid the transcription of any unwanted DNA.
The expression system of Fermify’s recombinant β-casein is based on the plasmid pET29b(+) (EMD
Biosciences), which originally contained a kanamycin-resistance marker gene. The antimicrobial
resistance marker was removed by substituting it using the ccdB/ccdA complementation system
(Peubez et al., 2010). This system is naturally occurring and stabilizes E. coli plasmid F (Tam and Kline,
1989). Briefly, the ccdB protein is specifically targeting bacterial gyrase, leading to the death of the cell,
unless the ccdA protein is present in the cell. To ensure the retention of the plasmid, the ccdB gene
was integrated into the genome of E. coli stF_24_139, whereas ccdA was integrated into the expression
plasmid.
All genetic modifications to the strain and plasmid were confirmed via polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
and Sanger sequencing. Additionally, whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed to confirm the
identity of the production strain and to ensure the absence of toxins, virulence factors, antibiotic

2.3. Production process
2.3.1. Description of the method of manufacture
Upstream process
A vial of E. coli stF_24_139 is taken from a working cell bank and used for an inoculation/seeding stage.
The seed is transferred to the production fermenter to produce biomass, followed by protein expression.
The expressed β-casein protein is produced intracellularly.
Downstream process
1. The cells harvested by centrifugation at the end of the fermentation are disrupted by high pressure

homogenization and subsequently washed by resuspension in fresh buffer.
2. Centrifugation is then performed to separate and remove cell debris and obtain inclusion bodies
(IBs).
3. The IBs separated from cell debris are solubilized to yield crude, soluble β-casein.
4. The solution is subjected to sequential precipitation and flocculation steps for the removal of
impurities, which are subsequently separated from the soluble product by centrifugation and
filtration.
5. Tangential flow filtration is performed to adjust protein titer and for final product formulation. The
product is retained by the ultrafiltration membrane and volumetrically concentrated to the target
final concentration. An in-house developed and validated reverse-phase high-performance liquid
chromatography (RP-HPLC) method is used to determine product concentration and purity during
the process and for the final product. Commercially available plate-based fluorescence assays are
used for determination of DNA and endotoxins on in-process samples and final products: Quant-
iT™ 1X dsDNA Assay Kits, Thermofisher Scientific and respectively.
6. Finally, the product is aliquoted and stored at maximum temperature of 4 ºC or 39.2 ºF.

PART 6. §170.250 NARRATIVE ON THE CONCLUSION OF GRAS STATUS
6.1. Introduction
β-casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 is a liquid product containing Fermify’s recombinant β-casein
at a concentration of 1.5 to 4% on a wet basis and is intended as a food ingredient in non-alcoholic
beverages, cheeses, cheese analogs, dairy analog products, frozen dairy desserts, milk products, and
plant protein products.
β-casein is a protein that is naturally present in bovine milk. Bovine milk contains on average about
3.5% protein. The proteins present in milk can be categorized into two principal groups: caseins and
whey (or non-casein) proteins. Caseins are phosphoproteins insoluble at pH 4.6 (the isoelectric pH) at
20 ºC or 68 ºF. Whey proteins are soluble under these conditions. On average, bovine milk consists of
80% casein and 20% whey protein (Yalçin, 2006). Isoelectric casein is known to consist of four primary
proteins (gene products), which are αS1-casein, αS2-casein, β-casein, and κ-casein, present in the
approximate ratio of 40:10:35:12 of the total protein fraction in milk (Fox and Mulvihill, 1990). Caseins
in milk form complex aggregates or micelles of proteins and mineral calcium phosphate. Caseins utilize
a calcium-sequestering mechanism to regulate the calcium phosphate concentration in their
environment (Fox & Brodkorp, 2008).
β-casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 contains min. 1.5% of Fermify’s recombinant β-casein, which
is comparable to the total casein concentration naturally present in bovine milk (ca. 2.8%).
The structure of β-casein in bovine milk can vary depending on the breed and genetic properties of
different cows. The two major subvariants for this protein are the A1 and A2 types, which differ by an
amino acid at position 67. The A1 genetic variant has a histidine amino acid at this position, while the
A2 genetic variant contains proline at position 67 (Poulsen et al., 2017). While the A1 and A2 genetic
variants are the most common variants, also other subvariants exist. Most commercial milks contain a
mixture of A1 and A2 β-casein, which can arrive from either heterozygous A1/A2 cows or from mixing
milk from A1/A1 and A2/A2 cows (Jianqin et al., 2016).
Fermify’s β-casein has an amino acid sequence that is based on the A2 genetic variant of β-casein and
contains a proline at position 67. In addition, Fermify’s β-casein contains an additional methionine at
the N-terminal end of the amino acid sequence, as a consequence of expressing the protein in E. coli.
In bacterial systems, protein expression typically begins with methionine due to the start codon (AUG),
and this methionine is typically not removed from the N-terminus. Based on the amino acid sequence,
amino acid composition and molecular weight characteristics of Fermify’s β-casein and native bovine
β-casein presented in Section 2.1.1, it can be concluded that both β-caseins are substantially
equivalent, and the safety of Fermify’s β-casein can be based on the safety of native bovine β-casein.
6.2. Absorption, digestion, metabolism, and excretion of β-casein

β-casein is a protein and is digested and metabolized in the same way as other dietary proteins. An
overview of the absorption, digestion, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) profile of dietary protein is
provided below.
Upon ingestion, β-casein is first exposed to the acidic environment of the stomach, where it undergoes
partial hydrolysis by gastric enzymes, primarily pepsin. This enzymatic action breaks down β-casein
into larger polypeptides. These polypeptides then move into the small intestine, where they encounter
pancreatic enzymes such as chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidases. These pancreatic
proteases further hydrolyze the peptides into smaller units, consisting of 6 to 8 amino acids. Free amino
acids are also formed to a small extent by the action of the carboxypeptidases. The resulting peptides
are further hydrolyzed by peptidases associated with the brush border membrane of enterocytes, which
have a specificity of oligopeptides consisting of 6 to 8 amino acids and break them down into small
peptides containing 2 to 3 amino acids. The dipeptides and tripeptides and free amino acids are
absorbed by the enterocytes through active transport mechanisms (Bhutia and Ganapathy, 2018).
Once absorbed into the bloodstream, free amino acids, di- and tripeptides are transported to the liver
via the portal vein. In the liver, they may be utilized for protein synthesis, converted into other biologically

The ADME profile of Fermify’s recombinant β-casein is expected to follow the ADME profile of dietary

6.3. Safety of β-casein
Due to the equivalence between native bovine β-casein and Fermify’s recombinant β-casein, the safety
of Fermify’s recombinant β-casein can be based on the long history of safe consumption of bovine milk

6.4. Safety of the parental strain
The subject of this GRAS notification is recombinant β-casein, which is produced by the bioengineered
strain E. coli stF_24_139, derived from E. coli BL21(DE3).
Escherichia coli, which naturally occurs in the intestinal microflora of humans and many animals, are
part of the Enterobacteriaceae family known for their Gram-negative, non-spore forming, and
facultatively anaerobic nature. Taxonomically, these E. coli strains fall into five ECOR phylogroups (A,
B1, B2, D, and E) based on housekeeping gene sequence similarities (Archer et al., 2011). Human
commensal strains are predominantly found in phylogroups A and B1, while groups B2, D, and E contain
non-related pathogenic strains. Among the numerous E. coli isolates, laboratory strains such as K-12,
B, and C, along with their derivatives, are identified as Risk Group 1 organisms according to biological
safety guidelines (Daegelen et al., 2009, Archer et al., 2011). The National Institute for Health (NIH)
guidelines classify Risk Group 1 organisms as “Agents not associated with disease in healthy adult
humans” (CDC/NIH, 2009). Among these strains, E. coli K-12 and its B derivatives (such as REL606
and BL21) are some of the most utilized for manufacturing biotechnology products, including those for
industrial, pharmaceutical, and food biotechnology applications.
The safety of the parental strain E. coli stF_24_139 has been evaluated in several GRAS notices,

including GRN 1015 (page 20), GRN 921 (page 24-25), GRN 571 (Appendix K, page 282-300), the
GRN 571 Supplement, and GRN 485 (page 15-18), all of which received “no questions” letters from the
FDA. In these GRAS notices, several studies are referenced to confirm the safety of the parental strain
E. coli BL21(DE3). E. coli BL21(DE3) lacks the pathogenic elements commonly found in E. coli strains
responsible for most gastrointestinal infections. Consequently, E. coli BL21(DE3) is regarded as non-
pathogenic, with a low likelihood of surviving in host tissues or causing disease (Chart et al., 2000).
This strain was among the first to have its entire genome sequenced, showing only minor differences
from the widely used production strain E. coli K-12 (Studier et al., 2009). The sequencing revealed that
it lacks genes for virulence factors such as invasion proteins, adhesion molecules, and enterotoxins
(Jeong et al., 2009). Additionally, an acute oral toxicity test found that the endotoxin from E. coli

Residual host strain protein
Disela et al. (2023) characterized the host cell proteome of two E. coli strains, E. coli HMS174 and E.

coli BLR(DE3) using mass-spectrometry-based proteomics. E. coli BLR(DE3) is a recA-deficient-
derivative of E. coli BL21(DE3) (Goffin and Dehottay, 2017), and therefore also closely related to the
production organism of Fermify’s β-casein, E. coli stF_24_139. Considering the close taxonomic
relationship between E. coli BLR(DE3) and E. coli stF_24_139, the proteome of E. coli BLR(DE3) is
considered to be representative of the proteome of E. coli stF_24_139. Table 11 provides an overview
of the 20 most abundant host cell proteins identified in E. coli BLR(DE3). The most abundant protein
appeared to be adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase F1 subunit epsilon. This protein generates ATP
from adenosine diphosphate (ADP) in the presence of a proton gradient across the membranes and
accounted for 73.03 molar % (mol %) of the total host protein fraction, making it the most abundant
protein by a high margin. This protein was also found to be the most abundant protein in E. coli HMS174.
ATP synthase F1 subunit epsilon, and the 19 other most abundant proteins that were identified in E.
coli BLR(DE3) are considered housekeeping proteins, which are responsible for the maintenance of
basic cellular functions required for survival. None of these proteins are considered to contribute to
virulence, pathogenicity and/or toxigenicity. Moreover, none of the major food allergens were identified.

Endotoxins
The batch variation data of β-casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 have shown the presence of
bacterial endotoxins at a level of ranging from 6,400 to 14,000 EU/mL on wet basis. The specification
for endotoxins in β-casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 was set at 20,000 EU/mL, which would
represent the worst-case scenario as highest tolerated level of endotoxins in the product. This value
translates to 660,000 EU/g on dry matter basis, considering a moisture level of 97%. Considering this
value, the mean and 90th percentile exposure to endotoxins through consumption of β-casein produced
by E. coli stF_24_139 accounts for 8.83 x 106 EU/day (or 162,000 EU/kg bw/day) and 1.84 x 107 EU/day

(or 374,000 EU/kg bw/day), respectively.
Bacterial endotoxins, found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria are members of a class
of phospholipids called lipopolysaccharides (LPS). LPS consists of long chains of sugar moieties
covalently linked to lipids. These chains create a dense network that forms a gelatinous layer on the
bacterial surface which keep the bacterial surface moist and slightly negatively charged to protect
against harmful compounds and allowing nutrients uptake (Wassenaar and Zimmermann, 2018). The
actual physical barrier separating the inside of a bacterial cell from the external environment is the
membrane, a double lipid layer with interspersed proteins, to which LPS is connected via lipid A, a
phosphorylated lipid. The toxicity of LPS primarily stems from lipid A, whereas the polysaccharides are
less toxic. In Gram-negative bacteria, LPS is anchored to the outer membrane through lipid A
(Wassenaar and Zimmermann, 2018). In the gut, intestinal phosphatase is produced, which detoxifies
lipid A by the removal of phosphate (Beumer et al., 2003). LPS is synthesized by enzymes, meaning
there are no genes directly coding for LPS itself, but there are genes for the enzymes that produce LPS
(Wassenaar and Zimmermann, 2018).
LPS are known to act as endotoxins when introduced into the bloodstream, eliciting strong immune
responses and potentially causing fever and inflammation. However, the route of exposure is critical in
determining the potential health risk posed by LPS. LPS is regularly consumed via the diet through
various foods without adverse effects. For instance, LPS is present in meat, dairy, fermented foods and
infant formula (Table 12).
If a cheese analog was to be produced containing the maximum tolerated level of 660,000 EU/g of β-
casein produced by E. coli stF_24_139 on dry matter basis (equal to the maximum specification of
20,000 EU/mL on a wet basis of the product with a moisture content of 97%), at the maximum inclusion
rate of 15 g/100 g of cheese analog (worst-case scenario), the product will contain endotoxins at a level
of 99,000 EU/g. This level is in line with some products already on the market, such as ground beef and
certain probiotic products (Table 12).

2.2.1 Amino acid sequence and molecular mass
Based on an SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) analysis,
it was determined that the molecular mass of the enzyme protein is 68 kDa, while the number of

2.3 Production Microorganism
2.3.1 Production Strain
The source material of Sumizyme PEG is the fungus Talaromyces versatilis sp. nov. IF550186
(Bridge, 2013). The former systematic name Penicillium funiculosum has been recently replaced
by Talaromyces versatilis (Samson et al. 2011).
The identification of the strain was confirmed by TechnoSuruga Laboratory Co., Ltd., based on
internal Transcribed Spacer 1 and 2 (ITS1 and ITS2) sequences and the 5.8S gene.
Talaromyces versatilis is a type of filamentous fungus. Its colonies exhibit a characteristic
pattern with a tendency to form aerial ropes (funiculose hyphae) interspersed with wooly
(floccose) regions. The reverse coloration typically ranges from yellow to orange or red, and on
malt agar, it demonstrates good sporulation. Conidiophores emerge perpendicular to the
funiculose hyphae, with those in marginal regions originating directly from the substrate hyphae.
They terminate in biverticillate, symmetric penicilli carrying conidial heads that are dark green to
bluish in color. The conidia, as well as the conidiophores, are smooth. The optimal growth
temperature for Talaromyces versatilis is 20-40 °C. It is capable of growing at a wide pH range,
though acidic conditions are more favourable. Talaromyces versatilis favours high oxygen
concentrations and therefore grows best on the surface of organic substrates. It uses asexual
reproduction via formation of conidiospores (Singh et al. 1986; van Reenen-Hoekstra et al.
1990).
The organism has not been genetically modified to produce the enzyme. The species
Talaromyces versatilis has been used for decades in the production of food and feed enzymes,
under its former systematic name Penicillium funiculosum. Talaromyces versatilis has a long
history of safe use in industrial-scale enzyme production, including a previous GRAS
determination for a cellulase enzyme from Penicillium funiculosum (GRN 584), which received
no questions from the FDA. More recently, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
authorized the use of the same enzyme that this the subject of this GRAS notice; endo-1,3(4)-β-
glucanase produced from Talaromyces versatilis strain PF8 (EFSA, 2024). Thus, Talaromyces
versatilis is recognized as a safe production organism for enzymes for food as well as feed
processing applications.

2.4 Description of Manufacturing Process
2.4.1 Manufacturing Site Information
The food enzyme is produced by Shin Nihon in accordance with current Good Manufacturing
Practices for Food (GMP) and the principles of Hazard Analysis of Critical Control Points
(HACCP).
2.4.2 Fermentation
The fermentation process to produce food enzymes from microbial sources is described below.
Fermentation commonly occurs in many different food products, and this fermentation process
has been used in the production of food enzymes for decades,
The fermentation processes used to produce Sumizyme PEG is a solid-state fermentation, with
the following main steps:
• Inoculum
• Seed fermentation
• Main fermentation

The raw materials used during the fermentation and recovery stages of the manufacturing
process are of food grade quality. Furthermore, all raw materials used for the production of
Sumizyme PEG are food, food additives, or food processing aids listed in the Food Chemical
Codex (13th edition) and/or the Code of Federal Regulations (“21 CFR”), and comply with their
respective specifications. Any antifoams used in the fermentation and recovery are used in
accordance with the Enzyme Technical Association submission to FDA on antifoams and
flocculants in April, 1998.
Materials used in the fermentation process (inoculum, seed and main fermentation) are:
• Potable water
• A carbon source
• A nitrogen source
• Vitamins
• Salts and minerals
• pH adjustment agents
• Foam control agents
2.4.3 Inoculum
A pure culture suspension of Talaromyces versatilis is transferred under sterile conditions to
fermentation medium in an inoculum flask. The culture is grown in the flask until a sufficient
amount of biomass is obtained, which can subsequently be used as inoculum for the seed
fermentation.
2.4.4 Seed Fermentation
Under sterile conditions, the inoculum is then transferred fermentation medium within the seed
fermentor. The seed fermentation is run under the following process conditions:
• Temperature: 30 °C
• For 1 to 3 days
• pH : 4.5 to 5.5
The fermentation is run under controlled agitation and controlled air supply. When a sufficient
amount of biomass has developed, the content of the seed fermenter is used for inoculation of the
main fermentation.
2.4.5 Main Fermentation
During the main fermentation, the production organism biosynthesizes the enzyme protein. The
fermentation in the main fermenter is operated as a batch process. The content of the seed
fermenter is mixed with the solid fermentation medium and subsequently transferred aseptically
onto fermentation trays or into a deep bed fermenter. In both cases, the fermentation is run under
a controlled atmosphere. Where necessary, agitation is applied in order to provide for suitable
Page 10 of 52
GRAS Determination:

oxygen supply in the whole fermenter. The solid state fermentation is run under the following
process conditions:
• Temperature: 30 °C
• Humidity 90 - 100 %
The fermentation process proceeds either for a set duration, until laboratory analyses confirm the
desired enzyme production has been achieved, or until the rate of enzyme production decreases

below a predetermined threshold. When either of these conditions are met, typically after 4 days,
the fermentation is completed.
2.4.6 Recovery
The purpose of the recovery process is:
• to isolate the desired enzyme protein from the fermentation substrate and biomass,
• to concentrate the desired enzyme protein and to enhance the enzyme activity/Total Organic
Solids (TOS) ratio
Throughout fermentation, the enzyme protein is secreted by the microorganism Talaromyces
versatilis into the fermentation medium. During the recovery process, the enzyme is isolated
from the biomass. Depending on the specific enzyme production plant, the nature, amount and
order of the different types of unit operations described below may vary:
• Pre-treatment
• Primary solid/ liquid separation
• Concentration
• Polish and germ filtration
Materials used during recovery of the food enzyme, if necessary, include filter aids, potable
water and pH adjustment agents.
2.4.7 Pre-Treatment
Depending on the process used for subsequent solid separation, water and diatomaceous earth are
added to the fermentation substrate.
2.4.8 Primary Solid/Liquid Separation
The purpose of the primary separation is to remove the biomass solids from the enzyme protein.
The solids consist of the biomass and fermentation substrate. During the primary separation, the
solid fermentation substrate is submerged in an aqueous extraction medium to separate the
enzyme protein from the fermentation substrate. It is performed at defined pH ranges (4 to 4.5) in
order to minimize the loss of enzyme activity. To achieve this, one or more of the following unit
operations are used:

2.4.9 Centrifugation
Centrifugation is applied to accelerate the natural sedimentation of the solids in the aqueous
extraction medium. The liquid (centrifugate) containing the enzyme protein is collected for
further recovery and formulation. The centrifugation equipment is tubular bowl centrifuges: Use
high centrifugal force and are used batch-wise to sediment particles.
2.4.10 Filtration
Filtration is a technique used to separate the aqueous extraction medium into a solid and a liquid
(filtrate) fraction by forcing the broth over a filter. This retains the solids and allows the liquid to
pass through. The filtrate containing the enzyme protein is collected for further recovery and
formulation. Here microfiltration is used, based on a continuous cross flow membrane filtration
process. The extraction medium is pumped over the filter membrane, during which the enzyme-
containing liquid (permeate) passes through the membrane pores, whereas the solids stream
(retentate) is pumped away.
2.4.11 Concentration
The solution containing the enzyme protein must undergo concentration to achieve the intended
enzyme activity and/or to increase the enzyme activity/TOS ratio prior to formulation.
Temperature and pH are regulated during this concentration step, and continues until the desired
concentration is achieved. Ultrafiltration is used in that step, which is a membrane filtration
process applied to increase the ratio of high molecular weight molecules (such as the enzyme
protein) versus the low molecular weight molecules. It increases the activity/TOS ratio.
2.4.12 Polish and Germ Filtration
For removal of residual solids from the fermentation and as a general precaution against
microbial contamination, filtration on dedicated germ filters is applied at various stages during
the recovery process. If required, pre-filtration (polish filtration) is integrated to eliminate
insoluble substances and facilitate the germ filtration using diatomaceous earth and filter press.
At the end of the recovery process, the final polish- and germ filtration (centrifugation and 0.2
µm ceramic filtration) produces a concentrated enzyme solution free of insoluble substances and

the production strain. The enzyme solution before formulation is defined as “food enzyme.”

2.4.16 Production Controls
Good Manufacturing Practice and HACCP
Potential Hazards
To comply with current GMP and HACCP principles for food manufacturing, the following
potential hazards associated with the production of the food enzyme are considered and
controlled throughout the production process:
Identity and Purity of the Producing Microorganism
It is of great importance to the manufacturer of the food enzyme to ensure that the production
microorganism effectively produces the desired enzyme protein. Hence, it is crucial to control
the identity and purity of the microorganism.
Microbiological Hygiene
For optimal production of the enzyme, it is critical to maintain hygienic conditions throughout
the whole fermentation process. Any microbial contamination would promptly hinder the growth
of the production organism, leading to reduced yield of the desired enzyme protein and
potentially resulting in product rejection.
Chemical Contaminants
It is also of importance that the raw materials used during the fermentation steps are of suitable
quality and are free of contaminants which may jeopardize the safety of the food enzyme and/or
impede the optimal growth of the production organism, which may consequently affect enzyme
yield.
Control Measures
The main measures to control the hazards identified above are:
Purity of the Producing Microorganism
The production of the required enzyme protein relies on a well-defined Master (MCB) and
Working Cell Bank (WCB). A Cell Bank consists of ampoules containing a pure culture, with

the cell line's history and the processes involved in producing, propagating, preserving, and
storing it being closely monitored and regulated.
The MCB is established from a selected strain, while the WCB is produced by sub-culturing of
one or more ampoules from the MCB. The acceptance of a WCB for production runs depends on
meeting specific standards, determined by assessing its identity, viability, microbial purity, and
productivity. An approved WCB serves as the seed material for the inoculum.

2.6 Enzymatic Activity
Beta-glucanase hydrolyses P-D-glucans with (1- 3)-linkages and/or (1- 4)-linkages. Beta
glucanases commonly use a broad range of substrates. In the present case, substrates include
cereal D-glucans, laminarin, lichenin, yeast glucan and other fungal glucans (Kikuchi et al. 2005,
Hua et al. 2011, Hong et al. 2002). This substrate versality demonstrates the usefulness of P
glucanase in various food processing applications, where related p-glucans are present.

processing of all food raw materials which naturally contain this substrate.
The benefits of the use of industrial β -glucanase in typical food or food ingredient processes are
described below for various applications. Food producers find these effects valuable as they
enhance processability and/or product quality. Additionally, these applications contribute to
more efficient production processes, thereby enhancing production efficiency and providing
environmental advantages such as reduced raw material usage and waste generation.
These benefits in certain food processes include:

Effect of the Presence of (Residues of) the Food Enzyme on the Final Food
It is not the food enzyme itself, but the result of the enzymatic conversion that determines the
effect in the food or food ingredient (including raw materials). This effect remains, irrespective
of whether the food enzyme is still present or removed from the final food.
The effect of β-glucanase is the cleavage of β-glucans in cereals, fruits, vegetables and yeasts
during food processing, resulting in glucan-oligomers and glucose. The enzyme does not exert
any (unintentional) enzymatic activity in the final food, due to a combination of various factors,
depending on the application and the process conditions used by the individual food producer.
These factors include depletion of the substrate, denaturation of the enzyme during processing,
lack of water activity, insufficient pH, etc. Consequently, the presence of residues of the food
enzyme in the final food does not lead to an effect in or on the final food.
Effect of the use of the Food Enzyme on the Final Food
The majority of food enzymes perform their technological function during food processing. In
many cases, they are used merely to improve the production process of a certain food or food
ingredient, and the impact of the enzymatic conversion is not noticeable in the final food
product. In other cases, however, the effect of the enzymatic conversion (depletion of a substrate
and/or development of a reaction product) might also result in a beneficial effect on the final
food. Below, the beneficial effects that can be obtained in the final foods when produced with the
help of β-glucanase are described.
Brewing:
By application of β-glucanase in the brewing process, the following characteristics

of the final product beer can be achieved:
• Prevention of β-glucan haze formation in the final product
Fruit and Vegetable Processing:
Due to better processing properties (e.g. reduced viscosity for better solid-liquid
separation) the beneficial effects are:
• Improved extraction of valuable substances from the fruits and vegetables in the juice (e.g.
enhanced nutrients levels and colour)
•Improving appearance and taste of juices, meeting consumers’expectations (by e.g. reducing
post-processing hazes (i.e. clearer product)
Wine Making:
Processing improvement (lowering viscosity, improving filterability and wine clarification) leads
to the following beneficial effects on the final food:

Fate of the Enzyme in Food
β-Glucanase performs its technological function during food processing. The food enzyme has
been used for many decades as a processing aid in food production (Pariza and Foster, 1983).
The enzyme catalyses the hydrolysis of the β-1,3- and / or β- 1,4-linkages in β-D-glucans like
cereal or fungal β-D-glucans. Like the endogenous β-glucanase present in the raw materials and
ingredients of common foods, it does not perform any technological function in the final food
product.
Based on the conditions of use described in Section 1.4 and the activity of β-glucanase
under such conditions, it can be concluded that the β-glucanase enzyme does not exert any
(unintentional) enzymatic activity in the final food.
Fate of the Enzyme Protein During Brewing
Beer is pasteurized before going onto the market to ensure the microbiological stability of the
product and are therefore denatured during the brewing process.
β-Glucanases are typically added in the mashing step or to the adjunct before addition of the
adjunct to the mash tun, and are therefore already denatured in the consecutive lautering or mash
filtration step. β-Glucanases can also be added during the fermentation step, for which in this
case, β-glucanases will be denatured during the pasteurization step.
Fate of the Enzyme Protein During Fruit and Vegetable Processing
Fruits and vegetables products, such as juices, jam, fruit preparations and canned fruits, are
pasteurized before going onto the market to ensure the microbiological stability of the product.
Β-Glucanases are therefore denatured during fruit and vegetable processing.
Fate of the Enzyme Protein During Wine Making
In the wine making process, the β-glucanase is added before clarification- or filtration steps. At
the end of the wine making process, one or more of the following unit operations are to be used:
- Bentonite is added into white and rosé wines prior to filtration (and bottling) in order to
stabilize the wine by the removal of thermo-labile proteins. Enzymes present in the wine are
absorbed and therefore removed with the help of bentonite addition.

2.8 Use Levels
Commercial food enzyme preparations are typically utilized in accordance with the Quantum
Satis (QS) principle, meaning they are applied at a level no higher than necessary to achieve the
desired enzymatic reaction, in accordance with GMP standards. The specific amount of enzyme
activity added to the raw material will be established by the respective food manufacturer on a
case by case basis, considering the intended effects and process conditions. Therefore, the
enzyme manufacturer can only provide a recommended dosage range, which serves as a starting
point for individual food producers to optimize their processes and determine the precise amount
of enzyme needed to achieve their intended effect. Therefore, from a technological standpoint,
there are no set "normal" or "maximum" usage levels, and Sumizyme PEG is used following the

QS principle. A food producer using significantly higher doses than necessary would incur
excessive costs and encounter adverse technological effects.
Microbial food enzymes contain not only the enzyme protein but also other substances derived
from the fermentation medium and production microorganism. These constituents include
organic materials such as proteins, peptides, amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids, as well as
organic salts. As defined by JECFA (FAO/WHO, 2006), the percentages of these organic
materials are combined and expressed as Total Organic Solids (TOS).

the relative purity of the enzyme. Whereas the dosage of a food enzyme depends on the enzyme

relevant from a safety point of view. Therefore, the use levels are expressed in TOS.

(the former name for Talaromyces versatilis) submitted in 2015 (GRN 584) to the FDA support
that consumption of enzymes from this source organism are non-toxic.

The source material for the food enzyme is Talaromyces versatilis. The organism has not been

genetically modified to produce the enzyme. The species Talaromyces versatilis has been used
for decades for the production of food enzymes, under its former systematic name Penicillium
funiculosum. Talaromyces versatilis has a long history of safe use in industrial scale enzyme
production and can be considered as a safe production organism for enzymes for food and feed
processing applications. In fermentation products derived from Talaromyces versatilis,

6.2.1 Safety of β-glucanase enzymes
β-glucanase enzymes are commonly found in a variety of natural sources, including plants,
bacteria, fungi and yeast (Nisha, 2022; Perrot et al. 2022). As such, there is a long history of
exposure to these enzymes within the human diet, for which they are expected to be digested in
the same manner as other dietary proteins. Furthermore, GRAS notifications on β-glucanase
derived from various microbial sources, intended for similar uses as those for Sumizyme PEG,
received letters with “no questions” from the FDA, such as GRN 149, 195, 479, 482, 535, 592
and 756. The FDA response to the first beta-glucanase GRAS notice, GRN 149, was in
September of 2004, demonstrating its safe use for over 20 years in the U.S. Microbially derived
β-glucanase enzymes have also been authorized for use in food production by other regulatory
agencies around the globe, including Health Canada, JECFA, Food Standards Australia New
Zealand (FSANZ) as well as EFSA, which recently authorized the use of the same enzyme that

versatilis strain PF8 (JECFA, 1995; EFSA, 2019, 2023, 2024; FSANZ, 2023; Health Canada,

The publicly available information that verifies the safety of other microbially derived β-

6.2.2 Information on Side Activities of the Enzyme Which May Cause Adverse Effects
As far as Erbslöh is aware, the β-glucanase described in this dossier does not possess any
enzymatic side activities which might cause adverse effects. Microbial food enzymes are
concentrates which typically contain minor amounts of other enzymatic activities (side activities)
naturally produced by the microorganism. These microorganisms may produce numerous
enzymes involved in the digestion of proteins, lipids and carbohydrates. Many of these hydrolase
enzymes are produced endogenously in human within the gut microbiota, and are widely sold as
digestive aids, in both foods and dietary supplements. These enzymes in digestive aids are sold at
levels of exposure magnitudes higher than the negligible exposure from food enzymes used as

processing aids in food manufacturing, are therefore enzymatic side activities are not relevant
from a safety point of view.
6.2.3 Allergenicity
Since they are proteins, enzymes could theoretically have the potential to cause allergic
responses. However, to address allergenicity by consumption, the following should be
considered:
• Bindslev-Jensen et al. (2006) evaluated the allergenic potential of enzymes in the publication:
"Investigation on possible allergenicity of 19 different commercial enzymes used in the food
industry". This study involved enzymes produced by both wild-type and genetically modified
strains as well as wild-type enzymes and Protein Engineered variants. 400 patients with a
diagnosed allergy to inhalation allergens, food allergens, bee or wasp were included in the study.
And it was concluded that in general, consumption of food enzymes are unlikely to pose a
concern regarding food allergies.
• Previously, the Association of Manufacturers and Formulators of Enzyme Products (AMFEP)
Working Group on Consumer Allergy Risk from Enzyme Residues in Food conducted a
thorough examination on the allergenic potential of enzyme products (Dauvrin et al., 1998).
Overall, it was concluded that, unlike exposure via inhalation, there are no scientific evidence to
suggest that the small quantities of enzymes present in food can sensitize or trigger allergy
reactions in consumers.

• Enzymes have been consumed daily as digestive aids for decades, at levels much higher (up to
1 million times) in comparison to enzymes levels in food. Wuthrich (1996) published a list of
enzymes used as digestive aids and concluded that they are not potent allergens by ingestion.
Thus, there are no scientific indications that small amounts of enzymes in food can sensitize or
induce allergic reactions in consumers.
• The majority of proteins do not cause food allergies, and the enzyme industry has not identified
enzyme proteins used in food that are homologous to recognized food allergens (The only
enzyme protein used in food that is recognized to have weak allergenic potential is egg
lysozyme).
• During food processing, the food enzyme is used in small amounts, resulting in very small
levels of enzyme protein in the final food products. Typically, a higher increases the risk of
sensitization, while low levels in the final food are correlated with reduced risks (Goodman et
al., 2008).
• When proteins undergo denaturation, the enzyme molecule's tertiary structure is destroyed.
Typically, these structural changes are linked with decreased antigenic reactivity in humans. In
the majority of instances evaluated, exhibit significantly lower immunogenicity compared to
their native counterparts (Valenta and Kraft, 2002; Valenta, 2002; Takai et al., 1997; Takai et al.,
2000; Nakazawa et al., 2005; Kikuchi et al., 2006).
• Furthermore, residual enzyme proteins in the final food undergo digestion in the
gastrointestinal tract, further reducing the risk of allergenicity of the enzyme. Although
resistance to digestion is viewed as a potential allergenic risk factor, it is hypothesized that small
protein fragments generated through digestion are less likely to induce allergies (FAO/WHO,
2001; Goodman et al., 2008).
• Enzymes in food processing have a long history of safe use, showing no evidence of adverse
effects or reactions. Additionally, a diverse array of enzyme classes and structures exist naturally
in food, unlike most recognized food allergens, which are typically confined to a limited range of
foods.
6.2.4 Allergenicity Search
To assess the potential risk of cross-reactivity between the β-glucanase enzyme and known

allergens, sequence homology testing was conducted. This testing involved an 80-amino acid
sliding window search and conventional FASTA alignment, with an overall homology threshold
of 35%, as recommended in the most recent literature (FAO/WHO, 2001; Ladics et al. 2007;
Goodman et al. 2008).
“AllergenOnline” database (http://www.allergenonline.org) was used to conduct the sequence
homology comparison analysis.

This search demonstrated sections throughout the peptide sequence with greater than 35%
identity to Asp f 7 from Aspergillus fumingatus, Der f 23 from Dermatophagoides farina and
villin 2 from Nicotiana tabacum. The maximum sequence identity was 42.40%, to Asp f 7.
FASTA alignments of the sequences above with recognized allergens also exhibited matches to
the Asp f 7 and Der f 23 (using E-value <0.1 as the cut-off) with 24.8 % and 32.4% identities
respectively (0.00012 and 0.011 E-scores respectively) when using the complete sequence search

However, Asp f 7 and Der f 23 are not recognized as food allergens by the World Health
organization and International Union of Immunological Societies (WHO/IUIS) Allergen
Nomenclature Sub-committee.3
Although warned against in Codex (2009), it was highlighted by Herman et al. (2009) and
expanded further by Ladics et al. (2011) along with information from AllergenOnline.org, that a
short sequence of amino acids matches may not necessarily indicate cross-reactivity and could be
overlooked by the more conservative 80 amino acid match (≥35%). However, some regulatory
bodies still require the search for isolated identity matches of 8 contiguous amino acids. When
performed with the amino acid sequence for Sumizyme PEG, this search yielded no sequence
matches with recognized allergens.
As for all enzyme products, the MSDS for Sumizyme PEG would include a precautionary
statement indicating that inhalation of enzyme mist/dust could lead to allergic respiratory
reactions, including asthma, particularly in susceptible individuals upon repeated exposure.
In summary, based on sequence homology alone, Sumizyme PEG is unlikely to present a risk of
food allergenicity. Considering the outcomes of the bioinformatics analysis to estimate potential
allergenicity based on similarity to known allergens, and taking into consideration the latest
scientific guidance on interpreting this data, along with the understanding that the enzyme is
usually denatured during food processing and any remaining enzyme in the final food undergoes
digestion in the gastrointestinal tract, it is improbable that the β-glucanase produced by
Talaromyces versatilis under assessment will trigger allergic reactions upon consumption of food
containing residues of these enzymes.

micronucleus assay was conducted to further investigate Sumizyme PEG’s genotoxicity under
physiologically relevant conditions. While in vitro tests play a key role in preliminary
genotoxicity assessments, they often yield false positives due to intrinsic limitations. In vitro
systems, particularly those using mammalian cell lines, may not reliably reflect human
metabolism, tissue distribution, or systemic interactions, all of which are important factors in

evaluating genotoxic potential (EFSA, 2011; FDA, 2012). The inability of in vitro models to
replicate these complex processes is one reason in vivo assays are preferred for follow-up
studies, as they provide a more accurate assessment of potential genotoxic effects in a living
organism.
In genotoxicity testing, commonly used cell lines have several limitations that may contribute to
a high rate of false positives. As noted in Kirkland et al. (2007), these cell lines often lack
endogenous metabolic activity and rely on external metabolic systems. Furthermore, many of
these cell lines have compromised p53 functions and altered DNA repair capabilities, which can
lead to exaggerated responses to DNA damage under test conditions. High concentrations of test
substances required by many in vitro protocols can also contribute to false-positive outcomes by
inducing cytotoxicity rather than genuine genotoxicity (Kirkland et al. 2007).
This issue is further emphasized in regulatory guidance, which suggests careful interpretation of
in vitro genotoxicity data, especially when tests yield positive results that are not corroborated by
in vivo evidence (FDA, 2012). According to both EFSA (2011) and FDA (2012) guidelines, in
vivo assays like the micronucleus test are valuable follow-ups because they address the
limitations of in vitro assays and help distinguish between biologically relevant genotoxic effects
and artifacts of the test system. Therefore, utilizing in vivo assays after an initial in vitro positive
result aligns with regulatory best practices and ensures that findings are robust, reducing the
likelihood of basing safety assessments on artifacts unique to in vitro conditions.
Overall, even though Sumizyme PEG was reported to induce structural chromosome aberrations,
(but not numerical chromosome aberrations (polyploidy)) in the in vitro chromosomal aberration

direct effect on DNA, and no clastogenic potential in the in vivo micronucleus assay. Thus, it can

Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) derived from the 90-day oral toxicity study by the Total
Theoretical Maximal Daily Intake (TMDI). The calculations are performed on the basis of the
maximum amounts of the food enzyme that could theoretically be carried over to final foods and
drinks. In the present case, the values found for wine making and yeast extract were used to
calculate the TMDI, which was found to be 0.4525 mg TOS/kg body weight/day. Consequently,
the Margin of Safety is 4,884, even when calculated using an exaggerated TMDI, as described in
Section 3.
In summary, the following information supports the safe use of the food enzyme:
• The enzyme was determined to be safe according to the decision tree by Pariza and Johnson
(2001)
• No mutagenic activity was observed under the given test conditions of the Ames test
•The induction of structural chromosome aberrations, but not numerical chromosome aberrations
(polyploidy) were observed under the given test conditions of the in vitro chromosomal
aberration assay
• No induction of micronucleated erythrocytes were observed in the in vivo Micronucleus assay
in rats, ruling out the concern for both structural and numerical chromosomal aberrations
• 90-day oral toxicity on rats: The No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) was determined
to be 2,210 mg TOS/kg bw/day, the highest dose tested in the study. The Margin of Safety was
determined to be 4,884.

6.3 Safety Assessment and GRAS Determination
Based on the information provided throughout this notification, Erbslöh has determined that their
β-glucanase enzyme preparation, Sumizyme PEG, is GRAS to be used Quantum Satis for its
intended purpose in the processing of beer, wine, yeast, fruits and vegetables. Considering the
high margin of safety, even when calculated using overestimated intake levels by the Budget
method, it is not necessary to restrict the use of the enzyme in food processing. There is a long
history of exposure to β-glucanases from natural sources within the human diet, as well as
widespread use of these enzymes from various microbial sources, for use in food processing. β-
glucanases have been approved by prominent regulatory agencies around the world, including
the FDA, EFSA, Health Canada, JECFA and FSANZ, for similar uses as those intended for the
subject of this GRAS notification. Sumizyme PEG is produced in accordance with GMP and
HACCP principles, and the final product is free of heavy metal and microbiological
contaminants. Furthermore, the safety of the production microorganism is well established and is
not considered pathogenic. Toxicological studies conducted with the food enzyme provide
corroborative evidence on the safe use of Sumizyme PEG for its intended uses, as the enzyme
was demonstrated to lack genotoxic potential, and the NOAEL was determined to be 2,210 mg
TOS/kg bw/day, which is 4,884 times higher than the TMDI of 0.4525 mg TOS/kg body
weight/day.

The production strain Escherichia coli EBASSC is a non-pathogenic, nontoxigenic strain generated

The genetically modified production organism complies with OECD (Organization for Economic
