Recipient strain:
The recipient strain E. coli W3110, devoid of rhamnose utilization gene, was used in the
construction of the alternansucrase production strain E. coli CAML357. The cassette used for
generating the rhamnose mutant contained the chloramphenicol marker for selection which was

Donor strain:
The alternansucrase gene donor microorganism - Leuconostoc mesenteroides - is a member of lactic
acid bacteria (LAB), which has a long history of safe use in food fermentations, industrial-scale
enzyme production and consumption as a probiotic, can be considered as safe for production of
enzymes for food as well as feed processing and numerous other industrial applications.
Importantly, EFSA has assigned L. mesenteroides a “Status of Qualified Presumption of Safety”
(QPS) (EFSA 2007, 2020) and is also included in the Inventory of Microbial Food Cultures with
Safety Demonstration in Fermented Food Products by the International Dairy Federation
(495/2018).1 Thus, expressing alternansucrase gene asr from this organism, therefore, doesn’t
cause a safety concern.
2.2.3 ALTERNANSUCRASE EXPRESSION PLASMID
The plasmid pAML369 contains the codon optimized sequence of the asr gene from L.

mesenteroides under the control of the rhamnose inducible promoter in the recipient host strain E.
coli CAML357. The production organism E. coli EBASSC is a host E. coli CAML357 transformed
with a plasmid pAML369. Since the gene sequence is of synthetic origin, no part of the production
strain or the expression plasmid contain original genetic elements from the donor strain. Production
efficiency was increased by fusion of the periplasmic signal sequence to the asr open reading frame
(ORF) to allow periplasmic secretion. Ectopic expression of the asr gene from the plasmid upon
induction with rhamnose eventually leads to the production of alternansucrase enzyme.
2.2.4 ANTIBIOTIC GENES IN THE PRODUCTION STRAIN
In addition to the asr gene that encodes alternansucrase, the pAML369 also contains a kanamycin
resistance gene as a selection marker. However, the enzyme product is free from the recombinant
DNA including the asr gene and the kanamycin resistance gene.
Phenotypically, E. coli EBASSC was evaluated for its susceptibility to different antibiotics by
following the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute’s guidelines (CLSI, 2015 and 2018) as
recommended by European Food Safety Authority (2018). Three batches of E. coli EBASSC were

When implemented, the fermentation process starts from an identical replica of the production strain
seed vial. Production stocks from the “Working Cell Bank” are used to start the fermentation
process. A Working Cell Bank is a collection of vials containing a pure culture. The cell line history
and the production of a WCB, propagation, preservation and storage are monitored and controlled.
The WCB is prepared from a selected strain. A WCB vial is only accepted for production runs if its
quality meets the required standards. This is determined by checking identity, viability, microbial
purity and productivity of the WCB vial. The accepted WCB vial is used as seed material for the
inoculum. Testimony to the stability of the strain is given by monitoring the growth behavior and
by comparable levels of alternansucrase activity in a number of fermentation batches made with E.
coli EBASSC. The activity measurements from parallel fermentations showed that the productivity
of the production strain remains similar, indicating strain stability.

A method was developed to check the presence of the production organism in the enzyme sample.

The production organism used for the production of alternansucrase covered in this dossier is
genetically modified E. coli EBASSC.
E. coli strains such as E. coli K-12, B, C, W and their derivatives are all classified as risk group 1

have a history of safe use. (Bauer et al., 2007, Gorbach, 1978)
In recent years, considerable knowledge and experience on the safe use of recombinant E. coli
strains at industrial scale has been accumulated. E. coli K-12 strain can be used under the lowest
containment level at large scale, GILSP, as defined by OECD (1993).
E. coli K-12 has been considered for over 30 years as safe to use for various biotechnological
applications as it does not produce toxins harmful for ingestion. E. coli K-12 has been widely used
in production of food ingredients, specialty chemicals and human drugs. Because of its history of
safe use, it has been exempted from the Environment Protection Agency (EPA), USA review of

betaglucosidase (Ferreira, 2018), and cellulases (Amraini et al, 2017).

The EFSA has provided positive scientific opinions for the use of substances produced by the
selected strains of E. coli in food. (EFSA Journal 2014, EFSA Journal 2019)
The United States FDA has also issued “no questions” letters in response to GRAS notices for
substances produced by an E. coli K-12 derivative and supporting its position as safe for use in food
production (GRN 624). The production of rennin by E. coli K-12 was affirmed as GRAS by the
FDA in 1990. Thus, E. coli strain K-12 and its derivatives such as W3110 can be considered as safe
production organisms for enzymes used in food / feed processing as well as numerous other
industrial applications.

2.3 Manufacturing process
2.3.1 OVERVIEW
Alternansucrase is produced by microbial fermentation process carried out following current Good
Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) and the principles of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points
(HACCP). The manufacturing facility is ISO 9001, ISO 22000 (Food Safety Management System)
and GMP certified in accordance with 21CFR§110 and 21CFR§117.
Fermentation is a well-known process that occurs in food and has been used for the production of
food enzymes for decades. Liquid state or submerged fermentation is used to produce the
alternansucrase.
As shown below, the key steps for the production of the alternansucrase are fermentation, recovery,

formulation, and packaging. The process is illustrated in Fig 5.
2.3.2 FERMENTATION
2.3.2.1 Raw materials
Materials used in the fermentation and post-fermentation processes (inoculum, seed, main
fermentation, recovery, and formulation), are all food-grade GRAS or approved food additives in
accordance with US federal regulations. The raw materials used in the fermentation conform to
current Food Chemicals Codex specifications except for those that do not appear in the FCC. There
are no ingredients based on milk, soy, or any of the named nine allergens in the Food Allergen
Safety, Treatment, Education & Research Act (FASTER Act, 2021).
2.3.2.2 Inoculum (Seed)
A suspension of a pure culture of E. coli EBASSC cells is aseptically transferred to an inoculum
flask containing fermentation medium.
Inoculum preparation is carried out by trained personnel in biosafety cabinets, installed in a class
100,000 cleanroom. Subsequent growth of the bacterium on a laboratory shaker is also carried out
in a similar cleanroom environment. The purity of the initial inoculum is ensured by monitoring the
inoculum’s specific growth pattern, direct microscopic evaluation, gram staining, and reviewing the
characteristics of viable growth on agar medium. The culture is grown in the flask under optimum
conditions in order to obtain a sufficient amount of biomass, which is subsequently used as inoculum
for the seed fermentation.
2.3.2.3 Seed Fermentation
The inoculum is aseptically transferred to the seed fermenter containing seed fermentation medium.
When a sufficient amount of biomass is developed (typically up to 8 hours), the content of the seed
fermenter is used for inoculation of the main fermentation.
16
Alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC
2.3.2.4 Main fermentation
The fermentation process is conducted in an entirely closed and sterile environment. Enzyme
production takes place at this stage. The fermentation is operated in fed batch mode. The production
microorganism E coli EBASSC grown in seed fermenter is aseptically transferred to the main
fermenter containing the sterilized and cooled fermentation medium. After the desired growth is
achieved in the fermenter, inducer is aseptically added in order to induce the synthesis of the
alternansucrase enzyme, which is produced and retained intracellularly. The fermentation process
is continued for a predetermined time or until laboratory test data show that the desired enzyme
production has been obtained or that the rate of enzyme production has decreased below a
predetermined production rate. When the desired enzyme level is reached, the fermentation is
complete.
The samples are checked microscopically for contamination with other microorganisms during seed
and fermentation stages at regular intervals. Microscopic observations for purity are also confirmed
by plating the samples on nutrient agar and incubating plates at 37°C for 24 hrs. A production batch
is stopped and discarded once any contamination is observed at any stage.
2.3.3 RECOVERY
The alternansucrase produced in the fermentation process is separated from the biomass and other
insoluble at this stage.
During fermentation, the enzyme protein alternansucrase is produced and retained by the E. coli
EBASSC, intracellularly. During recovery, the fermentation broth is subjected briefly to an elevated
temperature with due consideration to enzyme stability and passed through a cell homogenizer to
lyse the cells, this results in the release of the enzyme from the bacterial cells. The enzyme-
containing fermentation medium is then separated from the biomass.
The steps of enzyme recovery include:
 Primary separation (biomass and insoluble/unutilized media from liquid)

 Centrifugation
 Concentration
 Centrifugation
 Pre-filtration and micro (germ) filtration
 Spray drying
2.3.3.1 Primary Separation
Filter aids are added to promote biomass flocculation and filtration is carried out at a controlled pH
using a horizontal filter press. This enables separation of the biomass and other insoluble impurities
from the soluble enzyme containing liquid. The primary separation is performed at defined pH and
temperature ranges in order to minimize the loss of enzyme activity.

2.3.3.2 Centrifugation
The filtered liquid is passed through a high-speed centrifuge to separate and remove other insoluble
and partial soluble impurities.
2.3.3.3 Concentration and centrifugation
The primary filtration step is followed by ultrafiltration and diafiltration of the filtrate from the
primary recovery step to concentrate the enzyme containing filtrate and to reach the desired enzyme
activity. Temperature and pH are controlled during this step. The filtered liquid is passed through a
high-speed centrifuge to separate and remove other insoluble and partially soluble impurities.
2.3.3.4 Pre-filtration and micro-filtration (Germ filtration)
A filtration step on a dedicated micro (germ) filtration media is performed to ensure the removal of
the production strain cells and insoluble substrate components from the fermentation. The
concentrated enzyme liquid obtained after microfiltration, if required, is stabilized using suitable
food grade GRAS or approved food additive stabilizer.
2.3.3.5 Spray Drying
The concentrated enzyme solution is spray-dried in presence of GRAS or approved food additive
food-grade stabilizers (e.g., maltodextrin) to obtain the unformulated concentrate.
2.3.4 FORMULATION AND PACKAGING
Food enzyme alternansucrase is available in different enzyme activities.
If required, the spray-dried unformulated concentrate (not less than 3,000 U/g) is further formulated
with approved food grade formulating agents and adjusted to a declared enzyme activity.
The alternansucrase is tested by Quality Control for the quality specifications and released by
Quality Assurance. The final product is packed in suitable food packaging material before storage.
Warehousing and transportation are performed according to specified conditions mentioned on the
accordant product label for final preparations.
Allergenicity of enzyme preparations
The alternansucrase is not a known allergen (See section 6.2.2). Materials used in the fermentation
process (inoculum, seed, and main fermentation) of alternansucrase are food-grade substances.
There are no ingredients added based on milk, soy, or any of the listed nine allergens during
fermentation process and post fermentation process causing allergenicity or labelling concerns.
(FASTER Act, 2021). Allergen information for alternansucrase enzyme preparation is provided in
Annex B.

2.5 Technical Effect
2.5.1 MODE OF ACTION
Alternansucrase catalyzes a chemical reaction that transfers an alpha-D-glucosyl residue from
sucrose, alternately to the 6- and 3-positions of the non-reducing terminal residue of an alpha-D-
glucan, thereby creating a glucan (alternan) with alternating alpha-1,6- and alpha-1,3-bonds.

2.5.2 USES
In principle, the enzymatic conversions of sucrose with the help of alternansucrase can be of benefit
in the processing of all foods and food ingredients, which naturally contain sucrose.
Alternansucrase can be used for production of oligosaccharides by tailoring the reaction kinetics
with the help of acceptor molecules. Alternansucrase acts on sucrose and produces long chain
polymer called alternan consisting of altering α-(1,6) and α-(1,3) linked D-glucosyl residues (Sanz
et al., 2005; Wangpaiboon et al., 2018; Morales et al., 2001); and fructose is released as by-product.
This enzyme uses different types of acceptor molecules to start polymerization reaction. The
acceptor molecule drives the length and nature of oligosaccharide or polysaccharide formed. A well-
known acceptor for alternansucrase is maltose (Bivolarski et al., 2021; Sanz et al., 2005; Cote et al.,
2008); other saccharides such as raffinose (Cote et al., 2009), cellobiose (Morales et al., 2001), and
leucrose (Cote et al., 2008) also serve as chain initiation sites for alternansucrase. The nature of
alternan chains (degree of polymerization, composition, branching pattern etc.) formed in reaction
solely depends on acceptor molecule and its ratio with respect to sucrose.
Compared to other polysaccharides, alternan has unique physical properties like low viscosity (than
dextran) (Molina et al., 2020) and resistance to degradation by common digestive enzymes (Molina
et al., 2020; Cote, 1992). Therefore, alternansucrase can be used in the production of dietary
fibers/foods, which would have low glycemic index and prebiotic effects (Sanz et al., 2005).
Production of maltose alternan oligosaccharides:
Alternansucrase is intended to be used in the production of maltose alternan oligosaccharides using
sucrose as a substrate and maltose as an acceptor molecule. Unlike other glucosyltransferases,
alternansucrase utilizes a low-cost substrate (sucrose/ table sugar) for the production of
oligosaccharides (Wangpaiboon et al., 2021). The enzyme forms α-(1,3) linkage with maltose only
after the formation of α-(1,6) bond and incapable of forming two consecutive α-(1,3) linkages in a
growing chain; the oligosaccharide formed does not contain more than two consecutive α-(1,6)
linkages. It makes a polymer of a unique structure consisting altering α-(1,3) and α-(1,6) bonds
(Cote et al., 2008).
Alternansucrase produces panose as the first product after transferring glucose from sucrose to the
maltose acceptor, which subsequently acts as an acceptor for enzyme. Formation of alternan
oligosaccharides (i.e., DP lengths and their yields) is strongly influenced by maltose/sucrose ratio.
At higher concentrations, maltose competes for glucose hydrolyzed from sucrose and leads to the
24
Alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC
accumulation of oligosaccharides with lower DPs (Bivolarski et al., 2021). Therefore, the
concentration of maltose in reaction mixture is the key factor for production of different types of
maltose alternan oligosaccharides.

The production of alternan oligosaccharides achieved by continuous process where sucrose/refined
sugar is added in a reactor at definite time intervals and by-product fructose is simultaneously
removed from the system with the help of membrane filtration i.e., nanofiltration. The reaction is
initiated by addition of maltose, sucrose and alternansucrase enzyme that are then incubated at 37°C
up to 72 hrs (preferably 24 hrs). When the desired oligosaccharides are produced, the reaction is
terminated followed by removal of high molecular weight alternans and alternansucrase enzyme
using ultrafiltration. The maltose alternan oligosaccharide stream is then concentrated by water
removal to obtain a stable syrup (water ≤ 28%) or spray dried to powder (water ≤ 8%).
The benefits of the conversion of sucrose with the help of alternansucrase in production of maltose
alternan oligosaccharides are:
 Use of economical raw materials (commercial sucrose, maltose) to produce nutritionally
important oligo/polysaccharides - Chemical synthesis of oligo/ polysaccharides is complex and
expensive since it involves use of sugar derivatives as starting materials, which are less stable
or require protection/ de-protection during synthesis. On the other hand, alternansucrase utilizes
commonly available substrate like sucrose that makes production process viable at commercial
scale.
 Mild reaction conditions - Alternansucrase requires mild reaction conditions such as
temperature (37°C) and pH (4 to 6) for production of oligosaccharides unlike chemical
synthesis methods, which require harsher reaction parameters.
 The reaction can be tailored (with acceptor molecules) according to the product of interest- The
ratio of substrate to acceptor molecule (sucrose to maltose) is key factor in determining nature
of product formed. Additionally, alternansucrase works with multiple acceptor molecules such
as raffinose, cellobiose etc. providing flexibility in manufacturing process.
 Easy downstream processing- Enzymatic synthesis is regio-selective, therefore reduces by-
product formation during reaction. Thus, simple purification methods (like membrane
filtration) can be used for quick and easy recovery of finished product (oligo/ polysaccharides).

Bakery process (Bread making)
Sugar is a crucial ingredient in baking, primarily because it helps create golden brown crusts,
enhances crumb texture, and retains moisture in the crumb. However, refined sugar, commonly
used in baked goods, is high in calories and has a high glycemic index, offering no essential
nutrients or clear health benefits (Olagunju, 2019). While processing of bakery products,
alternansucrase can be added during the initial phase i.e. dough or batter mixing where it will
perform its technological function and reduce the sugar content. The sucrose in the dough will be
hydrolyzed by alternansucrase to release free fructose and glucose. The released glucose would be
utilized for oligosaccharide and/or polysaccharide (glucans) formation. The released fructose will
enhance the sweetness and make up for the flavor loss caused by the reduction in sucrose. The
resultant product will be low calorie. The glucans are resistant to enzymatic digestion and possess

dietary fiber potential. The glucans would also be responsible to improve bread volume and retain
moisture. Further, they would act as prebiotics.
The benefits of the conversion of sucrose with the help of alternansucrase in bakery process are:
 Sucrose reduction- The sucrose content in the final food would be reduced due to the
technological function of alternansucrase enzyme added in dough.
 Increase dietary fiber content- The oligosaccharides and/or polysaccharides (glucans) formed
are resistant to enzymatic digestion and exhibit dietary fiber potential (Vaze et al., 2024).
 Prebiotic potential- The resulting oligosaccharides are reported to possess prebiotic properties
i.e. they support growth of probiotic bacteria (Sanz et al., 2005).
 Moisture retention and mouth feel- The resulting glucans contribute to moisture retention and
mouth feel.
 Improved bread volume- The resulting glucans aids in improving bread volume

Fruit processing (Juice production)
Fruit-based products, such as juices, are valuable sources of vitamins but are also high in calories
due to presence of sugars (mono and disaccharides). Recent studies indicate that high consumption
of simple sugars can lead to negative health effects, including obesity, type II diabetes, and
cardiovascular disease (Giri et al., 2018).
Typically, oligosaccharides are added as functional food additives to various products after being
enzymatically produced from pure sugars. However, recent reports suggest a novel approach of
enzymatically producing oligosaccharides using the sugars already present in food products
(Vafeiadi, et al., 2016).
Alternansucrase can be added to the fruit juice to reduce its sugar content. This enzyme converts
sucrose into slowly and/or partially digestible oligosaccharides/polysaccharides, collectively
known as glucans. These glucans have dietary fiber properties and can act as prebiotics. The
resulting fruit juice thus offers greater health and nutritional benefits.
Benefits of conversion of sucrose with the help of alternansucrase in fruit processing are:
 Low sugar content- Addition of alternansucrase in juice processing converts sugar into
oligosaccharides and/or polysaccharides that are resistant to endogenous enzymatic digestion
in the body. Hence, the resulting product has low sugar content.
 Increase dietary fiber content - The oligosaccharides and/or polysaccharides formed in
presence of alternansucrase exhibit dietary fiber potential (Vaze et al., 2024).
 Prebiotic potential - The oligosaccharides produced by alternansucrase are known to support
growth of probiotics (Sanz et al., 2005).

2.5.4 ACTIVE AND INACTIVE ENZYME RESIDUES IN THE FINAL FOOD
Alternansucrase performs its technological function during food processing but has no technical
effect in final oligosaccharide food. The reasons why the alternansucrase does not exert enzymatic
activity in the final food can be due to a combination of various factors, depending on the application
and the process conditions used by the individual food producer. These factors include removal of
the enzyme from the food during the process, denaturation of the enzyme during processing,
depletion of the substrate, lack of water activity, unconducive pH, etc.
The fate of alternansucrase in production of maltose alternan oligosaccharides, baking process and
fruit juice processing is explained in more details below:
Production of maltose alternan oligosaccharides:
Post the enzymatic action of alternansucrase with maltose and sucrose forming maltose alternan
oligosaccharides, the physical separation of the enzyme is simple during the subsequent processing
of the oligosaccharides. The alternansucrase has high molecular weight and oligosaccharides have
a theoretical molecular weight far less than the alternansucrase enzyme. During the downstream
processing, ultrafiltration membranes are used in the purification of the oligosaccharides, which
allow the separation of the product of interest (oligosaccharides) while removing the high molecular
weight enzyme from the retentate stream. Also, pasteurization performed after the concentration
step inactivates any residual activity left during the process.

and beverages considered are maximum physiological levels of consumption—i.e. the daily
consumption of 0.1 litre of non-milk beverages per kilogram of body weight and the daily

beverages are assumed to be the highest maximum levels of the additive reported in any category
for foods and for beverages, respectively. The proportions of solid foods and beverages that may
contain the substance are set arbitrarily. EHC 240 refers to commonly used default proportions of
12.5% for foods and 25% for non-milk beverages. (WHO EHC Chapter 6, 2009) In the case of food

additives, a default proportion that is often used for European assessments is 12.5% for solid foods
and 25% for beverages (WHO EHC Chapter 6, 2009).

6.1. Safety of Donor and Production Strain
The microorganism used to produce alternansucrase is a non-pathogenic, non-toxigenic strain E coli
EBASSC. The microorganism has been genetically modified. The recombinant production strain E.
coli EBASSC is derived from Escherichia coli W3110 which is a well-characterized, non-
pathogenic laboratory strain by the addition of the plasmid pAML369. E. coli W3110 strain was
derived from the well characterized wild-type parent E. coli K-12, which is the most widely used
laboratory strain with a history of safe use. (Gorbach, 1978, Bauer et al., 2007, GRN 624). The E. coli
B, C and W strains and their derivatives are all classified as risk group 1 organisms in biosafety
guidelines (Bauer et al. 2007). The E. coli K-12 does not contain functional/intact gene sequences
encoding an O antigen polysaccharide (US EPA, 1997). It has also been reported that E. coli K-12
does not have the well-recognized pathogenic mechanisms required by strains of E. coli causing the
majority of enteric infections. The absence of pathogenic potential of E. coli K-12 is demonstrated
in the feeding studies by administration of E. coli K-12 to GI track of animals (Freter R. et al 1983,
Curtiss 1978). In mice, chickens, pigs and calves no pathogenic evidence of E. coli K-12 was

observed (Gorbach 1978). Additionally, the US Environment Protection Agency (EPA) has granted
tiered exempted to E. coli K-12, due to its extensive history of safe use. (US EPA, 1997)
E-coli K-12 has been widely used as safe laboratory organism because it doesn’t produce toxins that
cause illness to human by ingestion (US EPA, 1997) such as shiga-like toxins produced by some
other E. coli strains. No records of K-12 enterotoxin-induced disease for fermentation workers were
reported so far (US EPA, 1997). Also E. coli K-12 doesn’t carry known virulence genes. Finally, E.
coli K-12 is observed to be non-competitive and poor colonizers, making E. coli K-12 unlikely to
inhabit the GI track of humans or other animals (Freter et al., 1983).
Further, the asr gene donor microorganism- L. mesenteroides is a member of lactic acid bacteria
(LAB), which has a long history of safe use in fermented food production, industrial-scale enzyme
production and consumption as a probiotic and can be considered as safe for production of enzymes
for food as well as feed processing and numerous other industrial applications. Importantly, EFSA
has assigned L. mesenteroides a “Status of Qualified Presumption of Safety” (QPS) (EFSA 2007,
2020) and L. mesenteroides is included in the Inventory of Microbial Food Cultures with Safety
Demonstration in Fermented Food Products by the International Dairy Federation (495/2018).16
6.2 Safety of the Alternansucrase Enzyme
Alternansucrase has a history of use in the food industry. Alternansucrase is a member of the
glycosyltransferase family, specifically hexosyltransferases. Alternansucrase catalyzes a chemical
reaction that transfers an alpha-D-glucosyl residue from sucrose alternately to the 6- and 3-positions
of the non-reducing terminal residue of an alpha-D-glucan, thereby creating a glucan with

1982b) for the glucan based on its alternating linkage structure. The oligosaccharide acceptor
products formed by this enzyme have been studied for over 20 years (Cote and Robyt,
1982b; Pelenc et al., 1991) and are of interest because of their potential prebiotic activity.
These oligosaccharides have also shown potential as a low-glycemic index sweetener (Carlson and
Woo, 2004).
Alternansucrase from Leuconostoc citreum strain NRRL B-30894 has been evaluated for its safety
and technological need by the European Food Safety Authority and found no safety concern under
intended conditions of use. (EFSA Journal 2021b;19(1):6367)17
Sucromalt, produced by alternansucrase derived from Leuconostoc citreum, is approved for sale in
Canada. Health Canada notified that it has no objection to the sale of sucromalt as a food ingredient
that can be used as a partial or complete substitute for sweetening agents available in the Canadian
market, e.g., sucrose, corn syrup, high fructose corn syrup (HFCS), brown rice syrup and malt syrup.
The toxigenic potential of the alternansucrase preparation from E. coli EBASSC was evaluated in

animal and other cell-based toxicity model systems. The alternansucrase was found to be non-toxic,
non-mutagenic, non-clastogenic and non-aneugenic under the given test conditions at the highest
dose tested.
Heavy metal and mycotoxin contents in the alternansucrase produced by E. coli EBASSC were
within the specifications and below the detection limits of the test methods. Further, the
alternansucrase covered in this dossier and produced by E coli EBASSC does not contain any
detectable amount of full-length recombinant DNA as determined by the absence of amplicon for a
full-length recombinant gene of alternansucrase. This confirmed the absence of recombinant DNA
in the product (see Section 2.2.7 for details).

6.2.2 ALLERGENICITY
The allergenic potential of the alternansucrase was assessed following the pepsin digestion and
bioinformatics analyses of its amino acid sequence.
6.2.2.1 Evaluation of allergenicity of the alternansucrase following pepsin digestion method
Allergenicity of the alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC was evaluated following pepsin digestion
method. The pepsin digestion study is based on the recommendations made by the Joint FAO/WHO
Expert Consultation, 2001. The protocol used for this assay is based on the detailed study undertaken
by Thomas et al. (2004), which in turn takes into consideration the guidelines provided by the Codex
Alimentarius Commission, 2003.
Proteins that are susceptible to digestion by pepsin are less likely to elicit an allergenic response.
Hence, the digestibility of the alternansucrase by pepsin, was evaluated in vitro by exposing it to
the action of pepsin in the presence of simulated gastric fluid (SGF).
Results from this study showed that alternansucrase can be considered to be a labile protein, as it is
digested by pepsin, and therefore is not likely to be allergenic.

6.2.2.2 Sequence homology of the alternansucrase protein with the known allergens
Allergenic potential of the alternansucrase was assessed following the bioinformatics analyses of
its amino acid sequence. Over the last decade, bioinformatics methods have been widely used for
collecting, storing, and analyzing molecular and/or clinical information of importance for
determining the allergenic potential of proteins. In order to address the allergenicity potential of
alternansucrase, information obtained from bioinformatics, coupled with experimental data,
wherever necessary, is the approach postulated by the Joint Food and Agriculture Organization and
World Health Organization (FAO/WHO) Expert Consultation on Allergenicity of Foods Derived
from Biotechnology. This approach considers the evidence derived from several types of
information and data since no single criterion is considered to be sufficiently predictive (Report of
a Joint FAO/WHO Expert Consultation on Allergenicity of Foods Derived from Biotechnology,
2001).
As proposed in the FAO/WHO Report, cross-reactivity between a query protein and a known
allergen has to be considered when there is: (a) more than 35% identity in the amino acid sequence
of the enzyme, using a window of 80 amino acids and a suitable gap penalty, or (b) A stretch identity
of 6-8 contiguous amino acids.
The alternansucrase sequence was analyzed using the Structural Database of Allergenic Proteins
(SDAP) Program database.18 Bioinformatics searches showed that alternansucrase from E. coli

6.2.2.3 Comprehensive literature search and discussion on the possibility of the allergic reaction
Enzymes are proteins in nature. Like many other proteins, they may have the potential to cause
allergic responses. Allergens can activate the immune system through several routes of exposure,
including food, skin contact, and inhalation. Enzymes have been reported to cause allergies through
recurrent exposure via inhalation in sufficiently high doses and when they come into contact with
mucosal surfaces (eyes, nose). Only a few instances of enzyme-induced allergies have been
documented for enzyme allergy development from contact with eyes (Griffith et al. 1969;
Greenough et al. 1991). Cases of respiratory allergy / sensitization following occupational inhalation
of enzymes have been reported. (Vanhanen M. 2001; Bernstein et al., 1994).
Alternansucrase is a member of the glycosyltransferase family, in particular they are
hexosyltransferases. There are very few cases been reported so far stating allergic response triggered
by glycosyltransferase family members, particularly by alternansucrase. One case report was
published on oral allergy syndrome due to glycosyltransferases. In this case report, they claimed
that glycosyltransferases expressed in custard apple acts as an allergen when consumed orally and
it triggers IgE mediated allergic response with oral allergy syndrome. (Carrón-Herrero A et al,
2022).
Alternansucrase obtained from other Leuconostoc spp. i.e., Leuconostoc citreum was assessed for

allergenicity potential and showed no safety concern. EFSA has published a positive scientific
opinion for alternansucrase enzyme from Leuconostoc citreum NRRL B-30894. The EFSA panel
has estimated that risk of allergic sensitization and elicitation reactions upon dietary exposure to this
food enzyme is considered low (EFSA Journal 2021b;19(1):6367)19.
The donor organism Leuconostoc mesenteroides is a member of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) group
and Leuconostoc genus has received the status of Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) by the
European Food Safety Authority (EFSA 2007, 2020). Leuconostoc members are widely known for
their roles in several industrial and food fermentation processes (Buckenhuskes, 1993; Steinkraus,
2002) such as fermented sausages, fermented vegetables and cereal products, and dairy products
(e.g., butter, cream, fresh and raw milk, cheeses). This abundant presence of Leuconostoc strains in
various foods and the absence of a linkage between the fermented foods and allergies makes it highly

The microorganism used for the production of alternansucrase is a derivative of non-pathogenic,
nontoxigenic strain of E coli K-12. Bioinformatic observations have demonstrated that E. coli K-12
does not contain functional/intact gene sequences encoding an O antigen polysaccharide (US EPA,
1997). No evidence has been reported so far related to allergic response triggered due to non-
pathogenic strains of E. coli although in few cases E. coli strains have been used for attenuation of
allergic response. Oral administration of the probiotic strain E. coli (Nissle 1917) (ECN) helps in
prevention of papain induced respiratory barrier injury and severe allergic inflammation in mice
(Secher et al. 2018).
In general, there are no reports of sensitization to the enzyme products in the final commercial food
after ingestion. This may be due to the difference in exposure pattern of the inhalation route
compared to the digestive route, or it may be due to the fact that the enzymes, again generally, most
often are present in the final foods in low amounts and in inactive forms (Bindslev et al 2006).
Enzyme proteins used in food are not homologous to known food allergens.
The alternansucrase is not, itself, a known allergen. Alternansucrase is used in a very small amounts
during food processing and removed from the oligosaccharide food during processing, resulting in
miniscule quantities of the enzyme in the oligosaccharide or foods contain them. Goodman et al
(2008) discuss that a high concentration generally equals a higher risk of sensitization, whereas a
low level in the final food equals a lower risk. Additionally, it must be noted that the food enzyme
protein may undergo denaturation under various conditions of food processing, resulting in loss of

its tertiary structure. In general, these alterations in conformation are associated with a decrease in
the antigenic reactivity in humans. Usually, denatured proteins are much less immunogenic than the
corresponding native proteins (Takai et al., 1997; Valenta, 2012; Kikuchi et al., 2006). Additionally,
residual enzyme(s) still present in the final food will be subjected to digestion in the gastro-intestinal
system, which further reduces the risk of enzyme allergenicity.
Further, materials used in the fermentation process (inoculum, seed, and main fermentation) of
alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC are food-grade substances that are not known allergens and
are not one of the listed allergens of concern (FASTER Act, 2021)20 Moreover, no allergenic
ingredients are added post fermentation in enzyme preparation, causing no allergenicity or labelling
concerns.
In summary, the alternansucrase enzyme is readily digested by the pepsin, is not homologous to
know allergens, is present in the final food in very low amounts, is present in a microbial food
culture that is not known to elicit allergenic reactions in consumers of the food and is produced in
an organism similarly not known to elicit allergenic responses. Bioinformatics analyses do not show
any similarity of alternansucrase amino acid sequence with a known allergen. Based upon the

6.5 Decision Tree
The safety of alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC has also been established using the decision
tree for evaluating the safety of microbial enzyme preparations used in food processing (Pariza et
al., 2001). The decision tree is a widely used decision making tool by the enzyme industry and has

6.6 Safety Assessment and GRAS Determination
This section presents an assessment that demonstrates that the intended use of alternansucrase from
E. coli EBASSC is safe and is GRAS based on scientific procedures.
This safety assessment and GRAS determination involve two steps. In the first step, the safety of
the intended use of alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC is demonstrated. Safety is established by
demonstrating a reasonable certainty that the exposure of consumers to alternansucrase under its
intended conditions of use is not harmful. In the second step, the intended use of alternansucrase
from E. coli EBASSC is determined to be GRAS by demonstrating the safety of production
organism. The enzyme under its intended conditions of use is generally recognized among qualified
scientific experts and is based on publicly available and accepted information.
The regulatory framework for establishing whether the intended use of a substance is GRAS, in

accordance with Section 201(s) of the Federal Food Drug and Cosmetic Act, is set forth under 21
CFR §170.30. This regulation states that general recognition of safety may be based on the views
of experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety of substances directly
or indirectly added to food. A GRAS determination may be made either: 1) through scientific
procedures under §170.30(b); or 2) through experience based on common use in food, in the case
of a substance used in food prior to January 1, 1958, under §170.30(c). This GRAS determination
employs scientific procedures established under §170.30(b).
A scientific procedure GRAS determination requires the same quantity and quality of scientific
evidence as is needed to obtain approval of the substance as a food additive. In addition to requiring
scientific evidence of safety, a GRAS determination also requires that this scientific evidence of
safety be generally known and accepted among qualified scientific experts. This “common
knowledge” element of a GRAS determination consists of two components:
1. Data and information relied upon to establish the scientific element of safety must be generally
available; and
2. There must be a basis to conclude that there is a consensus among qualified experts about the
safety of the substance for its intended use.
The criteria outlined above for a scientific-procedures GRAS determination are applied below in an
analysis of whether the intended use of alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC is safe and is GRAS.
6.6.1 EVIDENCE OF SAFETY
As noted in the sections above, the production organism E. coli EBASSC, as well as the enzyme
alternansucrase derived from it, are well characterized and safe for intended usage. Publicly
available authorizations by various regulatory authorities, safety evaluations published in the peer-
reviewed scientific literature, reviews by qualified experts, corroborated by Advanced Enzymes’
unpublished safety studies, support such a conclusion.
The microorganism used for the production of alternansucrase is a non-pathogenic, non-toxigenic
strain E. coli EBASSC. The production strain does not produce secondary metabolites of
50
Alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC
toxicological concern to the human. The production strain E. coli EBASSC is generated from the
host strain E. coli W3110 which is a derivative of E. coli K-12, a non-pathogenic laboratory strain.
E. coli K-12 is considered as safe to use for various biotechnological applications as it does not
produce toxins harmful for ingestion. E. coli K-12 has been widely used in production of food
ingredients, specialty chemicals and human drugs, because of its history of safe use it has been
exempted from Environment Protection Agency (EPA), USA review of Toxic Substances Control
Act,1967 (TSCA) (EPA, 1997). Most common therapeutic proteins expressed in E. coli are Human
insulin (Nilsson et al, 1996), interleukin 2 (IL-2) (Roifman, 1985), etc. The E. coli B, C, and W
strains and their derivatives are all classified as risk group 1 organisms in biosafety guidelines
(Bauer et al., 2007).
The alternansucrase produced by the E. coli EBASSC was evaluated for antimicrobial activity and
the absence of antimicrobial activity was recorded against all the test micro-organisms. In addition,
heavy metals in the enzyme preparations were well within the specification and below the detection
limits of the analytical methods. No indications of toxicity were found in acute and repeated-dose
studies of oral toxicity or genotoxicity assays of alternansucrase obtained from E coli EBASSC.

Pepsin digestion analysis and bioinformatics studies on alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC
showed that it was a labile protein indicating a reduced risk of sensitization and did not share
homology with known allergens. Therefore, alternansucrase does not pose a concern in terms of
food allergy induction.
Further, the alternansucrase as described in this dossier and produced by E. coli EBASSC does not
contain the production microorganism and any detectable amount of full-length recombinant DNA
as determined by the absence of amplicon for full-length recombinant gene of alternansucrase. The
absence of this DNA in the final product eliminates the risk of unintended gene transfer.
The alternansucrase described in this dossier is manufactured following current Good
Manufacturing Practice for Food (cGMP) and the principles of Hazard Analysis of Critical Control
Points (HACCP).
Using the decision tree of Pariza and Johnson (2001), alternansucrase from E. coli EBASSC enzyme
preparation was determined to be acceptable for the proposed uses. Based on a highly conservative
(and highly unlikely) worst-case scenario, the maximum daily intake is 477 mg TOS/day which is
lower than the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) derived from the NOAEL from the 90-day sub-
chronic oral toxicity study i.e., 700 mg TOS per day. Therefore, the use of alternansucrase in the
production of maltose alternan oligosaccharides, bakery process and fruit juice production is not
expected to result in adverse effects in humans. A safety margin of 146.74 exists between the
established NOAEL and the estimated worst-case maximum daily human exposure level.
Based upon the totality of the evidence presented in this notice, Advanced Enzyme has determined
by scientific procedures that the alternansucrase from L. mesenteroides produced by E. coli
EBASSC and manufactured according to the principles of cGMP is Generally Recognized As Safe
for the intended processing aid uses in food.

B. Phenotypic Identity
Parabacteroides goldsteinii RV-01 is a strictly anaerobic, gram-negative, non-spore forming, rod-
shaped bacterium belonging to the Bacteroidota phylum. Colonies on agar plates are 1-2 mm in
diameter, grey to off-white–grey, circular, slightly convex and smooth. Parabacteroides goldsteinii are
saccharolytic bacteria, and major end-products are typically acetic and succinic acids; minor amounts
of isovaleric acid, propionic acid and formic acid are also produced. Parabacteroides goldsteinii can
also grow on medium containing 20% bile (Sakamoto and Benno, 2006). Further, P. goldsteinii RV-01
is reported to be non-pathogenic (Lin et al., 2024).

C. Genotypic Identity
The identification and grouping of P. goldsteinii RV-01 was achieved by a 16S rRNA sequence
analysis. Due to the full length 16S rRNA gene sequence showing 99.71% identity to the P.
goldsteinii JCM13446 in the NCBI Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) analysis1, the isolated
bacterial strain was identified as P. goldsteinii RV-01. The whole genome sequence and annotation of
P. goldsteinii RV-01 has been deposited at NCBI under the BioProject number PRJNA1153404.
Further, the genome of P. goldsteinii RV-01 has been deposited in the Japanese National Institute of

D. Manufacturing Processes
ReviveBio, Co.’s autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is produced in accordance with current Good
Manufacturing Practices (cGMP) according to the Taiwan Ministry of Health and Welfare. Further, the
ingredient is manufactured in accordance with ISO 22000:2018. Documentation supporting the
supplier’s Taiwan cGMP and ISO 22000:2018 compliance is found in Appendix 1, Appendix 2, and
Appendix 3. Production of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is also conducted according to Hazard
Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles (Appendix 4). All raw materials, processing
aids, and food contact substances used to manufacture autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 are food-
grade ingredients permitted by U.S. regulations or have previously been determined to be GRAS for
their respective uses, as attested in Appendix 5.
To avoid genetic drift, a 16S rRNA sequencing-validated working cell bank (WCB) is maintained at
the production facility (at -80°C in 10% glycerol) to store inoculum for culture initiation. Briefly, seed
culture is initiated using an aliquot from the WCB, and the seed culture is then used to inoculate the
production culture in the fermentation vessel where the product organism (P. goldsteinii RV-01) is
grown. Cells are separated from the growth medium (food grade soy peptones, sodium bicarbonate,
sodium chloride, sodium phosphate, sucrose2, and cysteine hydrochloride prepared in purified water)
by centrifugation, autoclaved at 121°C for 15 minutes, and stored at 4°C. The composition of each
batch of culture media is consistent between batches and within batches from seed culture to
fermentation culture. A flow chart of the production process is presented below in Figure 2, with
further details of each step of the production process outlined below.

1. Preparation of Seed Culture
An aliquot of the WCB (1 mL in 10% glycerol) is thawed at 37°C and used to inoculate freshly
prepared culture medium (50 – 200 mL). This culture is incubated at 37°C for 24 hours in an
anaerobic environment to generate the seed culture. Pre-culture inoculum from the seed culture is
added at a ratio of between 1:50 and 1:200, and cells are propagated between 36 and 37°C until end
log-phase, as determined by culture optical density. In general, a lower seed culture optical density
requires a higher seeding ratio to maintain cell density.

2. Initiation of Fermentation Culture
The production fermenter is prepared with fresh media and inoculated with seed culture at a ratio of
1:50 and 1:200. The fermentation time is dictated by fermentation conditions and the ratio of seed
culture to culture medium. The culture undergoes fermentation at 36°C to 37°C until harvesting cell
density is reached.
3. Cell Product Harvest
Twenty-four hours after fermentation, cells are harvested by pellet centrifugation for subsequent
lyophilization.
4. Autoclaving and Lyophilization
The P. goldsteinii RV-01 cells are autoclaved for 15 minutes at 121°C prior to being mixed with
maltodextrin (sourced from non-genetically modified corn) at a ratio of 1:6 w/w to achieve optimized
cell density and conditions. The resultant product, now referred to as the ingredient, is then freeze-
dried in a lyophilizer. This process results in a cake that is then ground to powder for storage. This
lyophilized powder is used to prepare the final product. The autoclave and lyophilization processes
occur in an aerobic environment.
5. Quality Control
Throughout the production process, line samples3 are taken for quality control analysis to ensure
process controls in place are met to guarantee optimized fermentation process reproducibility and
efficiency. Quality control (QC) steps are indicated in Figure 3, and involve calibration of all
equipment, and monitoring of temperature, pH, and optical density, as well as centrifugation speed.
Only if QC requirements are met in each phase is the production process allowed to move forward.
This includes the autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient meeting all specifications, including the
limit for live P. goldsteinii RV-01 cells. The autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient is then
packaged in food grade polyethylene packaging.

E. Ingredient Specifications and Analysis
While plate counts resulting in colony forming units (CFU) have long been the gold standard for
microbial analysis and are very useful for enumerating pathogenic or other undesired microbes, other
methods are required to accurately assess the number of dead bacterial cells. Flow cytometry using
specific functional dyes has been developed as the method of choice and is used here for the
enumeration of P. goldsteinii RV-01 (ISO, 2015; Foglia et al., 2020). This method, which is based on
membrane integrity (Nebe-Von Caron and Badley, 1995), can be used to monitor the number of dead
and intact cells represented as total fluorescent units (TFU). In the specific use described here, total
cell count of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is defined as TFU which represents the sum of dead
cells.

on the maximum permissible levels of these contaminants to ensure an acceptable final product. The

across the lifespan, from 1 mg/day in children aged 1-3 years, up to 10 mg/day in adults (Oregon

In terms of microbial contamination, the specification for Listeria monocytogenes established by

PART 6. NARRATIVE
A. Introduction
A review of the scientific and regulatory literature related to the use of P. goldsteinii in foods was
conducted through February 10, 2025. Various government databases were used to search for
applicable regulations across jurisdictions. To identify safety studies, literature searches were
conducted in PubMed using the terms; [("Parabacteroides goldsteinii" or "P. goldsteinii") and safety]
and [“Parabacteroides goldsteinii”].
The safety evaluation of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is conducted in a manner consistent with up-
to-date guidance documents that outline best practices and/or specific jurisdictional requirements for
the safety assessment of microorganisms intended for use in food. The guidance documents and
expert reviews from regulatory authorities and industry specialists that were utilized in the safety
evaluation of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 include the EFSA Qualified Presumption of Safety
guidelines (Barlow et al., 2007), the Guidelines for the Evaluation of Probiotics in Food (JECFA,
2002) issued by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Consultation on Evaluation of Health and Nutritional
Properties of Probiotics in Food, and the safety decision tree for evaluating microbial cultures
intended for human and animal consumption published by Pariza et al. (2015).
Parabacteroides goldsteinii strains were originally isolated and identified by Song et al. (2005) from
intestinal samples collected from 7 human patients with infections12 (4 with appendicitis, 1 with
peritonitis, and 2 with abdominal abscesses). However, Parabacteroides goldsteinii is actually a
human intestinal tract commensal known to contribute to metabolic regulation (Wu et al., 2019; Cui et
al., 2022). Parabacteroides goldsteinii and related species of the Parabacteroides genus have a
relative abundance of 1.27% in the feces. The species are obligate anaerobes that are important
contributors to the metabolism of simple sugars and are part of complex microbial populations that
form inter-organism nutritional webs involved in cross-feeding interactions with other gut microbes
(Cui et al., 2022). Further, production of SCFAs are important metabolic functions of these species
(Cui et al., 2022). The species has also been shown to assist in the maturation and development of
the immune system in mice (Cervantes-Barragan and Colonna, 2022). Further mouse studies have
shown that P. goldsteinii produces beta-hexosaminidase, a conserved enzyme identified in the
Bacteroidota phylum, which promotes the development of a subtype of CD4+ effector T cell that
regulates adaptive immunity in the intestinal mucosa, thereby playing an important role in maintaining
homeostasis (Bousbaine et al., 2022).
The P. goldsteinii RV-01 strain was originally isolated from the feces of a healthy adult (Lin et al.,
2024). To circumvent any possibility that live P. goldsteinii RV-01 may cause adverse effects in

D. Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism & Excretion (ADME)
It is expected that oral consumption of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 will traverse the intestine for
ultimate excretion in the feces. While infection with live P. goldsteinii has been reported on rare
occasions in humans, none of the cases involved oral consumption of live or autoclaved P.
goldsteinii; rather, each case resulted from the individuals suffering various injuries or
immunocompromising conditions (Awadel-Kariem et al., 2010; Ricco et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2024).
Further, the specifications for autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 limit the live P. goldsteinii RV-01 cell
count to < 10 CFU/g, significantly lowering the potential risk of infection.

analysis. The total DNA prepared from live P. goldsteinii RV-01 was used as the template for positive
PCR control (lane 1), and deionized water was used as the negative PCR control (lane 7). The size of
the tetQ PCR product is 1,859 base pairs and was not detected at any of the tested concentrations of
autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01. Also, in the left image of Figure 4, there appears to be a signal near

To further investigate the potential for antimicrobial resistance by P. goldsteinii RV-01, a minimum
inhibitory concentration (MIC) test was performed, as presented in Table 12. The MIC values are
compared to cut-off values for Parabacteroides species, established by the European Committee on
Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST).19 Further, a set of breakpoints for anaerobic bacteria
were used from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI, 2020). As suggested by both
organizations, B. fragilis ATCC 25285 was used as an anaerobic positive control strain. The results
indicate that P. goldsteinii RV-01 is resistant to aminoglycosides (gentamycin, kanamycin,
streptomycin, and apramycin), vancomycin, nalidixic acid, sulfonamide and trimethoprim. The MIC
values for these antimicrobials were similar among the three P. goldsteinii strains and two other
Parabacteroides species tested. Thus, resistance to these antimicrobials may be considered intrinsic,
given the lack of genes which confer resistance to these antimicrobials in the genome of P. goldsteinii
RV-01. In addition, P. goldsteinii RV-01 was susceptible to clindamycin, tetracycline, and
chloramphenicol according to the appropriate breakpoints. The susceptibility of P. goldsteinii RV-01 to
tetracycline indicates that the tetQ gene may have been mischaracterized or is inadequately
expressed by the live organism.

b. Virulence Factors
Analysis of the P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome was conducted to screen for potential virulence factor
genes using the Virulence Factor Database (VFDB). To identify potential virulence factor genes,
thresholds of > 60% coverage and > 80% identity for virulence factor identity were applied based on
relevant EFSA guidance (EFSA, 2021). There were no genes with > 60% coverage or > 80% identity
to known virulence factors identified in the P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome.
c. Secondary Metabolites
The P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome was submitted to the antibiotics and secondary metabolite analysis
shell (antiSMASH) tool version 7.0, as described by Blin et al. (2023), to identify any biosynthetic
gene clusters for secondary metabolites. Secondary metabolites include compounds which confer a
selective growth advantage to the organism. No biosynthetic gene clusters for secondary metabolites
were identified in the P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome.
d. Biogenic Amines
The genome of P. goldsteinii RV-01 was submitted to the BLASTx search tool to identify the biogenic
amine-producing genes histidine decarboxylase (hdcA), tyrosine decarboxylase (tyrdc), ornithine

decarboxylase (odc), agmatine deiminase (aguA and aguD), and lysine decarboxylase (ldc). The
potential for formation of biogenic amines is an important safety consideration because biogenic
amines are associated with the toxicological characteristics of food poisoning in humans (JECFA,

e. Mobile Genetic Elements
Considering the evidence of DNA degradation in the autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient
(Figure 4 and Figure 5), the presence of mobile genetic elements is not expected to pose a significant
safety concern.
f. Allergenicity
A genomic analysis was conducted by ReviveBio, Co. to evaluate the allergenic potential of proteins
present in P. goldsteinii RV-01. The GenBank P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome assembly, containing
5,241 protein coding sequences (CDS), was analyzed for potential allergenic proteins using
Allermatch.20 As per guidance from EFSA (2021), a threshold of 35% identity was used. Analyses
were performed using full-length sequences, 80-amino acid alignment, and 6-amino acid exact
matching. This analysis has been published by Lin et al. (2024).
In the full-length analysis, 33 hits with > 35% identity were identified. In the 80-amino acid alignment
analysis, 174 hits were identified with > 35% identity. Finally, 13 hits were identified with a minimum
of 6 exact amino acid matches. Of those 13 hits, 11 proteins were identified in the full-length
sequence homology search and 80-amino acid alignment. Upon closer evaluation, three proteins
(enolase21, adenosylhomocysteinase, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase A) had >
50% identity in both full-length homology search and 80-amino acid alignment. However, an important
consideration in the immunogenicity and cross-reactivity assessment of a protein is its structure. To
this end, the authors concluded, “therefore, although sequence homology to known allergens was
indicated, the autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient is not expected to possess allergenic
potential because the ingredient is prepared as an autoclaved and lyophilized powder which results in
protein denaturation” (Lin et al., 2024).

as it has been reported that enolase is found in cooked chicken meat samples (Wanniang et al.,
2022). However, the enolase homolog in P. goldsteinii RV-01 is related to an inhalation allergen
found in the fungus, Rhodotorula mucilaginosa.22 The activity and structure of enolase produced by

3. Subacute and Subchronic Toxicity Studies
Lin et al. (2024) conducted a 28-day repeat dose toxicity study with autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 in
male and female Sprague Dawley rats, in compliance with GLP and according to OECD Guideline
407. The animals (n = 5/sex/group) received vehicle control or autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 at 74,
370, or 1,500 mg/kg bw/day, corresponding to intakes of 4 x 109, 2 x 1010, or 8.1 x 1010 TFU/kg
bw/day, respectively, for 28 consecutive days via oral gavage. No mortality occurred and no clinically
adverse observations were made during the study. There were no statistically significant changes in
body weight, food intake, water intake, organ weights, or organ to brain weight ratios between
treatment and control groups. No gross lesions were observed in any of the animals and no
treatment-related histopathological findings were observed in high dose animals. Therefore, the no
observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 was determined to be
1,500 mg/kg bw/day, or 8.1 x 1010 TFU/kg bw/day, the highest dose level tested.

dosing to evaluate the reversibility or delayed onset of potentially adverse effects.

controls. This finding was not dose-dependent and was not observed in the high dose recovery
females compared to their respective controls. The mean APTT value in the middle dose
females (20.17 seconds) did deviate from the reference range of 13.0 – 18.0 seconds
(Derelanko, 2000), but each of the control and treatment groups in the main study and
recovery groups exceeded the reference range. This suggests that the animals used in the
study were predisposed to having slightly higher APTT than rats of the same age and strain by
some factor unrelated to treatment.
• Reduced serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was observed in middle dose males
compared to controls, but this change was not observed in the main or recovery high dose
groups and the mean value in the middle dose group (62.2 ± 6.5 U/L) did not deviate from the
reference range of 45.0 - 90.0 U/L (Derelanko, 2000).
• The incidences of renal tubular mineralization in control and high dose treated females were
6/10 and 4/10, respectively, and the incidence was 2/5 in both the recovery control and
recovery high dose females, indicating a lack of treatment-related effect. The incidence of
renal tubular mineralization in males was 1/10 and 0/10 in the control and high dose main
study groups, respectively, and 1/5 and 0/5 in the recovery control and recovery high dose
groups, respectively. These results support the findings of Rao (2002) and NRC (1995) that
control female Sprague Dawley rats spontaneously develop renal tubular mineralization and
show that treatment with autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 does not promote this lesion.
None of these observations change the conclusion that the NOAEL of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01
is 1,500 mg/kg bw/day (8.1 x 1010 TFU/kg bw/day) in male and female rats.

4. Other Animal Safety Studies
Lai et al. (2022) administered live P. goldsteinii MTS01 to male Balb/c mice (n = 10/group) for 12
weeks. The dose of P. goldsteinii MTS01 was 2 x 108 CFU/day for the first 10 weeks, followed by 1 x
109 CFU/day for the next 2 weeks, via oral gavage. Bodyweight and body temperature did not
significantly differ between treatment and control groups. Serum triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol
(TC), low density lipoprotein (LDL), and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) did not significantly differ
between groups. The P. goldsteinii MTS01 group had reduced serum high density lipoprotein (HDL)

compared to controls. Histopathological analysis of gastric tissue revealed no differences between
the P. goldsteinii MTS01 and control groups. Given that the test material was live, and a different
strain of P. goldsteinii, this effect on serum HDL is not expected to occur following oral exposure to
autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01. Further, there was no change in serum HDL between treatment and
control groups in the 90-day toxicity study of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01. Therefore, this study
provides supportive evidence of safety related to the intended use of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01.
5. Human Safety Studies
No clinical studies with P. goldsteinii, including live or autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01, have been
identified in the published literature.
Case reports involving infection with live P. goldsteinii have been reported in the published literature.
For example, an 82-year-old woman with a history of diverticular disease became infected with
several bacteria, including P. goldsteinii, after colonic perforation (Awadel-Kariem et al., 2010). This
patient died following 30 days of treatment for the infection which included several pathogenic
bacteria (including streptococci and Candida) as well as blood pressure abnormalities. Another
patient was likely immunocompromised due to treatment for lymphoma when they became infected
with several bacteria, including P. goldsteinii (Cobo et al., 2022). The patient was treated with
piperacillin-tazobactam (4 g/8 hours IV) for 10 days and fully recovered from the infection. Finally,
another patient became infected with P. goldsteinii following perineal lacerations, cervical lacerations,
and postpartum hemorrhage during childbirth (Peng et al., 2024). This patient underwent uterine
curettage and treatment via uterine cavity irrigation with metronidazole and intramuscular injection of
gentamicin and dexamethasone. The patient recovered and was discharged 30 days after admission.
None of the reported cases involved oral intake of P. goldsteinii prior to the reported infections.
Since the ingredient contains autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 and the specification for the live strain
is < 10 CFU/g, the ingredient is not expected to pose a significant risk of infection.

Amplification is provided in that the conclusion of safety is to include probable consumption of the

FDA’s operational definition of safety that serves as the framework against which this evaluation is
provided.
Furthermore, in discussing GRAS criteria, FDA notes that:
“…General recognition of safety requires common knowledge, throughout the expert
scientific community knowledgeable about the safety of substances directly or
indirectly added to food, that there is reasonable certainty that the substance is not
harmful under the conditions of its intended use.”
“‘Common knowledge’ can be based on either “scientific procedures” or on
experience based on common use of a substance in food prior to January 1, 1958.”
28
FDA discusses in more detail what is meant by the requirement of general knowledge and
acceptance of pertinent information within the scientific community, i.e., the so-called “common

knowledge element,” in terms of the two following component elements:
• Data and information relied upon to establish safety must be generally available, and this is
most commonly established by utilizing published, peer-reviewed scientific journals; and
• There must be a basis to conclude that there is consensus (but not unanimity) among qualified
scientists about the safety of the substance for its intended use, and this is established by
relying upon secondary scientific literature such as published review articles, textbooks, or
compendia, or by obtaining opinions of expert panels or opinions from authoritative bodies,
such as JECFA and the National Academy of Sciences.
General recognition of safety based upon scientific procedures shall require the same quantity and
quality of scientific evidence as is required to obtain approval of a food additive. General recognition
of safety through scientific procedures shall be based upon the application of generally available and
accepted scientific data, information, or methods, which ordinarily are published, as well as the
application of scientific principles, and may be corroborated by the application of unpublished
scientific data, information, or methods.

H. Common Knowledge Elements for GRAS Conclusions
The first common knowledge element for a GRAS conclusion requires that data and information relied
upon to establish safety must be generally available; this is commonly established by utilizing studies
published in peer-reviewed scientific journals. The second common knowledge element for a GRAS
conclusion requires that consensus exists within the broader scientific community.
1. Public Availability of Scientific Information
The regulatory framework for determining whether a substance is GRAS is in 21 CFR 170.30, which
states that GRAS status through scientific procedures shall ordinarily be based upon published
studies, which may be corroborated by unpublished studies and other data and information. These
criteria have been applied to the existing data for autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01.
All studies which have been reviewed and referenced in this dossier are published in the scientific
literature or are available online, including all pivotal safety information summarized throughout Part
6.
2. Scientific Consensus
The second common knowledge element for a GRAS conclusion requires that there be a basis to
conclude that consensus exists among qualified scientists about the safety of the substance for its
intended use.
ReviveBio, Co.’s autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient is manufactured according to Taiwan’s
cGMP, ISO 22000:2018, and HACCP principles. The specifications and analysis demonstrate

The potential for antimicrobial resistance was evaluated by analyzing the genome of P. goldsteinii
RV-01 for genes which are known to confer resistance to antimicrobials. One gene associated with
tetracycline resistance (tetQ) was identified in the genome; however, the gene is not detected in the
autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 ingredient. Further, in a MIC test with live P. goldsteinii RV-01, the
organism was susceptible to tetracycline. Therefore, autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is not expected
to demonstrate resistance to tetracycline or transfer any genes associated with antimicrobial
resistance to other microorganisms in the human gut. In the same MIC test, P. goldsteinii RV-01
demonstrated resistance to several antimicrobials. However, this is considered intrinsic to the species
as other strains of P. goldsteinii and other Parabacteroides species demonstrated the same
resistance profile, and no known genetic determinants of resistance to these antimicrobials were
identified in the genome of P. goldsteinii RV-01.

Analysis of the P. goldsteinii RV-01 genome using the VFDB and antiSMASH tools revealed no
known virulence factors or biosynthetic gene clusters for secondary metabolites, respectively.

homolog, which may catalyze the conversion of agmatine into N-carbamoylputrescine. However,
since the ingredient is autoclaved at 121°C, it is not expected to maintain the enzymatic activity
necessary to produce appreciable amounts of putrescine (the end product of metabolism of agmatine
and N-carbamoylputrescine). Further, live P. goldsteinii RV-01 is not cytotoxic to HEK293 or Caco-2
cells at a MOI up to 2,000.

J. Conclusion
In consideration of the aggregate safety information available, ReviveBio, Co. concludes that
autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 as defined in the subject notification is expected to be safe for use as
an ingredient in sports and energy drinks, ready-to-eat cereals (low sugar), yogurt, fermented milk
products, ice cream, cereal bars, nutrition bars, nut spreads, and candy containing chocolate at levels
up to 1 x 1010 TFU/serving, or 185 mg/serving. The intended use does not include infant formula or
USDA-regulated food. The mean and 90th percentile intakes of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 in the

general population are 223.8 mg/day (1.0 x 1010 TFU/day) and 475.9 mg/day (2.2 x 1010 TFU/day),
respectively.
The weight of the publicly available evidence from studies with autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01
provide a basis upon which to conclude that the proposed uses of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 as
described in this dossier satisfy the safety standard of Reasonable Certainty of No Harm and are
safe. Based on the pivotal, published data and information that are generally available, one may
conclude that the proposed uses of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 as produced consistent with ISO
22000:2018 and meeting the food grade specifications presented above, are Generally Recognized
As Safe (GRAS) based on scientific procedures. Support for these conclusions by a consensus of
qualified experts in the general scientific community is provided in Appendix 7 (Expert Panel Report).
Accordingly, autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 as produced in accordance with ISO 22000:2018 and
when it meets those specifications declared within the subject notification meets FDA’s definition of
safety in that there is “reasonable certainty of no harm under the intended conditions of use” as
described herein and, therefore, is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS).

Appendix 6 Intake Analysis Report
Proposed Use and Food Codes Utilized for Intake Calculation
The dietary exposure distributions were calculated using the Creme Food Safety® modeli, a scientific
cloud-based software service designed and developed to calculate dietary intakes of foods,
chemicals, and nutrients in populations of consumers. This is achieved by linking food consumption
data from the What We Eat In America (WWEIA) portion of the National Health and Nutrition
Examination Survey (NHANES) to the appropriate food composition and chemical occurrence data
using a number of validated and published models, available upon request from Crème Global
(https://www.cremeglobal.com/). Output calculations include daily average intakes, acute exposures,
as well as population statistics such as mean, percentiles, standard errors, and confidence intervals.
Results are output for “Consumers-Only” (i.e., consumers of the food / substance of interest), and
“Total Population” (consumers and non-consumers). Results of the exposure assessment are given in
absolute terms (mg per day) as well as relative to the consumer’s body weight (mg per kg body
weight per day). The per unit of bodyweight exposure is calculated on a subject level using the
bodyweight recorded by the NHANES data.
The proposed uses of autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01, are provided in Table 1 below. Autoclaved P.
goldsteinii RV-01 is intended to be used as an ingredient in the following conventional foods: sports
and energy drinks, ready-to-eat cereal (low sugar), yogurt, kefir, ice cream and frozen desserts,
cereal and nutrition bars, nut spreads, and candy containing chocolate. The target amount is up to 1 x
1010 total fluorescent units (TFU) or approximately 185 mg per daily serving in the finished food
product. The food codes utilized to calculate the estimated daily intake were selected from the
NHANES 2017 – 2020 Pre-pandemic survey. Food codes that most appropriately match the intended
use were selected. The final food code selections are found in Table 2.

Appendix 7 GRAS Associates Expert Panel Report
The Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) Status of the Proposed Uses of Autoclaved
Parabacteroides goldsteinii RV-01
April 22, 2025
Foreword
An independent panel of experts (“Expert Panel”) was convened by GRAS Associates, LLC on behalf
of their client, ReviveBio, Co., to evaluate the safety and Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS)
status of ReviveBio, Co.’s proposed uses of Autoclaved Parabacteroides goldsteinii RV-01 in
conventional foods. The members of this Expert Panel† are qualified to serve in this capacity by
qualification of scientific training and experience in the safety of food and food ingredients.
GRAS Associates and ReviveBio, Co. ensured that all reasonable efforts were made to identify and
select a balanced Expert Panel with expertise in food safety, toxicology, and nutrition. The Expert Panel
was selected and convened in accordance with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)’s guidance
for industry on "Best Practices for Convening a GRAS Panel"29. Efforts were placed on identifying
conflicts of interest or relevant “appearance issues” that could potentially bias the outcome of the
deliberations of the Expert Panel and no such conflicts of interest or "appearance issues" were
identified. The Expert Panel members received a reasonable honorarium as compensation for their
time; the honoraria provided to the Expert Panel members were not contingent upon the outcome of
their deliberations.
Discussion
Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is the result of heat-inactivation of P. goldsteinii RV-01, a strictly
anaerobic, gram-negative bacterium that is endogenously found in the human gastrointestinal tract
and is non-pathogenic and non-toxigenic. The strain was identified via 16S rRNA sequencing, whole
genome sequencing, and average nucleotide identity analysis.
The manufacturing process of Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is performed according to current
Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP) and utilizes food grade ingredients. The process includes the
seeding and growth of live bacterium in fermentation tanks, its harvest and centrifugation, followed by
autoclaving, mixing with maltodextrin, lyophilization, milling and storage. Genetic integrity of the strain

is ensured over repeated manufacturing processes through the use of a 16S rRNA sequencing-
validated working cell bank. Batch consistency is ensured with specifications that include qualitative
and quantitative identification parameters of the bacterium in addition to contaminants such as heavy
metal and other microorganisms. The efficacy of autoclaving is ensured with a parameter limiting the
number of viable P. goldsteinii RV-01 to “not detected”. Five non-consecutive batches were provided
as evidence of production consistency.
Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is intended to be used in sports and energy drinks, ready-to-eat
cereals (low sugar), yogurt, fermented milk products, ice cream, cereal bars, nutrition bars, nut
spreads, and candy containing chocolate at levels up to 1 x 1010 total fluorescent units (TFU)/serving.
It is not intended to be used in infant formula or USDA regulated foods and will not be marketed to
children. Under the intended conditions of use, the estimated mean and 90th percentile intakes in the
general population 1.2 x 1010 TFU/day (2.0 x 108 TFU/kg bw/day) and 2.6 x 1010 TFU/day (4.4 x 108
TFU/kg bw/day), respectively.
Safety information on Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 is generally available. Although genotypic
profiling of live P. goldsteinii RV-01 showed evidence of the tetQ gene, which is associated with
tetracycline resistance, the lack of its DNA in Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01, showed by PCR,
suggested DNA is degraded during the manufacturing process. The strain does not contain genomic
elements for secondary metabolites of concern or biogenic amines. Toxicological studies, including
GLP- and OECD-compliant genotoxicity studies (bacterial reverse mutation assay, in vitro
chromosomal aberration, and in vivo micronucleus assay) and subchronic, repeated-dose, oral
toxicity studies (28- and 90-day rodent studies) have shown Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 has no
toxicological concern under the conditions tested. Specifically, the no observed adverse effect level in
the 90-day, repeated-dose toxicological study was 1,500 mg/kg bw/day (8.1 x 1010 TFU/kg bw/day).
Based on this NOAEL, the margin of safety is 183 in the general population. Therefore, the composite
evidence from historical safe consumption and experimental studies collectively demonstrates the
safety of Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 for human food consumption at the above-described
intended use levels.
In summary, sufficient qualitative and quantitative scientific evidence in the composite is available to
support the safety-in-use of ReviveBio, Co.’s Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 preparation given the
following conditions:
ReviveBio, Co.’s Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 preparation continues to meet the designated

specifications; and
ReviveBio, Co.’s Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 preparation is produced in accordance with Current
Good Manufacturing Practices (CGMPs).
Conclusion

The ingestion of ReviveBio, Co.’s Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 from the intended uses results in

of no harm under the intended conditions of use” as described herein, and ReviveBio, Co.’s
Autoclaved P. goldsteinii RV-01 preparation is generally recognized as safe (GRAS).
It is also our opinion that other qualified and competent scientists reviewing the same publicly
available toxicological and safety information would reach the same conclusion. Therefore, we have
